questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient is found to have accumulation of glucocerebroside within cells. Dysfunction of which intracellular organelle is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lysosome

Glucocerebroside accumulation is the hallmark of Gaucher disease, a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of β-glucocerebrosidase (β-glucosidase). Defective lysosomal degradation of glucocerebroside leads to its accumulation within macrophage lysosomes, forming characteristic Gaucher cells with wrinkled (“crumpled tissue paper”) cytoplasm.

Why not the other options?

• B. Peroxisome: Involved in β-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids and α-oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids; disorders include Refsum disease, Zellweger syndrome, and X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.
• C. Golgi apparatus: Responsible for protein modification, glycosylation, and sorting; not involved in degradation of sphingolipids.
• D. Mitochondria: Site of ATP production, oxidative phosphorylation, and apoptosis; not involved in lysosomal substrate degradation.
questions.learning: Lysosome Glucocerebroside accumulation is the hallmark of Gaucher disease, a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of β-glucocerebrosidase (β-glucosidase).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The drug shown in the image below is administered for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malaria

The image given below shows artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), which is used in the treatment of falciparum malaria.

ACT consists of artesunate given for 3 days and sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine given for 1 day. It is supplied by the government of India under the national vector-borne disease control program (NVDCP).

It is given to all confirmed cases of Plasmodium falciparum infection, found positive by microscopy or rapid diagnostic tests. Primaquine with dose of 0.75 mg/kg of body weight is given on day 2 along with it. Artemether-lumefantrine is used for the treatment of falciparum malaria in the northeastern states of India.

This drug is not given in pregnancy and in children less than 5 kg of body weight.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following are causes of secondary osteoarthritis of the hip, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetes

Secondary osteoarthritis (OA) of the hip occurs due to an identifiable underlying condition that damages the hip joint.

• (a) Trauma — Correct: Previous hip trauma or fracture can lead to secondary OA.
• (b) Diabetes — Incorrect → Diabetes is not a classical direct cause of secondary hip OA.
• (c) Perthes’ disease — Correct: Childhood avascular necrosis of the femoral head can cause deformity and subsequent secondary OA.
• (d) Avascular necrosis — Correct: Collapse and deformity of the femoral head can result in secondary OA.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An 11-year-old child with a history of streptococcal pharyngitis presents you with fever and arthralgia. There is no past history of rheumatic heart disease or features of carditis or valvular disease. How often is 6,00,000 IU of benzathine penicillin recommended for prophylaxis of rheumatic heart disease?
options: Once in three weeks for 5 years or till the age of 18, whichever is longer
Once in three weeks for 10 years or till the age of 25, whichever is longer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Once in three weeks for 5 years or till the age of 18, whichever is longer

The given clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever (ARF). The secondary prophylaxis after an episode for a patient weighing <27 kilograms is 6,00,000 IU of benzathine penicillin injection once every three weeks for 5 years or till the age of 18, whichever is longer.

ARF is an autoimmune disease that develops in response to group A streptococcal infection. It is commonly seen in children between the age of 5-14 years. An upper respiratory tract infection with some M serotypes of the organism is the trigger. The concept of molecular mimicry is used to explain the pathogenesis of the condition.

Since one attack of ARF increases the risk for further episodes and development of RHD, secondary prophylaxis is recommended by the American heart association (AHA) as follows:

• Rheumatic fever without carditis: For 5 years after the last attack or till 18/21 years of age (whichever is longer).
• Rheumatic fever with carditis but no residual valvular disease: For 10 years after the last attack or till 21/25 years of age (whichever is longer).
• Rheumatic fever with persistent valvular disease, evident clinically or on echocardiography: For 10 years after the last attack or till the age of 40 (whichever is longer). Sometimes lifelong prophylaxis can be given.

Symptoms usually present after a latent period of about three weeks. Indolent carditis and chorea are the exceptions that can present even six months later. Migratory asymmetric polyarthritis which affects large joints and high-grade fever are common features. Cutaneous manifestations include erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules. Sydenham's chorea is commonly found in females and frequently affects the head and upper limbs. Acute rheumatic carditis can be seen as involvement of the endocardium, myocardium, or pericardium. Histopathological examination shows Aschoff bodies and activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells.

The image below shows Aschoff bodies.

In chronic rheumatic heart disease, there is a leaflet and tendinous cord thickening along with commissural fusion and shortening of the mitral valve. Ultimately the valve can undergo stenotic changes giving it a fish-mouth appearance as shown below.

The modified Jones criteria is used for diagnosis. Management of ARF is mainly symptomatic by the use of antibiotics and NSAIDs.
questions.learning: Once in three weeks for 5 years or till the age of 18, whichever is longer The given clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever (ARF).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient undergoes a vaginal delivery, after which a perineal tear is noted. The tear involves the muscle and less than 50% of the external anal sphincter, with the rectal mucosa remaining intact. What is the degree of the perineal tear?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Grade 3A

The clinical scenario describes a perineal tear involving muscle with less than 50% of the external anal sphincter, with the intact rectal mucosa, which is classified as a grade 3A perineal tear.

The perineal tear is more common in primigravida and results from over-stretching or sudden stretching of the perineum during childbirth. Trauma to the perineum can also result in perineal tears.

Clinical features include the inability to hold the flatus and feces. Soreness over the peri-anal region can be seen due to constant irritation by stool. Palpation reveals the decreased/absence of a sphincteric grip depending on the degree of tear.

All recent tears should be repaired immediately. If there is a delay of 24 hours, the repair has to be withheld and the patient has to be started on antibiotics to prevent infection. Complete perineal tears that were not repaired in the first 24 hours should be operated after 3 months. In 3 months of time, any local infection that might have been present would subside, and the general condition of the patient will also improve. However, if the perineal tear is untreated for more than 6 months, dense scar tissue forms making the surgery difficult.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient comes with a history of high fever for 5 days and altered sensorium. He also gave a history of two seizure episodes one day ago. Peripheral smear shows the following findings. What is the drug of choice in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Artesunate

The given scenario of high fever. altered sensorium and seizures and peripheral smear showing rings (headphones appearance) points towards the diagnosis of severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria, and the drug of choice for this condition is artesunate.

Artesunate-based combination therapy is given at a dose of 2.4 mg/kg stat IV, followed by 2.4 mg/kg at 12 and 24 hours, and then daily if necessary.

If artesunate is unavailable, artemether is given at a dose of 3.2 mg/kg stat IM, followed by 1.6 mg/kg QD, or quinine dihydrochloride is given at a dose of 20 mg of salt/kg infused over 4 hours, followed by 10 mg of salt/kg infused over 2–8 hours.

Major manifestations of severe falciparum malaria include more than two convulsions in 24 hours, unarousable coma/ cerebral malaria (failure to localize or respond appropriately to stimuli or coma persisting for >30 mins after generalized convulsion), acidosis, severe normocytic normochromic anemia, renal failure, pulmonary edema, hypoglycemia, shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Other manifestations include hemoglobinuria, hyperparasitemia, jaundice, and extreme weakness.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the classical triad of acute cholangitis?
questions.explanation: The classical clinical triad for acute cholangitis is known as Charcot's triad, which consists of right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and fever. This condition usually results from an obstruction in the biliary tree (often by stones) leading to a secondary bacterial infection. Regarding the distractors, shock (Option B) is not part of Charcot's triad but is a component of Reynolds' pentad, which also includes altered mental status and indicates severe, life-threatening obstructive suppurative cholangitis. While increased white blood cells (↑WBC) and elevated bilirubin (Options C and D) are common laboratory findings in this disease, they are not formal components of the recognized clinical triad. Early recognition of Charcot's triad is essential for initiating prompt antibiotic therapy and biliary decompression to prevent sepsis. Therefore, pain, jaundice, and fever are the defining features. is definitive for BCC

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient has markedly elevated plasma phenylalanine levels and low tyrosine levels. Phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme assay is normal. Which of the following cofactor deficiencies is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Biopterin

Conversion of phenylalanine → tyrosine requires:

• Enzyme: Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH)
• Cofactor: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄, biopterin)

In this case, PAH is normal, so the defect lies in the cofactor (BH₄) deficiency, leading to:

• ↑ Phenylalanine
• ↓ Tyrosine

BH₄ is also required for synthesis of neurotransmitters:

• Dopamine (via tyrosine hydroxylase)
• Serotonin (via tryptophan hydroxylase)

Thus, deficiency leads to: Neurological symptoms more severe than classical PKU

Why other options are incorrect:

• DHFR: Involved in folate metabolism
• PLP (Vitamin B6): Cofactor for transamination reactions
• THF: Involved in one-carbon metabolism (DNA synthesis)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman, G4P3L3, with 1 neonatal death (NND) and 2 previous lower segment cesarean sections (LSCS), presents at term with an active genital herpes infection. What is the preferred mode of delivery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Elective LSCS

For women with active genital herpes at the time of labor, elective cesarean section is the preferred mode of delivery to prevent neonatal herpes transmission. A standard lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) is typically performed unless there are other complications necessitating a different approach.

HSV infection in pregnancy can be caused by either HSV-1 or HSV-2 and transmitted by sexual contact. The infection can be primary, nonprimary, first episode, and recurrent.

HSV infection (both HSV 1 and 2) during pregnancy has a risk of vertical transmission of the infection to the fetus. The risk is higher in the primary than in the recurrent infection. The maximum risk of fetal infection is during labor, although it can occur in utero and post-natally from direct contact.

Suspicious lesions should be sent for PCR testing or culture. Antiviral treatment with acyclovir should be given if found positive. Women with no active genital lesions, asymptomatic, or those with active lesions in non-genital areas can undergo normal labor and delivery.

Management of HSV infection during pregnancy:

• Oral acyclovir or valacyclovir for primary or recurrent infections during pregnancy.
• IV acyclovir followed by oral acyclovir for severe or disseminated infection
• Oral analgesics or topical anesthetics for pain relief
• Catheterization for urinary retention

Cesarean delivery reduces the risk of vertical transmission during labor and is indicated in:

• Cases of active genital lesions - both primary and recurrent
• Prodromal symptoms like vulval itching or burning

Other options:

Option B: Classical Cesarean Section: Classical cesarean section involves a vertical incision on the upper part of the uterus and is generally reserved for specific cases such as abnormal uterine anatomy or placenta previa

Option C and D: Trial of Labor (VBAC) and Induction of Labor: Vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC) and induction of labor are contraindicated in women with active genital herpes due to the risk of transmitting the virus to the newborn during vaginal delivery.
questions.learning: Elective LSCS For women with active genital herpes at the time of labor, elective cesarean section is the preferred mode of delivery to prevent neonatal herpes transmission.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is used in the management of prostate cancer?
questions.explanation: The Gleason score is a critical grading system used to determine the aggressiveness of prostate cancer. It is calculated by examining biopsy samples under a microscope and assigning a grade to the two most common architectural patterns of the cancer cells, with the sum providing the total score. A higher Gleason score indicates a more poorly differentiated tumor that is likely to grow and spread faster. The Bethesda score (Option B) is primarily utilized for reporting thyroid cytopathology. The Alvarado score (Option C) is a clinical scoring system used to assist in the diagnosis of acute appendicitis based on symptoms, signs, and laboratory findings. The Nottingham score (Option D), also known as the Elston-Ellis modification of the Scarff-Bloom-Richardson system, is the standard grading method for breast cancer. Therefore, the Gleason score is the only tool listed specific to the pathological management and prognosis of prostate cancer

questions.text: A patient with dyspnea, respiratory distress due to pan-acinar emphysema, and liver dysfunction is due to a likely defect in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alpha 1 anti-trypsin deficiency

Pan-acinar emphysema with early-onset dyspnea and liver dysfunction is classic for α₁-antitrypsin deficiency.

Loss of α₁-antitrypsin leads to unopposed neutrophil elastase activity, causing diffuse alveolar destruction, predominantly in lower lobes.

Misfolded protein accumulation in hepatocytes explains the associated liver disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A pregnant woman with a prior mitral valve replacement is currently at 36 weeks of gestation. She has been on long-term warfarin therapy throughout pregnancy, and her INR is 3. In view of her advanced gestational age and cardiac history, which of the following is the most appropriate management approach at this stage?
options: Stop warfarin, start LMWH and aspirin
questions.explanation: In a pregnant woman with a mechanical mitral valve, continuous anticoagulation is essential to prevent valve thrombosis. However, at 36 weeks of gestation, continuing warfarin is unsafe because it crosses the placenta and increases the risk of fetal bleeding, especially intracranial hemorrhage during delivery. Therefore, warfarin must be discontinued at this stage. The preferred approach is to switch to low molecular weight heparin (LMWH). LMWH does not cross the placenta, making it safer for the fetus, and provides effective anticoagulation for the mother. It has a predictable dose-response and is widely used with anti-Xa monitoring in pregnancy. Other options are incorrect: (B) Unfractionated heparin is useful near delivery but is not the preferred option at this stage in stable patients. (C) Continuing warfarin poses significant fetal risk. (D) Adding aspirin is unnecessary and increases bleeding risk. Thus, at 36 weeks, the most appropriate management is to stop warfarin and initiate LMWH

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the Xray
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydro pneumothorax

The chest xray shows hydropneumothorax.

Chest radiography shows hydro pneumothorax with a collapsed right lung and an adjacent thoracic air–liquid level.

Hydro pneumothorax is a term given to the concurrent presence of a pneumothorax as well as a hydrothorax (i.e. air and fluid) in the pleural space.

On an erect chest radiograph, recognition of hydro pneumothorax can be rather easy and is classically shown as an air-fluid level.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 67-year-old patient with a history of thromboembolic stroke is currently taking aspirin and warfarin. He is complaining of a headache and appears confused after a fall in the toilet last night. NCCT of the head was done. What is the next best step in management? NCCT- Non contrast CT head
options: Vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma and neurosurgery consultation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma and neurosurgery consultation

The above clinical scenario and the plain computed tomography (CT) scan show a concave-convex-shaped hematoma on the left side suggestive of an acute subdural hematoma (SDH). Since, the patient is on anticoagulants, reversal with Vitamin K, FFP and immediate neurosurgical consultation would be the next best step.

Acute SDH results from the accumulation of blood between the arachnoid membrane and the dura. The tearing of a bridging vein running from the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses is the most common cause of acute SDH.

Radiographic features of subdural haemorrhages-Crescent-like distribution around the periphery of the brain.
Crescent-shaped hypodense lesion on axial CT: Chronic subdural haemorrhage
Crescent-shaped hyperdense collections on CT: Acute subdural haemorrhage.

On head CT scan, acute SDH appears as a hyperdense, crescent-shaped (concavo-convex) lesion (as seen in this question)

Open craniotomy for the evacuation of acute SDH is indicated for the following:

* Thickness >1 cm

* Midline shift >5 mm

Emergent decompression is also recommended for a comatose patient with an acute subdural hematoma less than 1 cm in thickness causing a midline shift of less than 5 mm if any of the following criteria are met:

*  GCS drops by two or more points from the time of injury to the hospitalization

*  The patient presents with fixed and dilated pupils

* ICP is >20mm Hg

Other options:

Option A: Aspirin and Clopidogrel are given in patients with ischemic stroke. It is not required for this patient.

Option C: Mannitol is used to lower intracranial pressure. Raised features of intracranial pressure like vomiting, papilledema are not mentioned.

Option D: Only observation would be inappropriate in the case of Acute SDH.

Pearl PF1866: Intracranial haemorrhage

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A farmer presents to the emergency department with diarrhea, sweating, excessive lacrimation, and salivation. Regarding the management of this condition, which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Atropine is used as an antidote for OP poisoning
Pralidoxime has a role in reversing the enzyme in carbamate poisoning
Succinylcholine use is avoided in rapid sequence intubation
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms are characteristic of a cholinergic crisis caused by organophosphate (OP) or carbamate poisoning. A critical pharmacological difference is that carbamates bind reversibly to the acetylcholinesterase enzyme, which typically results in a shorter duration of toxicity. In contrast, organophosphates bind irreversibly through a process called "aging." Atropine is the essential antidote for both to block muscarinic symptoms (Option B). Pralidoxime (Option C) is generally considered ineffective or controversial in carbamate poisoning because the bond is already reversible, and it is primarily used for OP poisoning. Succinylcholine (Option D) is avoided because its metabolism depends on pseudocholinesterase, which is inhibited by these poisons, leading to prolonged muscle paralysis. Therefore, the statement claiming carbamates bind irreversibly is incorrect

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per Biomedical Waste Management guidelines, cotton swabs used for cleaning a wound contaminated with pus and maggots should be disposed of in which color-coded bag?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Yellow non chlorinated bag

Cotton swabs used for cleaning wounds contaminated with blood, pus, or body fluids are categorized under “soiled waste,” which the guidelines specify should be disposed of in yellow-colored non-chlorinated plastic bag.

According to biomedical waste management guidelines, soiled waste items such as dressings, plaster casts, cotton swabs, and bags containing residual or discarded blood and blood components must be collected in yellow bags and treated by incineration, plasma pyrolysis, or deep burial.

Other options:

Option A and B: Red bags are used for contaminated recyclable wastes like tubing, intravenous tubes and sets, catheters, urine bags, syringes(without needles, and gloves).

Option D: Yellow chlorinated bags are not recommended, as the guideline specifies non-chlorinated yellow bags.

questions.text: A manufacturer substitutes a drug partly by another drug and doesn’t add it in the label. What is this type of drug called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Spurious drug

A spurious drug is one that is substituted wholly or partly by another drug or substance and this substitution is not declared on the label, making the product deceptive in identity and composition. Such drugs may falsely represent their contents, strength, or manufacturer, and are treated as counterfeit products under drug laws. The key feature is intentional substitution with misrepresentation, which fits this scenario precisely.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Misbranded drug: Involves labeling errors or misleading claims without actual substitution.

B. Adulterated drug: Refers to contamination or quality compromise, not identity deception.

C. Unethical drug: Not a recognized legal classification in pharmacovigilance or drug law.
questions.learning: Spurious drug — A spurious drug is one that is substituted wholly or partly by another drug or substance and this substitution is not declared on the label, making the product deceptive in identity and composition.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male presented with discharge as shown in the image. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fistula in ano

The diagnosis, considering the purulent discharge shown in the image, is a fistula in ano.

A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal hollow tract or cavity that is lined with granulation tissue and that connects a primary opening inside the anal canal to a secondary opening in the perianal skin. The most common cause is a perianal abscess. Other causes include tuberculosis or Crohn's disease.

Symptoms:

• Perianal pain
• Discharge- intermittent purulent discharge (which may be bloody)

Goodsall’s rule can be used as a guide in determining the location of the internal opening of the fistula.

• Fistulas with an external opening anteriorly connect to the internal opening by a short, radial tract.
• Fistulas with an external opening posteriorly track in a curvilinear fashion to the posterior midline.

Exceptions to Goodsall’s Rule

However, exceptions to this rule often occur: Fistulas with an anterior external opening greater than 3 cm from the anal margin usually track to the posterior midline.

Investigations:

The investigations done for fistula-in-ano are as follows:

• Fistulogram
• Endoanal ultrasound
• MRI
• Computed tomography (CT) scan
• Endocoil MRI
• Hydrogen peroxide–enhanced 3-D endoanal ultrasonography

MRI is the gold standard investigation for fistula imaging. It helps us to identify the secondary extensions of the track, which when missed may cause persistence of the fistula.

Treatment:

• Control of constipation
• Sitz bath
• Fistulotomy
• Fistulectomy
• Ligation of intersphincteric fistula tract (LIFT)
• Setons
• Advancement flaps

Other options:

Option B: A fissure in ano is a linear ulcer usually found in the midline, distal to the dentate line. It is one of the most common causes of anal pain and bleeding. They typically start with a tear in the anoderm within the distal half of the anal canal which then triggers cycles of recurring anal pain and bleeding, which lead to the development of a chronic anal fissure. The exposed internal sphincter muscle within the bed of the fissure frequently spasms, which not only contributes to severe pain but also can restrict blood flow to the fissure, preventing its healing.

Option C: Hemorrhoids are cushions of submucosal tissue containing venules, arterioles, and smooth muscle fibers located in the anal canal. External hemorrhoids are distal to the dentate line and are covered with anoderm; these may engorge, causing pain. Thrombosis of these external hemorrhoids causes severe pain.

Option D: Pilonidal sinus disease is commonly seen in the natal cleft, more in men, usually after puberty. Drivers and hairdressers are more commonly affected. The pilonidal sinus opening is usually seen in the midline between the sacrococcygeal joint's level and the coccyx's tip. The other sites that can be affected include the interdigital cleft and axilla.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presented with fever, headaches, myalgia, and drowsiness. He later developed dizziness and altered consciousness. His mother reports that he had consumed palm fruit on their recent trip to Kerala and has not been feeling well since then. Keeping the patient's history in mind, which of the following viruses should be considered in your differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nipah virus

This patient with fever, headaches, myalgia, drowsiness, dizziness and altered consciousness, with a history of consuming palm fruit is likely to have been infected with the Nipah virus.

Nipah virus is a zoonotic virus, which is transmitted by animals to humans.

It is an emerging paramyxovirus that belongs to the genus Henipavirus. It has caused disease in humans who have had contact with infected animals.

It has a wide range of hosts and is associated with high mortality rates. Its natural host is a certain species of fruit bat while pigs may be an intermediate host for transmission to humans.
Its transmission can occur by the following methods:

* Unprotected exposure to the secretions from the pigs, or unprotected contact with the tissue of a sick animal.

* Consumption of fruits or fruit products (such as raw date palm juice) contaminated with urine or saliva from infected fruit bats of the family Pteropodidae.

* Human-to-human transmission through close contact with people's secretions and excretions.

* The incubation period ranges from 4 to 14 days.

Patients present with symptoms of headaches, myalgia, vomiting, and sore throat. This is followed by the onset of encephalitis, which manifests as dizziness, drowsiness, and altered consciousness. Patients may also present with acute respiratory distress. Encephalitis and seizures occur in severe cases, progressing to coma within 24 to 48 hours.

Diagnosis is by means of real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) from bodily fluids and antibody detection via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) methods. The virus can be isolated by cell culture.

There is no treatment or vaccine available for either people or animals. The primary treatment for humans is supportive care.
questions.learning: Nipah virus — This patient with fever, headaches, myalgia, drowsiness, dizziness and altered consciousness, with a history of consuming palm fruit is likely to have been infected with the Nipah virus.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl presents with itchy lesions on her arm as shown. Her family history is positive for asthma. What could be the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atopic dermatitis

The clinical scenario depicting pruritic lesions at a flexural site along with a family history of atopy (asthma) is suggestive of atopic dermatitis (AD) or atopic eczema (AE). The scratch marks and excoriations shown in the image are due to pruritis, which is the hallmark feature of AD.

AD is a chronic relapsing inflammatory condition. It presents with erythematous macules, papules and vesicles that often start in early childhood, usually less than 2 years old. The lesions later become excoriated and lichenified. It is frequently associated with dryness of the skin and secondary infections. In infancy, the lesions initially appear on face (sparing the napkin area) and later on extensor aspect of knees and elbows as the child starts crawling. In later childhood and in adults, the principal site of involvement is flexures.

The filaggrin monomers in keratinocytes in the epidermis bind and aggregate keratin bundles and intermediate filaments to form the epidermal barrier. Any damage/dysfunction of this barrier is associated with an increased risk of developing AD. Damage to this barrier can be due to environmental factors (detergents, hard water, UV light) or local inflammatory reactions. Dysfunction of the barrier can be due to genetic mutation of the FLG gene leading to reduced filaggrin production or local immunomodulatory effects leading to reduced filaggrin expression.

Other options:

Option A: Seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by erythema, pruritus, scaling, flaking, or crusting of the skin. It is often associated with Malasezzia fungal infection. A milder form of seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp is commonly known as dandruff.

Option C: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is an inflammatory condition caused due to a delayed hypersensitivity reaction (Type 4 hypersensitivity) to a specific allergen that comes into direct contact with the skin.Patients usually present with pruritus, erythema, swelling, papules, and papulovesicles. Some common allergens include nickel (found in artificial jewelry), PPD/Para phenylene diamine (in hair dye), chromate (in cement), rubber or latex, cosmetics, etc. Patch test (image below) is used for the diagnosis of ACD.

Option D: Erysipelas is a bacterial skin infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) characterized by raised, erythematous sharply demarcated rapidly spreading skin lesions, along with systemic symptoms like fever and chills. The skin may also have a peau d'orange or orange peel-like appearance.
questions.learning: Atopic dermatitis — The clinical scenario depicting pruritic lesions at a flexural site along with a family history of atopy (asthma) is suggestive of atopic dermatitis (AD) or atopic eczema (AE).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: OCPs are not protective for?
questions.explanation: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs) are not protective against breast cancer and may actually be associated with a slight increase in risk (approximately 25%), especially in long-term users who started at a young age. However, this risk generally disappears within ten years of stopping the medication. In contrast, OCPs provide significant, well-documented protection against other malignancies. They reduce the risk of endometrial cancer (Option C) by over 30% and ovarian cancer (Option D) by 30–50% by suppressing ovulation and endometrial proliferation. There is also evidence that OCP use is protective against colorectal cancer (Option B), reducing the risk by roughly 15–20%. Cervical cancer risk may also be increased by OCPs, but breast cancer is the most classic "non-protected" malignancy listed. Therefore, while OCPs have significant non-contraceptive benefits, breast health requires separate screening protocols
questions.learning: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs) are not protective against breast cancer and may actually be associated with a slight increase in risk (approximately 25%), especially in long-term users who started at a young age.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the drug of choice for gastrointestinal stromal tumors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Imatinib

Imatinib is the drug of choice for gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST).

Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. It has a dominant role in tumors involving ABL, KIT, or EGFR kinases. It is the chemotherapy agent of choice in the chronic phase of chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML) and GIST.

Adverse effects:

* Gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting

* Fluid retention, edema, and periorbital swelling

* Myelosuppression

Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) are mesenchymal tumors originating from the interstitial cells of Cajal, located in the gastrointestinal myenteric plexus. The most common mutation is the c-KIT mutation. GIST can also occur with SDH mutation and NF-1 mutation in neurofibromatosis-1.

GIST has specific tumor markers i.e., CD117 (c-KIT mutation) and DOG-1.

Succinyl dehydrogenase deficient (SDH) deficient GIST is commonly seen in Carney’s triad.

Carney’s triad:

* Gastric GIST (succinyl dehydrogenase deficient)

* Pulmonary chondroma

* Extra adrenal paraganglioma

Microscopically, GIST has elongated spindle cells or plumper epithelioid cells, or a mixed pattern.The below image shows the microscopy of GIST composed of bundles, or fascicles, of spindle-shaped tumor cells.

Imatinib can be used to treat GIST with mutations in KIT or PDGFRA. Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) - deficient GIST is imatinib-resistant, so sunitinib, sorafenib, or regorafenib can be used instead.

During surgical resection of GIST, care must be taken to prevent capsule rupture, which causes seeding of nearby tissues leading to relapse in 100% of the cases. If capsule rupture occurs, adjuvant therapy with imatinib is indicated regardless of tumor extent.

Other options:

Option A: Sunitinib is a multiple kinase inhibitor that is used in imatinib-resistant GIST and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.

Option C: Sorafenib is also a multiple kinase inhibitor that is used in the treatment of renal cancer and imatinib-resistant GIST.

Option D: Dasatinib is a BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor and is used in imatinib-resistant CML.
questions.learning: Imatinib Imatinib is the drug of choice for gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not a derivative of neural crest cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinal pigment epithelium

Retinal pigment epithelium is not a derivative of neural crest cells.

Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is derived from the neuroectoderm. The RPE develops from the outer layer of the optic cup, a structure that arises from the neural tube (neuroectodermal origin), not from neural crest cells.

Neural crest cells are a group of cells that migrate during embryonic development and give rise to various structures, including parts of the nervous system, face, and heart.

Neural crest cells (NCC) are present adjacent to the neural tube and are sometimes referred to as the fourth germ layer. It contributes to the formation of many organs and tissues:

In the trunk region, they form:

• Melanocytes (Option D)
• Sensory ganglia
• Sympathetic and enteric neurons
• Schwann cells
• Adrenal medulla cells

In the cranial region, they contribute to the:

• Craniofacial skeleton
• Neurons for cranial ganglia-Ciliary ganglion  (Option C)
• Ciliary muscles  (Option A)
• Satellite glial cells
• Melanocytes

Some of the other neural crest derivatives are:

• C cells of the thyroid gland
• Conotruncal septum in the heart
• Odontoblasts
• Smooth muscle cells to blood vessels to the face and forebrain.
questions.learning: Retinal pigment epithelium Retinal pigment epithelium is not a derivative of neural crest cells. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is derived from the neuroectoderm.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A middle-aged man working in sandblasting developed hemoptysis, and a productive cough. Chest X-ray is suggestive of tuberculosis. Which of the following is associated with the same?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

Silicosis is associated with tuberculosis.

Silicosis occurs in industries such as sandblasting, pottery and ceramics, mining, and construction. Silicosis patients are prone to developing tuberculosis, in a condition called silico-tuberculosis.

Silica causes pulmonary alveolar macrophage dysfunction and hence, patients with silicosis have a higher risk of developing lung infections from organisms like M. Tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, and fungi.

Radiographic imaging of silicotuberculosis shows cavitation.

In silicotuberculosis: it is still unclear whether silico-tuberculotics are really tubercular or purely silicosis, because

* Sputum is rarely AFB+ve

* Children and women of silicotuberculosis patients do not develop tuberculosis

* The post-mortem on silicotuberculosis fail to prove the existence of tuberculosis disease

* Radiological evidence of both the condition is similar

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old male patient presents to the OPD with abdominal striae. He denies any history of long-term drug use. On examination, he has centripetal obesity, buffalo hump and hypertension. After diagnosis by dexamethasone suppression test, which of the following is the next appropriate investigation?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of adrenal gland
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasma ACTH levels

After confirming endogenous Cushing syndrome with a screening test (e.g., overnight dexamethasone suppression test), the next step is to measure plasma ACTH levels to determine whether the hypercortisolism is ACTH-dependent or ACTH-independent. This guides the subsequent imaging investigation.

• Plasma ACTH is the first investigation after biochemical confirmation of Cushing syndrome.
• Interpretation:

• Low ACTH → ACTH-independent (adrenal adenoma/carcinoma) → CT/MRI adrenal
• Normal or high ACTH → ACTH-dependent (pituitary adenoma or ectopic ACTH secretion) → Pituitary MRI ± Inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS)

Why not the other options?

• A. MRI of brain: Done only after ACTH is elevated or inappropriately normal, suggesting a pituitary source (Cushing disease).
• C. CECT of adrenal gland: Indicated only if ACTH is suppressed, suggesting an adrenal cause.
• D. Non-contrast CT of adrenal gland: Also performed after low ACTH confirms ACTH-independent disease, not immediately after diagnosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which ligament is tested in the following test?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates the Anterior Drawer Test, a common clinical maneuver used to evaluate the integrity of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL). To perform the test, the knee is flexed to 90 degrees, and the examiner pulls the tibia forward while stabilizing the femur. Excessive forward displacement of the tibia indicates an ACL tear. The Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL) (Option B) is assessed using the Posterior Drawer Test, where the tibia is pushed backward instead. The Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL) (Option C) is tested using the valgus stress test to check for gapping on the inner side of the knee. The Lateral Collateral Ligament (LCL) (Option D) is evaluated with the varus stress test to check the outer side of the joint. Because the image shows the tibia being pulled anteriorly, the ACL is the correct target of this specific test

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following causes a decrease in serum parathyroid hormone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calcitriol

The active form of vitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), directly suppresses PTH gene expression

Calcitriol is the active form of vitamin D. It increases calcium absorption from the intestines and helps maintain adequate serum calcium levels. When calcium levels rise, this triggers a negative feedback mechanism on the parathyroid glands, leading to decreased secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH). PTH's primary role is to raise blood calcium levels, so when calcium is sufficient, the need for PTH decreases, resulting in lower PTH levels.

Vitamin D and its derivatives are the primary treatment for hypoparathyroidism. Dihydrotachysterol (DHT), a reduced form of vitamin D2, has a quicker onset, shorter duration, and stronger impact on bone mobilization than traditional vitamin D, making it a preferred option. While most hypoparathyroid patients respond well to any form of vitamin D, calcitriol may be preferred for temporary treatment of hypocalcemia while waiting for the effects of a slower-acting vitamin D form. Calcium is used to address calcium deficiency and as a dietary supplement. Vitamin D is the primary treatment for hypoparathyroidism.

Severe hypermagnesemia or hypomagnesemia can also inhibit PTH secretion.

Other options:

Option B: Risedronate is a bisphosphonate that inhibits bone resorption, but it doesn't directly affect PTH secretion.

Option C: Furosemide is a diuretic that can increase calcium excretion, potentially raising PTH as the body tries to conserve calcium.

Option D: Lithium can actually increase PTH secretion by affecting calcium-sensing receptors in the parathyroid glands.
questions.learning: Calcitriol — The active form of vitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), directly suppresses PTH gene expression Calcitriol is the active form of vitamin D.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A diabetic patient presents with facial pain and a black eschar in the nasal cavity. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mucormycosis

Mucormycosis (rhino-orbito-cerebral form) is an aggressive angioinvasive fungal infection classically seen in uncontrolled diabetes, presenting with facial pain and black necrotic eschar in the nasal cavity.

·    Causative organisms: Mucor, Rhizopus species

·    Pathogenesis: Angioinvasion → thrombosis → tissue necrosis → black eschar

·    Predisposing factors:

o    Diabetes (especially DKA)

o    Immunocompromised states

·    Rapid progression to orbit and brain if untreated

Why not other options:

·  Acute sinusitis: No necrosis or black eschar

·  Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis: Allergic mucin, not invasive or necrotic

·  Nasal polyposis: Pale, non-necrotic masses

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a suspected tubal (ectopic) pregnancy with an inconclusive transvaginal ultrasound, what is the next step in management?
questions.explanation: In a clinically stable patient with a suspected ectopic (tubal) pregnancy and an inconclusive transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) (e.g., no pregnancy is seen in the uterus or adnexa), the mandatory next step is to obtain serial serum beta-hCG levels. The relationship between the hCG level and the TVS findings (the "discriminatory zone") is the cornerstone of diagnosis. If the hCG is above the discriminatory zone (typically ) and no intrauterine sac is seen, an ectopic pregnancy is highly likely. If it is below the zone, serial levels are monitored every 48 hours; a slow rise or plateau confirms an abnormal pregnancy. Methotrexate (Option B) is a treatment for ectopic pregnancy, not a diagnostic test. Laparotomy (Option C) and Diagnostic laparoscopy (Option D) are more invasive surgical steps reserved for when the diagnosis remains unclear after biochemical testing or if the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable. This biochemical-radiological correlation is essential for safe and effective early pregnancy management
questions.learning: In a clinically stable patient with a suspected ectopic (tubal) pregnancy and an inconclusive transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) (e.g., no pregnancy is seen in the uterus or adnexa), the mandatory next step is to obtain serial serum beta-hCG levels.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As an epidemiologist, you are assigned to calculate the maternal mortality ratio in your area. Which of the following parameters will you not take into account while calculating this ratio?
options: Maternal deaths due to road traffic accidents
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Maternal deaths due to road traffic accidents

Total live births and deaths due peripartum infections and postpartum haemorrhage will be taken into account while calculating the maternal mortality ratio (MMR).

MMR = (Number of maternal deaths in a given year / Number of live births in the same area and year) x 1,00,000 (or 1000).

Maternal mortality refers to deaths during pregnancy or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, from causes related to pregnancy.

Pearl PF0987: Maternal Mortality Ratio

Maternal death is defined as the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management but not from accidental or incidental causes.

* Maternal mortality ratio is the number of maternal deaths in a given period per 100,000 live births during the same period.

* MMR = Number of maternal deaths in a period x 100,000 (or 1000)/Number of live births in the same period

* Main global causes of maternal deaths are severe bleeding, indirect causes (anemia, malaria, heart diseases), infections, unsafe abortions, eclampsia, obstructed labor and other direct causes like ectopic pregnancy, anesthesia related complications, etc.

* In India, the most common causes of maternal deaths are hemorrhage (leading cause), sepsis, obstructed labor, hypertensive disorders, etc.
questions.learning: Maternal deaths due to road traffic accidents Total live births and deaths due peripartum infections and postpartum haemorrhage will be taken into account while calculating the maternal mortality ratio (MMR).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the constituent of the marked area in the electron microscopic picture of muscle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alpha actinin

Alpha actinin is the constituent of the marked area.

The image depicts sarcomere and the arrow points towards Z-line. Alpha actinin binds actin to Z-lines.

The orderly arrangement of actin, myosin, and related proteins that produces this pattern. The area between two Z-lines is called sarcomere.

The thick filaments, which are about twice the diameter of the thin filaments, are made up of myosin, which are lined to form A bands; the thin filaments are made up of actin, tropomyosin, and troponin. The array of thin filaments extends out of the A band and into the less dense staining I bands.

The lighter H bands in the center of the A bands are the regions where, when the muscle is relaxed, the thin filaments do not overlap the thick filaments.  The Z lines allow for anchoring of the thin filaments.

Actinin, titin and desmin are additional structural proteins.Titin connects Z-lines to the M line and provides the scaffolding to the sarcomere.  Desmin adds structure to Z-lines by connecting Z-line to plasma membrane.

Note: Some sources say that even titin is a component of Z-disc so if alpha actinin is not given in the options titin is the second best answer.
questions.learning: Alpha actinin Alpha actinin is the constituent of the marked area. The image depicts sarcomere and the arrow points towards Z-line.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A male presented with complains of decreased sexual desire. He was recently diagnosed with depression and started on a drug for the same. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fluoxetine

Fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) that is associated with the side effects of sexual dysfunction.

Fluoxetine is used in the treatment of major depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, bulimia and anorexia nervosa, generalized anxiety disorders, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder.

Other adverse effects include dry mouth, urinary retention, insomnia, GI disturbances, risk of suicidal behavior, and weight gain.

Adverse effects of specific antidepressants:

Drug

sedation, antimuscarinic, hypotension, arrhythmia, seizures

Fluoxetine

Nausea, anorexia, loss of libido, insomnia

Sedative, priapism, hypotension

Seizures, mild tachycardia, hypertension

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents to the OPD with palpitation and weight loss. On examination, both of her legs had the following lesion given below. On applying pressure, the indentation does not persist on release. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. What is the probable etiological cause for the oedema?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myxedema

A bilateral presentation of non-pitting oedema in the lower limbs along with features of palpitation and weight loss in the given scenario point towards a diagnosis of pretibial myxedema. And most probably it is due to the underlying thyroid disease.

Pretibial myxedema/Thyroid dermopathy  (localized edematous and thickened pretibial plaque formation) in seen secondary to Grave's disease.

Other options:

Option C: While chronic lymphangitis and acute lymphatic filariasis can also cause non-pitting oedema, they usually have a unilateral/localized presentation and the given clinical history is not relevant to this condition.

Option B and D: Nephrotic syndrome and heart failure cause bilateral pitting oedema. Also, the clinical scenario given above does not fit either of them.

Causes of generalized oedema include:

* Heart failure

* Chronic renal failure

* Nephrotic syndrome

* Liver cirrhosis

Causes of localized oedema:

* Thrombophlebitis

* Chronic lymphangitis

* Resection of regional lymph nodes

* Filariasis
questions.learning: Myxedema — A bilateral presentation of non-pitting oedema in the lower limbs along with features of palpitation and weight loss in the given scenario point towards a diagnosis of pretibial myxedema.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which therapy is given for cervical cancer?
questions.explanation: Platinum-based chemotherapy, specifically Cisplatin, is the gold standard for treating advanced, recurrent, or metastatic cervical cancer. It is most commonly used in "concurrent chemoradiation," where Cisplatin is administered alongside radiotherapy to act as a radiosensitizer, significantly improving survival rates in locally advanced cases. Option B (Hormonal therapy) is incorrect because cervical cancer is not hormone-dependent, unlike breast or endometrial cancers. While targeted therapy (Option C, e.g., Bevacizumab) and immunotherapy (Option A, e.g., Pembrolizumab) are increasingly used as adjuncts for specific indications, they are not the primary, first-line systemic treatment across all advanced stages. Carboplatin may also be used in patients who cannot tolerate Cisplatin due to renal issues. Therefore, because of its foundational role in standard chemoradiation protocols, platinum-based therapy is the most accurate answer for general cervical cancer management

questions.text: The difference between the incidence of disease among exposed and incidence among non exposed is given by which of the following variables?

Correct answer: B. Attributable risk

The difference between the incidence of disease among exposed and incidence among non-exposed is given by attributable risk.

Attributable risk is often expressed as a percentage.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Thermogenin protein is mainly found in ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mitochondria

Thermogenin is an uncoupling protein found in the mitochondria of brown adipose tissue (BAT); this protein is abundantly found in neonates.

* It is used to generate heat by non-shivering thermogenesis and makes an important contribution to countering heat loss in neonates.

* The uncoupling mechanism of thermogenin is by increasing the permeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane, allowing protons that have been pumped into the intermembrane space to return to the mitochondrial matrix. It uncouples the electron transport chain, allowing for fasting substrate oxidation with a low rate of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following hormones have an inhibitory effect on hormone-sensitive lipase?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Leptin

Leptin and insulin inhibit hormone-sensitive lipase, whereas the other hormones given in the options stimulate it.

Leptin is a hormone produced by adipose tissue in proportion to the amount of body fat. It acts as a long-term regulator of energy balance. It functions by signalling the brain, specifically the hypothalamus, to regulate appetite and energy expenditure. It suppresses appetite and increases energy expenditure to maintain body weight within a certain range.

In addition to its central effects, leptin also has peripheral effects on adipose tissue. Leptin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) activity, which reduces the breakdown of triglycerides into fatty acids in adipocytes. This inhibition of HSL leads to reduced release of free fatty acids into the bloodstream, contributing to the overall regulation of energy storage and utilization.

Other options:

Option A: Glucagon is produced by the pancreas, glucagon stimulates hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) to break down triglycerides into free fatty acids, which can be released into the bloodstream for energy production.

Option B: Epinephrine is produced by the adrenal glands, and epinephrine is released during the body's stress response. It activates HSL, promoting the breakdown of stored fat to provide energy in fight-or-flight situations.

Option C: ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic Hormone) is produced by the pituitary gland, ACTH indirectly stimulates HSL activity. ACTH signals the adrenal glands to release cortisol, which can lead to the mobilization of fatty acids from adipose tissue.
questions.learning: Leptin Leptin and insulin inhibit hormone-sensitive lipase, whereas the other hormones given in the options stimulate it. Leptin is a hormone produced by adipose tissue in proportion to the amount of body fat.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the OPD as he is always fatigued and has muscle cramps after exercise and the blood sample collected soon after exercise showed low glucose and lactate level. He also has a history of one episode of hypoglycaemia while playing. He became normal after resting for a while. Which of the following diseases is he most likely to be suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. McArdle disease

McArdle disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type V) is caused by deficiency of myophosphorylase, the enzyme responsible for breakdown of glycogen in skeletal muscle.

• Muscle cannot convert glycogen → glucose-1-phosphate
• Leads to failure of glycolysis during exercise
• Hence, ↓ lactate production after exercise (key diagnostic clue)

Clinical features explained:

• Exercise intolerance & early fatigue
• Muscle cramps after exercise
• Low lactate levels post-exercise
• Second-wind phenomenon (symptoms improve after rest due to use of blood glucose)
• Occasional hypoglycemia during exertion

Why other options are incorrect:

• Hers disease (GSD VI): Liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency → mild hypoglycemia + hepatomegaly
• Cori disease (GSD III): Debranching enzyme deficiency → hepatomegaly + abnormal glycogen
• Andersen disease (GSD IV): Branching enzyme deficiency → liver cirrhosis, not exercise intolerance

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the main substrate and metabolic fuel used by RBCs during fasting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glucose

Glucose is the main substrate and metabolic fuel used by RBCs during fasting. RBCs lack mitochondria and are dependent fully on glycolysis (anaerobic) and pentose phosphate pathway during fasting state.

Glucose is always required by brain and RBCs. Brain can meet only about 20 percent of energy requirements by using ketone bodies and the remaining is supplied by glucose. Metabolic changes occuring during fasting state and starvation therefore serve to preserve glucose and glycogen reserves for brain and RBCs.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A female was brought for autopsy with an alleged history of being found at a lake in the village. All of the following are suggestive of antemortem drowning except:
options: White leathery foam around mouth and nostrils
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Washerwoman's hands and feet

Washerwoman's hands and feet are a non-specific sign of submersion. They occur due to the imbibition of water into the outer skin layers. They can be seen in antemortem as well as postmortem drowning victims.

The presence of water in the stomach, white leathery foam around the mouth and nostrils, and a positive diatom test are suggestive of antemortem drowning.

Given below are the features of antemortem drowning.

• Froth - The presence of copious amounts of fine, shaving-lather-like froth at the mouth and the nostrils is the most characteristic finding of antemortem drowning. It is caused by the vigorous agitation of the tracheal and bronchial mucous secretions, edema fluid, and alveolar surfactant during respiratory efforts.
• Cutis anserina - The contraction of the erector pilorum muscles causes puckering and grainy appearance of the skin. This resembles goose skin; hence, it is called cutis anserina.
• Washerwoman’s hand - Maceration of the skin on the palms and soles gives a wrinkled, sodden, and bleached appearance due to submersion.
• Cadaveric spasm - Gravel, weed, soil, grass, etc. is firmly held in the clenched hands due to cadaveric spasm. This is a vital sign of antemortem drowning. The material also indicates the place of submersion.
• Rigor mortis - This appears early in cases of a violent antemortem struggle.
• Face - It is bloated and discolored, with cyanosis.
• Eyes - Conjunctiva are suffused and pupils dilated.
• Tongue - It may be swollen and protruded.
• Antemortem injuries - These may be sustained by striking objects, such as rocks, during the fall into the water body. Examination for such injuries must be performed only after the body is dry.

Internal findings:

• Lungs - They appear voluminous and distended and show ballooning. The cut section will exude copious amounts of frothy, bloodstained fluid.
• Larynx, trachea, and bronchioles - The presence of sand, silt, and aquatic vegetation in the trachea and lower respiratory tract are characteristic findings of antemortem drowning.
• Heart and blood vessels- Gettler test can be done to estimate the chloride content in the right and left sides of the heart to differentiate between freshwater and saltwater drowning.
• Diatom test- Diatoms are microscopic algae. Their presence in the organs, particularly in the bone marrow, is suggestive of antemortem drowning.
• Stomach and small intestines- These organs may contain water in some cases. Water present in the small intestine is positive evidence of death by drowning.
• Middle ear - The presence of water in the middle ear is highly suggestive of antemortem drowning.
• Brain - It is congested, and edematous, with loss of gray-white junction.
questions.learning: Washerwoman's hands and feet Washerwoman's hands and feet are a non-specific sign of submersion. They occur due to the imbibition of water into the outer skin layers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Where are the Ito cells in the liver located?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Space of disse

Ito cells/Hepatic stellate cells are located in the space of Disse. They are mesenchymal in origin.

The space of Disse or the perisinusoidal space (or space of Disse) is a location in the liver between hepatocytes and the liver sinusoid.

Significance of Ito cells:

Ito cells are in a dormant state for the majority of the duration. They store the fat-soluble vitamin A in their lipid droplets and are a signiﬁcant source of growth factors involved in liver homeostasis and regeneration.

When there is liver injury, Ito cells get activated. They replace damaged hepatocytes with collagenous scar tissue and secrete intralobular matrix components, including collagen type III (reticular) ﬁbres. This leads to hepatic ﬁbrosis.

Note: A narrow space which separates limiting plate (a sleeve of modified hepatocytes) from the connective tissue of the portal area is known as space of moll.

questions.text: Based on the given ECG, identify which wall of the myocardium was affected in this patient?
questions.explanation: The ECG shows ST-segment elevation in precordial leads V1–V4, which correspond to the anterior wall of the left ventricle supplied mainly by the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. These leads directly reflect anterior myocardial activity, so ST elevation here indicates an anterior wall myocardial infarction (MI). Key ECG localization: 1. V1–V4 → Anterior wall 2. V5–V6, I, aVL → Lateral wall 3. II, III, aVF → Inferior wall 4. Posterior MI → ST depression in V1–V3 (mirror image) Why other options are incorrect: (A) Inferior wall: Would show ST elevation in II, III, aVF, not seen here (C) Posterior wall: Shows ST depression in V1–V3, not elevation (D) Lateral wall: Involves I, aVL, V5–V6, not the primary changes here Thus, ST elevation in V1–V4 confirms anterior wall involvement

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During the puerperium, what is the accurate order of vaginal discharge?
options: Lochia serosa > Lochia rubra > Lochia alba
Lochia rubra > Lochia alba > Lochia serosa
Lochia alba > Lochia rubra > Lochia serosa
Lochia rubra > Lochia serosa > Lochia alba
questions.explanation: Lochia is the vaginal discharge occurring after childbirth, consisting of blood, mucus, and placental tissue. It progresses through three distinct stages based on its color and composition. Lochia Rubra is the first stage (Days 1–4), appearing bright red due to high blood and decidual content. Lochia Serosa follows (Days 5–9), appearing pinkish or brownish as the discharge becomes thinner and contains more serous fluid, leukocytes, and cervical mucus. The final stage is Lochia Alba (Day 10 to about 4–6 weeks), which is yellowish-white or pale and consists primarily of leukocytes, epithelial cells, and fat. Options A, B, and C provide incorrect sequences that do not follow this physiological progression. Understanding the normal order and duration of lochia is essential for healthcare providers to distinguish healthy postpartum recovery from complications like secondary postpartum hemorrhage or endometritis (infection)
questions.learning: Lochia is the vaginal discharge occurring after childbirth, consisting of blood, mucus, and placental tissue. It progresses through three distinct stages based on its color and composition.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The catalytic efficiency of enzyme is best expressed by which of the following kinetic constants:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kcat/Km

The catalytic efficiency of an enzyme is expressed as Kcat/Km.

Kcat is the rate constant, which is the limiting rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction at saturation. It is given by Vmax divided by number of active sites of the enzyme. Km is the Michaelis-Menten constant, which is defined as the substrate concentration at which the initial velocity(Vi) is half the maximum velocity (Vmax/2).

For some enzymes, when a substrate (S) binds to the active site of the enzyme (E), and forms an enzyme-substrate complex (ES), the product is instantaneously formed. For such enzymes, the reaction of E+S→ES becomes the rate-limiting step. Its rate is determined on the rate of diffusion of the molecules in a solution. Hence, these enzymes are called diffusion-limited or catalytically perfect.

Examples of the catalytically perfect enzymes, where the catalytic efficiency reaches the diffusion limit of 108-109 M−1s−1:

• Triosephosphate isomerase
• Carbonic anhydrase
• Acetylcholinesterase
• Adenosine deaminase
questions.learning: Kcat/Km — The catalytic efficiency of an enzyme is expressed as Kcat/Km. Kcat is the rate constant, which is the limiting rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction at saturation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Hospital management wants to estimate the average time a doctor spends with each patient to decide whether staffing levels need adjustment. Which management technique would be most suitable for assessing this?
questions.explanation: Work sampling is a statistical management technique used to analyze the time spent by workers on various categories of tasks. It involves making a large number of instantaneous observations at random intervals to determine what proportion of a worker's time is dedicated to specific activities, such as patient interaction. This is the most appropriate method for determining average interaction duration because it provides objective data without the continuous presence of an observer. Option A refers to theoretical simulations. Option B is a broad administrative process rather than a measurement tool. Option C involves hiring, training, and policy development rather than time-task analysis. Work sampling allows hospital management to identify workflow bottlenecks and justify staffing adjustments to enhance the quality of care. By quantifying non-repetitive work, it helps in optimizing the ratio of clinicians to patients, ensuring that the health system functions efficiently and meets patient needs

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient develops hypotension and cardiac arrhythmias after receiving a supraclavicular brachial plexus block using 0.5% bupivacaine. What is the first-line management for this complication?
questions.explanation: The development of hypotension and arrhythmias shortly after a regional nerve block with a local anesthetic (like bupivacaine) is diagnostic for Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST). Bupivacaine is particularly cardiotoxic as it binds tightly to cardiac sodium channels. The specific first-line treatment and antidote for LAST is the rapid administration of a 20% intravenous lipid emulsion (Intralipid). The "lipid sink" theory suggests the emulsion absorbs the lipophilic anesthetic molecules from the blood and tissues, reducing their toxic effects on the heart and brain. While Invasive ventilation (Option A) and Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (Option D) may be required in severe cases of cardiac arrest, Intralipid is the targeted pharmacological intervention to reverse the toxicity itself. Sodium bicarbonate (Option C) is not the primary treatment for LAST. All settings where regional anesthesia is performed must have a "lipid rescue kit" readily available. Early recognition of the prodromal signs of toxicity, such as metallic taste or perioral numbness, is essential to prevent cardiovascular collapse
questions.learning: The development of hypotension and arrhythmias shortly after a regional nerve block with a local anesthetic (like bupivacaine) is diagnostic for Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During the 14th century, what was the prescribed duration of isolation for individuals suspected of having the plague when quarantine measures were enforced?
questions.explanation: The term "quarantine" originates from the Italian word "quaranta giorni," which literally means forty days. This duration was established during the Black Death in the 14th century when the port city of Venice required ships coming from plague-infested areas to anchor offshore for forty days before landing. This specific timeframe was chosen as it was believed to be sufficient for a disease to manifest and for the "cleansing" of the ship and crew. Option A (14 days) is the modern quarantine period used for diseases like COVID-19 but was not the historical standard. Options B (35 days) and D (28 days) are incorrect as they do not correspond to the etymological or historical root of the practice. The choice of forty days may have also had religious significance, echoing the biblical duration of the Great Flood or Lent. This historical precedent laid the foundation for modern public health isolation and containment strategies used in infectious disease control globally

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The renal feed of a patient suffering from end-stage renal disease (stage 5) should ideally be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Low volume, high calories

The renal feed of a patient suffering from end-stage renal disease should ideally be low volume, high calories.

Dietary factors may have an effect on the progression of kidney disease and its complications. A low-volume feed is preferred in order to avoid:

• Sodium and volume overload
• Hyperkalemia
• Hyperphosphatemia
• Accumulation of toxic metabolites of protein degradation

A high-calorie feed is preferred in order to combat the patient's risk of malnutrition and wasting seen in ESRD.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with jaundice characterized by conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and intrahepatic cholestasis. Liver biopsy reveals eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The laboratory finding of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is never physiological (Option D) and always requires investigation. The definitive diagnostic clue in this case is the liver biopsy finding: eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules. These granules are characteristic of Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (A1AT) Deficiency, which is a leading cause of genetic neonatal hepatitis (Option B). The granules represent misfolded A1AT protein accumulated within hepatocytes. Hypoplasia of the biliary tract (Option A) and Choledochal cysts (Option C) are structural causes of cholestasis but would not show these specific intracellular PAS-positive granules. Neonatal hepatitis can eventually lead to cirrhosis and liver failure. Diagnosis is confirmed by serum A1AT levels and protease inhibitor (Pi) phenotyping. Therefore, given the pathognomonic histological evidence of A1AT protein accumulation, neonatal hepatitis is the correct clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: The laboratory finding of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is never physiological (Option D) and always requires investigation. The definitive diagnostic clue in this case is the liver biopsy finding: eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man was abducted from his home and was presumed to be dead after long time of search. His son subsequently claimed the rights to his property. According to section 111 of BSA, till how much time the son is not entitled to claim the inheritance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 7 years

Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), Section 111 (similar to earlier Evidence Act provisions), a person who has been missing and not heard of for 7 years is presumed dead.

• If a person is not heard of for 7 years by those who would naturally have heard from him, the law presumes death after 7 years
• Until completion of 7 years, the person is legally considered alive

Implication for inheritance:

• Legal heirs cannot claim inheritance before 7 years
• After 7 years → presumption of death → property rights can be claimed

Important clarification: The law presumes death, but exact time of death is not presumed
