questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient is asked to copy the face of a clock, and the resulting drawing is shown below. What is the correct term used to describe this finding?
questions.explanation: The image displays a classic result of the "Clock Drawing Test" where the patient has crowded all the numbers onto the right side of the clock face, completely ignoring the left side. This is the hallmark of Hemispatial Neglect (Option B) (also known as unilateral neglect). This condition usually results from a lesion in the right parietal lobe (often after a stroke), causing the patient to lose awareness of the left half of their environment. Confabulation (Option A) is the fabrication of memories seen in Korsakoff syndrome. Kinetic apraxia (Option C) is the loss of ability to perform fine, skilled movements despite normal strength. Asterixis (Option D) is a "flapping tremor" of the hands seen in hepatic or metabolic encephalopathy . Because the patient has completely failed to represent one side of the spatial layout, hemispatial neglect is the only accurate neurological term. This test is a simple and effective bedside screening tool for parietal dysfunction
questions.learning: The image displays a classic result of the "Clock Drawing Test" where the patient has crowded all the numbers onto the right side of the clock face, completely ignoring the left side.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A diabetic truck driver presents to you with cough and breathlessness. A diagnosis of pneumonia was confirmed, and histopathological examination revealed dichotomous branching, as shown below. What is the likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aspergillus

The most likely causative agent based on the clinical features and image showing dichotomous branching at acute angles given is Aspergillus.

Aspergillus fumigatus is the most common pathogenic species. It can cause invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients. This can be due to prolonged treatment with steroids or retro-positive status. It starts as pneumonia, which can later spread to involve other organs. Voriconazole is the drug of choice.

Other manifestations include allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis where central bronchiectasis is usually seen. Aspergilloma and superficial infections like otomycosis or mycotic keratitis are the other presentations.

Histopathological examination of the tissue section shows characteristic dichotomous branching at an acute angle. The hyphae stain poorly with hematoxylin and eosin, so periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stain is used.

Other methods for diagnosis include detection of galactomannan (Aspergillus cell-wall component) and culture isolation. Aspergillus fumigatus grows dark green colonies, while Aspergillus niger appears black. Yellow-green colonies are seen in case of Aspergillus flavus. Microscopic examination of colonies stained with lactophenol cotton blue would show septate hyphae and conidiophores.

Other options:

Options A and B - Rhizopus and Mucor are zygomycetes that are responsible for mucormycosis. Non-septate, broad hyphae are seen on tissue samples stained with hematoxylin and eosin.

The image below shows broad aseptate and irregularly-branched non-septate hyphae of Mucor.

Option C - Candida, the causative agent for candidiasis, appear as budding gram-positive cells on wet films and smears. Mycelial forms suggest colonization. Culture colonies are creamy-white and have a yeasty odor. Candida albicans, the most commonly implicated pathogenic species, form chlamydospores on corn meal agar.

The image below shows candidal hyphae and chlamydospores.
questions.learning: Aspergillus — The most likely causative agent based on the clinical features and image showing dichotomous branching at acute angles given is Aspergillus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Orthotolidine test is used to determine ________
options: Free and combined chlorine in water
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Free and combined chlorine in water

Orthotolidine (OT) test is used to determine free and combined chlorine in water.

Pearl PF0273: Chlorination of Water

* Chlorination is widely used for large scale purification of water and for drinking water.

* It is bactericidal and moderately virucidal but not sporicidal, except in high doses.

* Alongside its anti-pathogenic attributes, it oxidizes iron, manganese and hydrogen sulphide. It also destroys some taste and odor producing components. It controls algae and slime organisms and aids in coagulation.

* Action of chlorine:

* Hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid are formed when chlorine is added to water. Hypochlorous acid ionizes to form hydrogen and hypochlorite ions.

* H2O + Cl2 → HCl + HOCl
HOCl → H + OCl

* The disinfecting action of chlorine is predominantly due to hypochlorous acid. Hypochlorous acid is the most effective form of chlorine and it is almost 70 – 80 times more effective than hypochlorite ions.

* Chlorine acts best in water that has a pH of around 7.

* Principles of chlorination:

* The water to be disinfected must be clear of turbidity as turbidity impedes efficient chlorination.

* The chlorine demand of water is the difference between the amount of chlorine added to the water and the amount of residual chlorine remaining at the end of a specific period of contact (usually 60 minutes) at a given temperature and pH of the water. This has to be estimated before chlorination is done.

* The point at which the chlorine demand of water is met is called the breakpoint. It is beyond this that residual free chlorine begins to appear.

* Contact period of free chlorine for at least one hour is required to kill bacteria and viruses.

* Minimum recommended concentration of free chlorine is 0.5 mg/litre for one hour. Free residual chlorine provides a margin of safety against microbial contamination that occurs in storage or transport.

* The sum of the chlorine demand of the specific water plus free residual chlorine of 0.5 mg/litre constitutes the correct dose of chlorine to be applied.

* Methods of chlorination

* Chlorine gas: It is the first choice as it is cheap, quick and efficient in action and easy to apply. Special chlorinating equipments like Paterson’s chloronome are used for application of chlorine gas.

* Chloramines: These loose compounds of chlorine and ammonia give more persistent forms of residual chlorine. They have slow action and thus are not widely used.

* Perchloron or high test hypochlorite (H.T.H.): It is a calcium compound that has 60 – 70% of available chlorine.

* Break point chlorination:

* The point at which the chlorine demand of water is met is called the breakpoint.

* Free chlorine (HOCl and OCl) appears when chlorine is added beyond the breakpoint.

* In other words, at the breakpoint, if chlorine is added, then all the combined chlorines have been completely destroyed and free residual chlorines begin to appear.

* This corresponding dosage to achieve appearance of free residual chlorine is called breakpoint dosage and this method is called breakpoint chlorination.

* It is also called controlled superchlorination

* Superchlorination followed by dechlorination is used to disinfect highly polluted waters whose quality fluctuates greatly.

* Orthotolidine (OT) test:

* It is a test for chlorination and determines free and combined chlorine in water, rapidly and accurately.

* The reagent used is analytical grade Orthotolidine dissolved in 10% solution of hydrochloric acid.

* When added to water which contains chlorine, it turns yellow with varying intensity. This is faster in the presence of free chlorine and slower in the presence of combined chlorines.

* Orthotolidine - arsenite (OTA) test:

* This is a modification of the OT test which nullifies the errors caused due to interfering substances like iron, nitrites, manganese, etc.

* It determines free and combined chlorines separately.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most common electrolyte imbalance observed in pyloric stenosis?
questions.explanation: In pyloric stenosis, repeated projectile vomiting leads to loss of gastric contents, resulting in a characteristic hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Among electrolyte abnormalities, hypokalemia is considered the most consistent and prominent finding in exam context. Mechanism: 1. Vomiting causes loss of H⁺ and Cl⁻, leading to metabolic alkalosis 2. Alkalosis causes shift of K⁺ into cells, lowering serum potassium 3. Volume depletion activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system 4. Aldosterone increases renal potassium loss, worsening hypokalemia Why other options are incorrect: (A) Hyponatremia: May occur due to dehydration, but not the most consistent finding (C) Hypochloremia: Common due to HCl loss, but hypokalemia is more consistently emphasized as the key metabolic disturbance (D) Hypophosphatemia: Not typically associated Thus, the most common electrolyte imbalance (exam answer) is hypokalemia
questions.learning: In pyloric stenosis, repeated projectile vomiting leads to loss of gastric contents, resulting in a characteristic hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with joint pain, swelling, and difficulty in movement. Examination reveals a tender, swollen knee, and the history is notable for a recent sore throat. Laboratory investigations show elevated antistreptolysin O (ASO) titers, while renal biopsy findings are consistent with post- streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Considering the association with both acute rheumatic fever and PSGN, which streptococcal species is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of migratory arthritis (joint discomfort/swelling) followed by symptoms of glomerular disease (PSGN) after a recent throat infection is diagnostic for the sequelae of Streptococcus pyogenes infection. Streptococcus pyogenes, also known as Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci (GABHS), is the only organism responsible for both acute rheumatic fever and PSGN. High ASO titers confirm the immune response to a recent GABHS pharyngeal infection. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A) causes pneumonia and meningitis. Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B) (Option C) is the leading cause of neonatal sepsis. Streptococcus mutans (Option D) is associated with dental caries and subacute endocarditis. While PSGN can follow either a throat or skin infection, acute rheumatic fever characteristically follows only a pharyngeal infection with GABHS. Understanding this shared etiology is fundamental in pediatric medicine for emphasizing the need for prompt treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of migratory arthritis (joint discomfort/swelling) followed by symptoms of glomerular disease (PSGN) after a recent throat infection is diagnostic for the sequelae of Streptococcus pyogenes infection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which statement correctly describes the location and clinical significance of McBurney’s point in a patient with acute appendicitis?
options: McBurney point is located in the left lower quadrant of the abdomen.
McBurney point corresponds to the site of maximal tenderness in acute appendicitis.
McBurney point is used to assess rebound tenderness in acute appendicitis.
McBurney point is located at the umbilicus in acute appendicitis.
questions.explanation: McBurney's point is the most common site of clinical landmarking for the base of the appendix. It is anatomically located one-third of the distance from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. In cases of acute appendicitis, this point corresponds to the site of maximal tenderness on physical examination. Option A is incorrect because the point is in the right lower quadrant, not the left. Option C is inaccurate; while tenderness at McBurney's point is common, "rebound tenderness" is a generalized peritoneal sign known as Blumberg's sign, not specifically synonymous with McBurney's point itself. Option D is incorrect as the point is lateral to the umbilicus. Pain in appendicitis typically begins in the periumbilical region (visceral pain) and then localizes to McBurney's point (somatic pain) as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed. Identifying tenderness at this specific anatomical landmark remains a fundamental diagnostic skill in the evaluation of acute abdominal pain
questions.learning: McBurney's point is the most common site of clinical landmarking for the base of the appendix. It is anatomically located one-third of the distance from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with small cell lung carcinoma presents with confusion and seizures. Laboratory findings show: • Serum sodium: 112 mEq/L • Serum osmolality: Low • Urine osmolality: High Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypertonic saline (3% NaCl)

Symptomatic severe hyponatremia (e.g., confusion, seizures) due to SIADH, commonly associated with small cell lung carcinoma, is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment with hypertonic saline (3% NaCl). Hypertonic saline rapidly raises serum sodium and reduces the risk of cerebral edema and herniation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Fluid restriction – first-line for chronic or mild SIADH but too slow in patients with severe neurologic symptoms.
• C. Demeclocycline – used for long-term management of chronic SIADH; not appropriate for acute emergencies.
• D. Tolvaptan – may be used in selected cases of euvolemic hyponatremia but is not the initial treatment for symptomatic severe hyponatremia with seizures.
questions.learning: Hypertonic saline (3% NaCl) Symptomatic severe hyponatremia (e.g., confusion, seizures) due to SIADH, commonly associated with small cell lung carcinoma, is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment with hypertonic saline (3% NaCl).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following zymogens requires gamma-glutamyl carboxylase?
options: Factors II, VII, IX, and X
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factors II, VII, IX, and X

Clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X are zymogens of serine proteases that contain glutamic acid residues. These residues undergo vitamin-K-dependent carboxylation via gamma-glutamyl carboxylase to form gamma-carboxyglutamic acid residues. These residues chelate calcium ions, allowing the binding of clotting factors to the platelet surface.

Zymogens are the proprotein form of enzymes (proenzymes) that require proteolytic activation to carry out their function.

The reduced form of vitamin K acts as a cofactor in the post-synthetic modification of these zymogens and their activation. This reduced form of vitamin K is recycled back from its oxidized form by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, which is inhibited by warfarin.

The absence of vitamin K or the presence of warfarin inhibits carboxylation of the glutamate residues, leading to the release of abnormal precursors of clotting factors in the blood.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following parameters is used to assess the extent of drug absorption in a plasma concentration vs. time graph?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Area under the curve

The area under the curve of plasma concentration vs. time curve gives the extent of absorption, which is calculated by the trapezoidal rule.

The following image shows a plasma concentration vs. time graph:

Two drugs may have the same rate of absorption but a different extent of absorption or bioavailability.

The factors upon which the extent of drug absorption depends are:

• Lipophilicity - If too lipophilic (e.g., acyclovir), the drug is not soluble enough to cross the water layer adjacent to the cell.
• Hydrophilicity - If too hydrophilic (e.g., atenolol), the drug cannot cross the lipid cell membrane.
questions.learning: Area under the curve — The area under the curve of plasma concentration vs. time curve gives the extent of absorption, which is calculated by the trapezoidal rule.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the size of the given blade used for incision and drainage of a superficial abscess?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 11

The size of the surgical blade shown is the 11-size blade (stab knife) that has a triangular shape with an oblique edge and a sharp-pointed tip.

Uses:

• Incision and drainage (I & D) of an abscess
• Insertion of drains and arteriotomy.

Other options:

Option A: The 10-size blade is used for skin incisions. It has a curved cutting edge that tapers to a pointed tip.

Option C: The 22-size blade is often used for abdominal incisions. It has a flat, unsharpened back edge and a curved front cutting edge.

Option D: The 15-size blade is used for minor surgical procedures (lipoma excision) and precise skin incisions. It is a smaller blade with a small cutting edge.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A boy was diagnosed with a medical condition, which is believed to have been passed down from his grandmother to his father, and now to him. What is the pattern of inheritance in this particular case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Autosomal dominance

The said disease shows an autosomal dominant pattern.

In the autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, both males and females are equally affected, and the affected individual has a 50% chance of passing it on to the offspring.

The following flow chart helps in making out the pattern of inheritance from a given pedigree chart.

Pearl PF0346: Pedigree chart for different inheritance patterns

Autosomal Dominant Disorders:

* With every autosomal dominant disorder, some patients do not have affected parents. Such patients owe their disorder to new mutations involving either the egg or the sperm from which they were derived.

* Clinical features can be modified by variations in penetrance and expressivity.

* In many conditions, the age at onset is delayed, and symptoms and signs may not appear until adulthood (as in Huntington disease).

X-linked Recessive Conditions:

* All sex-linked disorders are X-linked, and almost all are recessive.

* Several genes are located in the “male-specific region of Y;” all these are related to spermatogenesis.

* Males with mutations affecting the Y-linked genes are usually infertile, and hence, there is no Y-linked inheritance.

* An affected male does not transmit the disorder to his sons, but all daughters are carriers.

* Sons of heterozygous women have, of course, a one-in-two chance of receiving the mutant gene.

* Heterozygous females express the disorder partially because of random inactivation of one X chromosome.

Pearl PF1577: Autosomal Dominant Disorders

A Very Powerful DOMINANT Human

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 37-week primigravida has mild labor pains for 20 hours and the cervix is persistently 1 cm dilated but non-effaced. What would be the appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sedation and wait

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of either prolonged latent phase. The appropriate management is to sedate the patient and wait.

The first stage of labour consists of two phases :

* Latent phase: It is considered to begin at the time the woman first perceives regular uterine contractions and is characterized by gradual cervical change (up to 5 cm of cervical dilatation).

* Active phase: This follows the latent phase and is characterized by regular painful uterine contractions, cervical effacement, and rapid cervical dilatation from 5 cm to full dilatation.

A latent phase that exceeds 20 hours in primigravidae or 14 hours in multiparae is termed as a prolonged latent phase of labour. Bed rest is the preferred treatment unless there is any indication for expediting the delivery.

The presence of false labour pains for a long time may be confused with a prolonged latent phase. The differences between them include

True labour pains

Augmentation with oxytocin is done only in those patients who even after therapeutic rest continue to be in a prolonged latent phase. There is no indication of the cesarean section unless cephalopelvic disproportion is present. Amniotomy is not useful and should be avoided in patients with prolonged latent phases due to the risk of infections.

Pearl PF1871: Partograph

Partograph types:

WHO Modified Partograph (2000)

* No latent phase

* Vaginal examination: This should be done no less than every 4 hours to assess cervical dilatation, descent of the fetal head, and moulding of skull bones. More frequent examination is only undertaken if indicated.

* Charting starts at 4 cm of cervical dilation.

* Colour of liquor mentioned as C-clear, B-blood stained, M-meconium stained.

* Moulding mentioned:

* bones are separated and sutures can be easily felt - (0)

* bones touching (1+)

* bones overlapping but can be reduced(2+)

* bones severely overlapping and irreducible ( 3+).

* Alert line reflects the average rate of cervical dilation of the slowest quintile of term primigravidas, if dilation slows or ceases, the partograph plot will cross the alert line.

* Alert line: at 4 cm dilation and expected dilation of 1 cm/hour.

* Action line is 2–4 hours after the alert line, which prompts interventions to accelerate labor or perform cesarean delivery.

* Higher rates of perinatal mortality are associated with delays of 4 hours or more after the alert line.

* Contractions measured for a span of 10 min (duration noted) and measured every 30 min (1 square = half hour).

* Pulse: record every 30 minutes and mark with a dot (•).

* Blood pressure: record every 4 hours and mark with arrows, unless the patient has a hypertensive disorder or pre-eclampsia, in which case record every 30 minutes.

* Temperature: record every 4 hours.

WHO Composite Partograph: It is same as modified except for it has latent phase and charting done at 3 cm.

WHO Simplified Partograph: WHO further modified the partograph for use by skilled attendants in health centers. This simplified partograph is colour coded.

* The area to the left of the alert line in the cervicograph is coloured green, representing normal progress.

* The area to the right of the action line is coloured red, indicating dangerously slow progress in labour.

* The area in between the alert and action line is coloured amber, indicating the need for greater vigilance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents with fever, headache, cranial nerve palsy, and hydrocephalus. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination shows low glucose, elevated protein, and predominant lymphocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tuberculous meningitis

Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is a subacute or chronic meningitis caused by hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the meninges. It classically involves the basal meninges, leading to cranial nerve palsies, hydrocephalus, and vasculitis with cerebral infarction.

• The combination of fever, headache, cranial nerve palsy, hydrocephalus, and CSF findings of low glucose, high protein, and lymphocytic pleocytosis is characteristic of tuberculous meningitis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pyogenic meningitis: Acute presentation with neutrophilic predominance, markedly elevated protein, and low glucose.
• C. Fungal meningitis: Usually occurs in immunocompromised patients and has similar CSF findings but is less commonly associated with basal meningeal involvement and cranial nerve palsies in children.
• D. Viral meningitis: Typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis but normal CSF glucose with only mildly elevated protein.
questions.learning: Tuberculous meningitis Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is a subacute or chronic meningitis caused by hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the meninges.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the management of bacterial vaginosis (BV), certain antibiotics are not advised according to CDC guidelines. Which antibiotic is specifically not recommended for treating BV?
questions.explanation: Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) results from a shift in vaginal flora where lactobacilli are replaced by anaerobes like Gardnerella vaginalis. According to CDC guidelines, Erythromycin (Option D) is not recommended for the treatment of BV as it has poor activity against the causative organisms. The first-line recommended treatments include Metronidazole (Option A) (either oral or vaginal gel) and Clindamycin (Option C) (cream or oral). Tinidazole (Option B) is an alternative oral regimen recommended by the CDC. BV is diagnosed clinically using Amsel's criteria: thin white discharge, vaginal pH , positive "whiff" test, and "clue cells" on microscopy. Treatment is indicated for symptomatic women and all pregnant women to reduce the risk of preterm birth. Partners are generally not treated as it does not prevent recurrence. It is important to advise patients on Metronidazole to avoid alcohol to prevent a disulfiram-like reaction

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Arrange the following steps of ventricular action potential in the correct order.

A. Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels
B. Repolarizing K+ currents
C. Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels
D. Transient outward flow of potassium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C, D, A, B

The correct sequence for ventricular action potential is as follows:

C. Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels
D. Transient outward flow of potassium
A. Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels
B. Repolarizing K+ currents

The events of action potential occur in the following sequence:

• Phase 0: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus (rapid depolarization phase)
• Phase 1: Inactivation of voltage-gated Na+ channels and transient outward flow of K+ causes rapid repolarization (rapid repolarization phase)
• Phase 2: Opening of slow voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels causes the influx of calcium into the cells and results in the plateau phase (plateau phase)
• Phase 3: Opening of various K+ channels results in the efflux of K+ from the cells and results in slow repolarization (slow repolarization phase).
• Phase 4: Return to resting membrane potential
questions.learning: C, D, A, B — The correct sequence for ventricular action potential is as follows: C. Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels D.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An HIV-positive patient presents with the following finding. What is the diagnosis & WHO clinical stage of HIV?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oral candidiasis & WHO Stage 3

Oral candidiasis (Thrush) is categorized as WHO clinical stage 3.

Oral Candidiasis (Thrush), and oral hairy leukoplakia, are oral lesions characterized in WHO clinical Stage 3. They generally occur in patients with CD4+ T cell counts of <300/μL.

Differentiating oral candidiasis and oral hairy leukoplakia:

* Oral Candidiasis (Thrush) appears as a white, cheesy exudate, on an erythematous mucosa in the posterior oropharynx. The diagnosis is made by direct examination of pseudohyphal elements.

* Oral hairy leukoplakia presents as white, frondlike lesions, generally along the lateral borders of the tongue and sometimes on the adjacent buccal mucosa(image below). Despite its name, oral hairy leukoplakia is not considered premalignant. Lesions are associated with immunosupression and Ebstein-Barr virus (EBV).

Pearl PF1360: Clinical stages of HIV in children/ infants

Stage 1

* Asymptomatic

* Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy

Stage 2

* Unexplained persistent hepatosplenomegaly

* Papular pruritic eruptions

* Extensive wart virus infection

* Extensive molluscum contagiosum

* Recurrent oral ulcerations

* Unexplained persistent parotid enlargement

* Linear gingival erythema

* Herpes zoster

* Recurrent or chronic upper respiratory infections (otitis media, otorrhoea, sinusitis, tonsilitis)

* Fungal nail infections

Stage 3

* Unexplained moderate malnutrition not adequately responding to standard therapy

* Unexplained persistent diarrhea (14 days or more)

* Unexplained persistent fever (above 37.6 °C intermittent or constant, for longer than one month)

* Persistent oral candidiasis (after first 6-8 weeks of life)

* Oral hairy leukoplakia

* Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis/periodontitis

* Lymph node TB

* Pulmonary TB

* Severe recurrent bacterial pneumonia

* Symptomatic lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis

* Chronic HIV-associated lung disease including bronchiectasis

* Unexplained anemia (<8 g/dL), neutropenia (<0.5 x 109/L) or chronic thrombocytopenia (<50 × 109/L)

Stage 4

* Unexplained severe wasting, stunting or malnutrition not responding to standard therapy

* Pneumocystis pneumonia

* Recurrent severe bacterial infections (e.g., empyema, pyomyositis, bone or joint infection, meningitis, but excluding pneumonia)

* Chronic Herpes Simplex infection; (oro-labial or cutaneous of more than one month's duration or visceral at any site)

* Extrapulmonary TB and disseminated non-tuberculosis mycobacterial infection

* Kaposi Sarcoma

* Oesophageal candidiasis (or candidiasis of trachea, bronchi or lungs)

* Central nervous system toxoplasmosis (after one month of life)

* HIV encephalopathy

* Cytomegalovirus infection; retinitis or CMV infection affecting another organ, with onset at age over 1 month)

* Extrapulmonary cryptococcosis (including meningitis)

* Disseminated endemic mycosis (extrapulmonary histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis)

* Chronic cryptosporidiosis and isosporiasis

* Cerebral or B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma

* Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

* Symptomatic HIV-associated nephropathy or HIV-associated cardiomyopathy
questions.learning: Oral candidiasis & WHO Stage 3 Oral candidiasis (Thrush) is categorized as WHO clinical stage 3. Oral Candidiasis (Thrush), and oral hairy leukoplakia, are oral lesions characterized in WHO clinical Stage 3.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following are characteristic features of Turner syndrome, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prominent occiput

Turner syndrome (45,X) shows classic somatic features like webbed neck, shield chest with wide-spaced nipples, and short 4th metacarpal due to SHOX gene haploinsufficiency.

Classic Phenotype

• Short stature
• Webbed neck
• Shield chest
• Wide spaced nipples
• Streak ovaries → primary amenorrhea

Skeletal abnormalities and lymphatic dysgenesis are characteristic.

Prominent occiput is not a recognized feature of Turner syndrome and is more associated with certain craniofacial anomalies in other syndromes.

A. Prominent occiput- Incorrect statement

• Not a feature of Turner syndrome
• Seen more in:

• Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)
• Some neural tube defects

B. Short 4th metacarpal

• Gives knuckle dimpling when making a fist
• Also seen in:

• Pseudohypoparathyroidism

C. Webbed neck

• Due to cystic hygroma in fetal life
• Leaves behind lateral neck folds
questions.learning: Prominent occiput Turner syndrome (45,X) shows classic somatic features like webbed neck, shield chest with wide-spaced nipples, and short 4th metacarpal due to SHOX gene haploinsufficiency.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4 day old baby is active and feeding well. He has a bilirubin level of 8 mg/dl. What is the next step in the management of the baby?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Continue breastfeeding

Since this child has a bilirubin level of only 8 mg/dl on the 4th day, it points to physiologic jaundice. The child is active and feeding well, the mother should be encouraged to continue breastfeeding frequently and exclusively.

All the other options would be possible treatment choices if the child had pathological jaundice.

Physiological jaundice/Icterus neonatorum is due to increased bilirubin production from the breakdown of fetal red blood cells combined with transient limitation in the conjugation of bilirubin by the immature neonatal liver. It first appears on the 2nd or 3rd days usually peaks on the 4th day at 5-6 mg/dL and decreases to <2 mg/dL between the 5th and 7th days after birth.

On the other hand, in pathological jaundice, appearance is within the first 24 hours after birth and may be present at or beyond the age of 2 weeks in term babies and 3 weeks in preterms babies. There may be an elevated direct (or conjugated) bilirubin level. Jaundice visible on the palms and soles, unresponsiveness to phototherapy, and a rapid rise in bilirubin levels during phototherapy indicate pathological jaundice.

Phototherapy is initiated in babies with pathological jaundice when the bilirubin levels exceed the 95th percentile on the total serum bilirubin (TSB) normogram. Babies are kept at a distance of 30-45 cm from the UV lamp (460-490 nm) with eyes and gonads covered. It is avoided in babies with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to the risk of bronze-baby syndrome. Dehydration and hypocalcemia are potential complications and breastfeeding is encouraged.

Exchange transfusion (ET) is done in cases of bilirubin encephalopathy, Rh incompatibility with significant hemolysis, and bilirubin values exceeding TSB cutoffs for ET.
questions.learning: Continue breastfeeding Since this child has a bilirubin level of only 8 mg/dl on the 4th day, it points to physiologic jaundice. The child is active and feeding well, the mother should be encouraged to continue breastfeeding frequently and exclusively.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 3-day-old newborn baby boy is brought to the hospital with difficulty breathing, cyanosis and coughing whenever he is fed. The baby was born full-term via vaginal delivery, and his mother had an uneventful pregnancy. He had a birth weight of 2.8 kg and was discharged from the hospital after 48 hours of observation. On examination, the baby appears to be in respiratory distress, with increased work of breathing and decreased oxygen saturation levels. What would be the best contrast of choice for study?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iohexol

A neonate with cyanosis, coughing, and respiratory distress during feeding suggests tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF)/esophageal atresia.

For contrast study in suspected TEF:

• Use a non-ionic, water-soluble contrast (e.g., Iohexol)
• It is less irritating to lungs if aspirated
• Safer than hyperosmolar agents like Gastrografin

Avoid:

• Barium → causes severe chemical pneumonitis if aspirated
• Gastrografin → hyperosmolar, risk of pulmonary edema

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal bleeding. A transvaginal ultrasound reveals an endometrial thickness of 8.0 mm. What should be the next step in management? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Histopathological examination of curettage

Postmenopausal bleeding must always be evaluated for endometrial carcinoma until proven otherwise. Transvaginal ultrasound is used to measure endometrial thickness:

• Endometrial thickness ≤4 mm → low risk of malignancy
• Endometrial thickness >4 mm → requires endometrial sampling

This patient has:

• Postmenopausal bleeding
• Endometrial thickness of 8 mm

Therefore, the next step is histopathological evaluation of the endometrium by endometrial biopsy or curettage.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Hysterectomy is not performed before tissue diagnosis
• Progesterone therapy should not be started without excluding malignancy
• Follow-up sonography alone is inappropriate in symptomatic women with thickened endometrium

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not ligated for the control of epistaxis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Internal carotid artery

The internal carotid artery is not ligated in epistaxis control due to a high percentage of cerebral complications and high mortality.

The first step in treating epistaxis is to pinch the nose with the thumb and index finger for about 5 minutes. The patient should sit leaning slightly forward over a basin to spit out blood and breathe through the mouth (Hippocratic or Trotter’s method).

If the bleeding point is localized, cauterization can be done with electrocautery. In cases of uncontrolled bleeding or when the bleeding is posterior into the throat, anterior or posterior nasal packing may be required, respectively. If bleeding continues despite these measures, endoscopic procedures or vessel ligation can be considered.

The sphenopalatine artery is ligated first through a trans-nasal endoscope (Transnasal endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation). However, if the bleeding persists, maxillary artery ligation is done. If bleeding is still not controlled, external carotid artery ligation is done. It is important to note that if the bleeding site is located superior to the level of the middle turbinate, the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries should be ligated.
questions.learning: Internal carotid artery — The internal carotid artery is not ligated in epistaxis control due to a high percentage of cerebral complications and high mortality.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 60-year-old individual presents with an ulcer near the medial canthus of the eye. The lesion has rolled-out, beaded margins. Histopathological examination reveals nests of cells showing peripheral palisading. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of an ulcer with rolled-out, beaded margins located at the medial canthus is a classic presentation of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), the most common skin cancer. The diagnosis is confirmed by histopathology, which characteristically shows nesting of basaloid cells with a distinctive peripheral palisading pattern of nuclei. Regarding the distractors, Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Option A) typically presents with a scaly or keratinized appearance and lacks the pearly, beaded margins. A nevus (Option B) is a benign lesion and would not show these malignant histological features. Melanoma (Option D) usually presents as an irregularly pigmented macule or nodule rather than a slow-growing ulcer with palisading cells. BCC is slow-growing and rarely metastasizes but can be locally invasive. Therefore, the combination of clinical margins and palisading histology
questions.learning: The clinical description of an ulcer with rolled-out, beaded margins located at the medial canthus is a classic presentation of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), the most common skin cancer.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The punishment for the death of a patient by spurious drug:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Life imprisonment

The punishment for the death of a patient by a spurious drug is imprisonment for life.

In case of an adulterated, spurious, or any drug that when used by any person for or in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation, or prevention of any disease or disorder is likely to cause ill health or is likely to cause such harm on his body as would amount to grievous hurt within the meaning of Section 320 of IPC, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term that shall not be less than 3 years but that may extend to a term of life.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The following clinical examination was performed. What lesion would cause an exaggerated reflex?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Upper motor neuron

The examination being performed is the ankle jerk reflex, also known as the Achilles reflex. Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesions are associated with exaggerated deep tendon reflexes.

Hyperreflexia is a feature of UMN nerve injury. There may be an acute decrease in reflexes, but this is normally followed by hyperreflexia. LMN lesions on the other hand will present with depressed reflexes.

UMNs refer to corticospinal tract neurons and brainstem neurons that control spinal motor neurons. Injury to UMNs leads to:

• Spasticity
• Hypertonia
• Hyperreflexia
• Abnormal plantar extensor reflex (positive Babinski sign).

Other options:

Options A, B and D: Polyneuropathy/ neuropathic weakness and radiculopathy are types of lower motor neuron weakness and will not cause exaggerated reflexes.

The following image shows the Babinski reflex:
questions.learning: Upper motor neuron — The examination being performed is the ankle jerk reflex, also known as the Achilles reflex. Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesions are associated with exaggerated deep tendon reflexes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following statements about the Piezoelectric Effect are true, except:
options: Transducers produce waves by piezoelectric effect
Transducers receive waves by reverse piezoelectric effect
Lead Zirconate Titanate (PZT) has marked piezoelectric effect
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Used in USG and MRI

• Piezoelectric effect is the ability of certain crystals to generate an electric charge when mechanically stressed.
• In ultrasonography (USG), piezoelectric crystals are used in the transducer:

• Direct piezoelectric effect: returning echoes deform the crystal and generate electrical signals.
• Reverse piezoelectric effect: applied electrical energy causes the crystal to vibrate and produce ultrasound waves.

• Lead Zirconate Titanate (PZT) is the most commonly used piezoelectric material in ultrasound transducers.
• MRI does not use the piezoelectric effect for image generation; it is based on magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 23-year-old woman presents to the surgery out-patient with a left-sided breast lump which she noticed on self breast examination 3weeks ago. She has no other complaints. On palpation, the lump seems to be mobile and firm. Mammogram revealed a benign lesion. What is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reassurance and follow-up

The most probable diagnosis based on the clinical scenario is fibroadenoma and the best next step in the management of Fibroadenoma is to Reassure the patient and do regular follow-up.

Fibroadenoma is one of the aberrations of normal development and involution of the breast (ANDI). The most common age group affected is 15-25 years (early reproductive period) with a peak incidence in the second decade.

It arises from hyperplasia of a single lobule and presents as a well-circumscribed, smooth, firm, non-tender, freely mobile mass (mouse in the breast). It is a biphasic tumor consisting of fibroblastic stroma and epithelium-lined gland. Popcorn calcification is seen in mammography.

Option A : Biopsy is not required for Fibroadenoma unless there is a suspicion of Malignancy but based on the clinical and imaging findings the given lesion is benign.

Option C:Excision is not advised unless there is suspicious histology on fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC). Giant fibroadenomas are >5 cm in size, common in adolescent girls, and require excision by submammary incision.

Option D: Tamoxifen is a SERM-Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator used in the management of ER positive Breast carcinoma.
questions.learning: Reassurance and follow-up — The most probable diagnosis based on the clinical scenario is fibroadenoma and the best next step in the management of Fibroadenoma is to Reassure the patient and do regular follow-up.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which adverse effect is considered the most clinically significant with tamoxifen therapy?
questions.explanation: Tamoxifen is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) primarily used in the treatment of ER-positive breast cancer. It acts as an estrogen antagonist in breast tissue but has an agonistic (estrogen-like) effect on the uterus. This stimulation of the uterine lining can lead to endometrial hyperplasia, which significantly increases the risk of developing endometrial cancer. Tamoxifen actually decreases the risk of cancer in the opposite breast (Option A). In postmenopausal women, tamoxifen helps prevent osteoporosis due to its bone-protective estrogenic effects (Option B). While it can affect hormonal cycles, "endometrial hyperplasia" is the most clinically significant and well-documented serious side effect requiring routine gynecological monitoring. Patients on tamoxifen are typically advised to report any abnormal vaginal bleeding immediately to rule out malignancy. Thus, the tissue-specific estrogenic action on the endometrium is its most concerning toxicity
questions.learning: Tamoxifen is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) primarily used in the treatment of ER-positive breast cancer. It acts as an estrogen antagonist in breast tissue but has an agonistic (estrogen-like) effect on the uterus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 2-year-old undergoing chemotherapy for leukemia presents for vaccination counselling. Which of the following statements regarding live vaccines is accurate for this patient?
options: Live vaccines are contraindicated even after chemotherapy is completed.
Live vaccines can be safely administered during chemotherapy as long as the patient is afebrile.
Live vaccines are contraindicated in immunocompromised states, but household contacts can safely receive them.
Live vaccines are contraindicated in leukemia patients only if they are in remission.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Live vaccines are contraindicated in immunocompromised states, but household contacts can safely receive them.

• A child undergoing chemotherapy for leukemia is severely immunocompromised.
•

Live attenuated vaccines (e.g., BCG, OPV, MMR, varicella) are contraindicated in such patients due to risk of vaccine-derived infection.

•

Household contacts of immunocompromised patients can and should receive live vaccines (e.g., OPV replaced by IPV in India; MMR, varicella are safe).

• This indirectly protects the immunocompromised child by reducing exposure risk.
questions.learning: Live vaccines are contraindicated in immunocompromised states, but household contacts can safely receive them. • A child undergoing chemotherapy for leukemia is severely immunocompromised. • Live attenuated vaccines (e.g., BCG, OPV, MMR, varicella) are…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Arrange the following events in the sequence in which they occur, after 'p wave' in ECG:

1. a wave in JVP
2. First heart sound
3. Rapid filling of ventricles
4. T wave in ECG
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-2-4-3

The correct sequence of events that occur after the p-wave is 1-2-4-3, ie:-

a wave in JVP → First heart sound  → T wave in ECG  → Rapid filling of ventricles.

The sequence of the events in this question can be better understood with the following diagram:

• The p wave in the ECG represents atrial depolarization, which causes contraction of the atria, represented by the 'a' wave in the JVP. Atrial contraction causes final filling of the ventricles (fourth phase of ventricular diastole)
• Atrial contraction is followed by the closure of the mitral valve, which causes the first-heart sound.
• This is followed by the isovolumetric contraction of the ventricle, which causes c wave in JVP, due to bulging of the tricuspid valve. This is followed by the rapid ejection phase of the ventricle.
• The T wave of ECG occurs during ventricular repolarization, which is followed by the opening of the mitral valve, followed by rapid filling phase of the ventricle (second  phase of ventricular diastole).

Note: Passive rapid filling occurs as the mitral valve opens just before atrial contraction occurs.
questions.learning: 1-2-4-3 The correct sequence of events that occur after the p-wave is 1-2-4-3, ie:- a wave in JVP → First heart sound → T wave in ECG → Rapid filling of ventricles.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A smoker has hoarseness for 2 months. Examination shows an ulcerative lesion involving one vocal cord with fixation and cartilage invasion extending outside the larynx. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Total laryngectomy with neck dissection

This vignette describes T4a laryngeal carcinoma — the presence of vocal cord fixation with cartilage invasion and extension outside the larynx (into strap muscles/soft tissue) defines T4a disease per AJCC staging. This is a critical staging cutoff that dictates management.

Why A is correct:

• Once cartilage destruction/extralaryngeal spread is present, the tumor biology and bulk make it a poor candidate for organ-preservation strategies. Primary surgical management (total laryngectomy) with neck dissection (for nodal staging and clearance, given the high risk of occult/overt nodal metastasis) is standard of care.
• Adjuvant radiotherapy (± chemotherapy if positive margins or extracapsular nodal spread) typically follows.

Distractor-by-distractor breakdown:

| Option | Why it's wrong

| ------ | --------------

| B. Concurrent chemoradiation | This is the organ-preservation approach for T3 (or select early T4a without cartilage invasion) laryngeal cancer — the landmark trial defining this (RTOG 91-11) specifically excluded patients with cartilage invasion/massive tumor extension, since CRT alone yields poor local control and high rates of salvage laryngectomy in this subgroup. Cartilage invasion is a classic "trap" cue meant to push you away from chemoradiation.

| C. Radiotherapy alone | Inadequate as monotherapy for T4 disease — local control rates are poor once cartilage is invaded.

| D. Laryngectomy with radiotherapy | Close, but incomplete/imprecise — omits neck dissection, which is standard given T4 disease's high nodal metastasis risk, and doesn't specify the adjuvant (post-operative) sequencing. In a single-best-answer format, B is more precise and complete.

High-yield pearl:

• "Cartilage invasion = surgery, not organ preservation."
• Any stem mentioning cartilage invasion, extralaryngeal extension, or vocal cord fixation with bulky disease should trigger total laryngectomy ± neck dissection, not chemoradiation — regardless of how tempting "voice-preserving" options look.
questions.learning: Total laryngectomy with neck dissection — This vignette describes T4a laryngeal carcinoma — the presence of vocal cord fixation with cartilage invasion and extension outside the larynx (into strap muscles/soft tissue) defines T4a disease per AJCC staging.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Who is chiefly responsible for registering eligible couples for family planning services and maintaining their records under the national health system?
questions.explanation: Under the Indian National Health System, the Multipurpose Worker (Female), also known as the Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM), is primarily responsible for maintaining the Eligible Couple Register (ECR) at the sub-centre level. Her duties include identifying married women aged 15–49, recording their contraceptive choices, and ensuring proper follow-up. While Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA) (Option A) play a vital role in motivating couples and distributing contraceptives, they do not maintain the official legal records for registration. Village Health Guides (Option C) focus on basic health education and minor treatments at the village level but are not involved in formal family planning registration. Anganwadi Workers (Option D) primarily focus on nutrition and preschool education under the ICDS program and are not responsible for the ECR. Consequently, the ANM remains the key figure for family planning record-keeping within the administrative health framework
questions.learning: Under the Indian National Health System, the Multipurpose Worker (Female), also known as the Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM), is primarily responsible for maintaining the Eligible Couple Register (ECR) at the sub-centre level.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the nasal fracture.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chevallet fracture

A Chevallet fracture usually results from a blow to the nose from below. This fracture line runs vertically. It extends from the anterior nasal spine upwards to the junction of the bony and cartilaginous dorsum of the nose.

Injuries to the nasal septum can result from trauma to the nose from the front, side, or below. The septum may get buckled on itself, fracture vertically and horizontally, or get crushed

A Jarjaway fracture (option B) results from a blow to the nose from the front. The fracture line runs horizontally backwards. It begins just above the anterior nasal spine and extends just above the junction of the septal cartilage with the vomer.

Early recognition and treatment of septal injuries are crucial, including drainage of hematomas.

Dislocated or fractured septal fragments should be repositioned and supported between mucoperichondrial flaps using mattress sutures and nasal packing. Nasal pyramid fractures often coincide with septal fractures and should be treated simultaneously.

Neglecting injuries to the septum can lead to deviations in the cartilaginous nose, as well as asymmetry in the nasal tip, columella, or nostrils.

Other options:

Option C: Simple fractures refer to the fractures of the nasal bone without displacement. Simple fracture describes the nature of the fracture.

Option D: Le Fort fractures are a group of fractures that affect the midface of the skull and collectively involve a partial or complete separation of the midface from the skull.
questions.learning: Chevallet fracture — A Chevallet fracture usually results from a blow to the nose from below. This fracture line runs vertically.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman with primary infertility is found to have a 5–6 cm ovarian endometrioma on pelvic ultrasonography. She desires future fertility. Which of the following is the most appropriate fertility-preserving treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Laparoscopic cystectomy (cyst wall excision)

For women with ovarian endometrioma ≥4 cm who desire future fertility, the preferred fertility-preserving treatment is laparoscopic cystectomy (complete excision of the cyst wall).

Compared with drainage or ablation, laparoscopic cystectomy:

• Improves spontaneous pregnancy rates
• Reduces recurrence of endometrioma
• Provides tissue for histopathological examination
• Relieves pain more effectively

Why not the other options?

• A. Oophorectomy: Not appropriate in a young nulliparous woman as it reduces ovarian reserve and fertility.
• B. Cauterization (ablation) of the cyst wall: Higher recurrence rates and lower spontaneous pregnancy rates than cystectomy.
• C. Transvaginal cystectomy: Not the standard approach; laparoscopic surgery is preferred.
questions.learning: Laparoscopic cystectomy (cyst wall excision) For women with ovarian endometrioma ≥4 cm who desire future fertility, the preferred fertility-preserving treatment is laparoscopic cystectomy (complete excision of the cyst wall).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A young athlete presented with chest pain and dyspnea. His brother passed away due to sudden cardiac death. He is diagnosed with HCM. A harsh systolic murmur is heard in the left sternal border. Which of the following will increase the murmur?

HCM - Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Valsalva

The clinical vignette of an athlete with chest pain and dyspnea whose family history is suggestive of sudden cardiac death due to HCM and a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border are all in favour of HCM murmur. It increases in intensity while performing the Valsalva manoeuvre.

The murmur of HCM is an ejection systolic murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border.

The intensity of the mid-systolic murmur is

Increased by -Valsalva strain phase, Standing posture, and exercise
Decreased by - Squatting, passive leg raising, and handgrip.

Valsalva manoeuvre involves the performance of forced expiration against a closed glottis.

HCM is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young adults. It is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy of >15mm on ECHO. The left ventricular myocardium is poorly compliant. This leads to abnormal diastolic filling and intermittent ventricular outflow obstruction, i.e.,  primarily diastolic dysfunction.

Gross features of HCM:

• Massive myocardial hypertrophy usually without ventricular dilation
• Asymmetric septal hypertrophy- disproportionate thickening of the ventricular septum relative to the left ventricle free wall
• Banana-shaped left ventricle- due to bulging of the ventricular septum into the lumen

The image given below shows changes in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy compared to a normal heart. HCM shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and a thickened left ventricle wall.

Histologic features of the HCM:

Massive myocyte hypertrophy- with transverse myocyte diameters frequently greater than 40 μm, normal is approximately 15 μm.
Myofiber disarray- haphazard disarray of bundles of myocytes, individual myocytes, and contractile elements in sarcomeres within cells
Interstitial fibrosis and replacement fibrosis
The image given below is a histologic section of cardiac muscle showing myocyte disarray and extreme hypertrophy seen in an abnormal HCM septum.

Pathophysiology:

HCM is characterized by reduced stroke volume due to impaired diastolic filling. Approximately 25% of patients with HCM have dynamic obstruction to the left ventricular outflow as the anterior mitral leaflet moves toward the ventricular septum during systole. The compromised cardiac output in conjunction with a secondary increase in pulmonary venous pressure explains the exertional dyspnea seen in these patients.

Major clinical problems in HCM are atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus formation leading to embolization and stroke, cardiac failure, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden death.

ECG - findings:

Prominent abnormal Q waves
P wave abnormalities
Left axis deviation
Deeply inverted T waves

Echocardiography:

LV wall thickness ≥15 mm
Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
LVOT obstruction
The management options in patients with HCM:

Beta-blockers
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
Disopyramide
Drugs to be avoided in patients with significant LVOT obstruction:

Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
Nitroglycerin
Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, ARBs
Diuretics
Preventive intra-cardiac defibrillator is indicated for patients with HCM and documented cardiac arrest or sustained ventricular tachycardia.

Note: Valsalva maneuver decreases the intensity of all murmurs except MVP (mitral valve prolapse) and HCM.
questions.learning: Valsalva — The clinical vignette of an athlete with chest pain and dyspnea whose family history is suggestive of sudden cardiac death due to HCM and a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border are all in favour of HCM murmur.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with severe pain and swelling in his knee joint since 10 days. He also complains of pain and discomfort during urination. He says that he had diarrhoea one month ago and he has been unwell since then. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reactive arthritis

The given scenario describes acute arthritis following an infection which is also associated with urethritis and generalized malaise. These features are suggestive of reactive arthritis.

Reactive arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthritis that occurs as a consequnece of a recent enteric or urogenital infection. It is associated with HLA B27. It is also associated with extra-articular manifestations:

* Urogenital- urethritis, prostitis, cervicitis

* Ocular- conjuctivitis, anterior uveitis

* Mucocutaneous- oral ulcers, keratoderma blennorrhagica, circinate balanitis

It presents as a triad of arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis in some patients.
questions.learning: Reactive arthritis — The given scenario describes acute arthritis following an infection which is also associated with urethritis and generalized malaise.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the given organism?
questions.explanation: The provided image (located at the top of Page 9) displays characteristic large, smooth-walled, club-shaped macroconidia arranged in clusters, which are diagnostic features of Epidermophyton floccosum. A key distinguishing feature of this genus is the absence of microconidia, which separates it from other common dermatophytes. This fungus is a frequent cause of tinea cruris, tinea pedis, and tinea unguium. Microsporum gypseum (A) produces thin-walled, ellipsoidal macroconidia with up to six cells. Microsporum audouinii (B) typically shows very rare conidia and is known for pectinate hyphae. The genus Trichophyton (D) is characterized by abundant microconidia and rare, smooth, pencil-shaped macroconidia. Because the visual evidence specifically highlights the "beaver-tail" or club-shaped morphology and lacks smaller spores, the identification is definitively Epidermophyton. Morphology of dermatophytes is a high-yield topic for FMGE, and correctly differentiating between these three main genera based on microscopic conidial structure is essential for clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: The provided image (located at the top of Page 9) displays characteristic large, smooth-walled, club-shaped macroconidia arranged in clusters, which are diagnostic features of Epidermophyton floccosum.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During delivery, the head is delivered, but the shoulders become stuck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency occurring when the fetal head has delivered but the anterior shoulder becomes wedged behind the mother's pubic symphysis. This is often recognized by the "turtle sign," where the head retracts against the perineum. Cephalopelvic Disproportion (CPD) (Option A) refers to a mismatch between fetal size and the pelvic canal, leading to failure of the head to engage or descend, rather than entrapment after head delivery. Occipito-posterior position (Option B) involves a malpresentation of the head that can slow labor but does not inherently cause the shoulders to stick. Breech presentation (Option D) occurs when the buttocks or feet are the presenting part, which is the opposite of the described cephalic delivery. Shoulder dystocia requires immediate maneuvers such as McRoberts maneuver (hyperflexion of maternal thighs) and suprapubic pressure to dislodge the shoulder. This is a high-risk scenario for brachial plexus injury or neonatal hypoxia
questions.learning: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency occurring when the fetal head has delivered but the anterior shoulder becomes wedged behind the mother's pubic symphysis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A single mutation in a nucleotide base pair resulting in a termination codon is known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nonsense mutation

A single mutation in a nucleotide base pair resulting in a termination codon is known as a nonsense mutation.

A codon is a sequence of three bases present on the mRNA (messenger RNA), and it codes for amino acids. Out of the 64 codons possible, only 61 code for the 20 amino acids. Three codons, UAA, UAG, and UGA  do not code for any of the 20 amino acids. These are known as nonsense/punctator/termination/stop codons and function as translation termination signals. The UGA codon is traditionally considered a stop codon, but it codes for selenocysteine (21st amino acid).

The tRNA (transfer RNA) contains the anticodon which recognizes specific codons present on the mRNA. The sequence of the anticodon is complementary to the codon. The pairing between the codon and anticodon can wobble at the third base. For example, GGU, GGC, and GGA all pair with the anticodon CCI. The wobble phenomenon along with degeneracy reduces the effect of mutations.

A mutation involving a single nucleotide base is known as a point mutation. A nonsense mutation is a type of point mutation where a codon previously coding for an amino acid is changed to a stop codon. This results in premature termination of translation and the formation of a truncated protein. mRNA containing premature stops are removed by the nonsense-mediated degradation pathway.

Other options:

Option A: A missense mutation is a type of point mutation where the new codon, formed by the changed base, codes for a different amino acid.

Option C: Stop mutation is a term that can be used interchangeably with nonsense mutation. Here, nonsense mutation is the best answer.

Option D: Silent mutations are point mutations where the new codon formed still codes for the same amino acid as the codon before the mutation.
questions.learning: Nonsense mutation — A single mutation in a nucleotide base pair resulting in a termination codon is known as a nonsense mutation. A codon is a sequence of three bases present on the mRNA (messenger RNA), and it codes for amino acids.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man seeks treatment for erectile dysfunction and prefers a medication that does not require precise timing before sexual activity because of an unpredictable schedule. Which phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitor would be most suitable due to its longer duration of action?
questions.explanation: Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors are the first-line pharmacological treatment for erectile dysfunction. Among the commonly prescribed agents, Tadalafil is distinct due to its exceptionally long half-life of approximately 17.5 hours. This provides a "window of opportunity" that lasts up to 36 hours, earning it the nickname "the weekend pill." This prolonged duration allows for greater spontaneity, as the patient does not need to time the dose immediately before sexual activity. In contrast, Sildenafil (Option A) and Vardenafil (Option C) have much shorter durations of action, typically lasting 4–6 hours. Avanafil (Option D) is characterized by a very rapid onset of action (15 minutes) but has a shorter duration compared to Tadalafil. All PDE-5 inhibitors require sexual stimulation to be effective and are contraindicated in patients taking nitrates due to the risk of severe hypotension. Tadalafil’s unique pharmacokinetic profile makes it the preferred choice for patients seeking flexibility and long-lasting efficacy
questions.learning: Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors are the first-line pharmacological treatment for erectile dysfunction. Among the commonly prescribed agents, Tadalafil is distinct due to its exceptionally long half-life of approximately 17.5 hours.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which unit is used to express the strength of the magnetic field?
questions.explanation: The "Tesla" (T) is the international unit used to measure the strength of a magnetic field. In clinical practice, most MRI scanners operate at magnetic field strengths of 1.5T or 3.0T. Higher field strengths generally provide a better signal-to-noise ratio, allowing for higher-resolution images and faster scan times. Hounsfield Units (Option B) are used in "CT scans" to represent tissue density (radio-density). Kilohertz (Option C) is a unit of frequency used in signal processing and radio waves. Hg or Mercury (Option D) is a unit used to measure "pressure," such as blood pressure or intracranial pressure. Understanding the strength of an MRI magnet is essential for safety protocols, as higher Tesla magnets create stronger attractive forces on ferromagnetic objects and can interact more intensely with implanted medical devices. The safety zone surrounding an MRI scanner is strictly maintained to prevent accidents related to this powerful magnetic field
questions.learning: The "Tesla" (T) is the international unit used to measure the strength of a magnetic field. In clinical practice, most MRI scanners operate at magnetic field strengths of 1.5T or 3.0T.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common reason for women discontinuing the use of an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD)? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Abnormal uterine bleeding

The most common reason for discontinuation of intrauterine contraceptive devices (IUCDs), especially copper-containing IUCDs, is abnormal uterine bleeding. Common bleeding-related complaints:

• Menorrhagia
• Intermenstrual bleeding
• Increased menstrual duration
• Dysmenorrhea

Copper IUCDs increase local endometrial inflammatory response, which can increase menstrual blood loss and cramping. Other complications of IUCDs:

• Expulsion
• Pelvic inflammatory disease (rare)
• Ectopic pregnancy (rare overall, but relatively more likely if pregnancy occurs with IUCD in situ)

Important distinction:

• IUCDs do not commonly cause infertility
• Uterine rupture is not a typical complication
questions.learning: Abnormal uterine bleeding — The most common reason for discontinuation of intrauterine contraceptive devices (IUCDs), especially copper-containing IUCDs, is abnormal uterine bleeding.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following methods is regarded as the gold standard for the measurement of intraocular pressure?
questions.explanation: The Goldmann Applanation Tonometer (GAT) is universally recognized as the gold standard for the measurement of intraocular pressure (IOP). It operates on the Imbert-Fick principle, which states that the pressure inside a sphere is equal to the force needed to flatten a fixed area of its surface. GAT is highly accurate and is the reference against which all other tonometers are calibrated. Option A (Gonioscope) is used to examine the drainage angle of the eye, not measure pressure. Option C (Hertel's) is used to measure the degree of proptosis (eyeball protrusion). Option D (Tonopen) is a portable handheld device useful for bedridden patients or irregular corneas but is not as accurate as GAT. GAT measurements can be influenced by central corneal thickness (CCT); therefore, clinicians often adjust readings based on pachymetry. Accurate IOP measurement is fundamental in the diagnosis and management of glaucoma to prevent irreversible optic nerve damage

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: The serotonergic cell bodies of the analgesia pathway projecting to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord are located in which part of the brain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nucleus raphe

The descending pain inhibitory (analgesia) pathway modulates pain transmission at the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.

Key components of this pathway:

1.      Periaqueductal gray (PAG) in the midbrain receives pain signals.

2.      PAG activates neurons in the nucleus raphe magnus (raphe nuclei) in the medulla.

3.      Serotonergic neurons from the nucleus raphe descend to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.

4.      These neurons stimulate enkephalin-releasing interneurons, which inhibit pain transmission from primary afferent neurons.

Important neurotransmitters:

• Serotonin (5-HT) from raphe nuclei
• Enkephalins in the spinal cord

Other structures:

• Locus ceruleus: provides noradrenergic modulation of pain.
• PAG: initiates the descending analgesic pathway but is not the source of serotonergic projections.
questions.learning: Nucleus raphe — The descending pain inhibitory (analgesia) pathway modulates pain transmission at the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Periaqueductal gray (PAG) in the midbrain receives pain signals.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Match the following intracranial bleed:
options: A -i B-ii C- iii D- iv
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A -ii B-iv C-i D-iii

Epidural hematoma:

Noncontrasted axial computed tomography scan showing a lenticular area of increased density in left parietal region.

• Typically occur in the groove of the middle meningeal artery associated with temporal bone fractures that have resulted in a tear of middle meningeal artery.
• They tend to not to cross suture lines of the skull.

Subdural hematoma:

A non contrasted computed tomography scan of acute subdural hematoma shows a cresentric area of increased density in the right posterior parietal region between brain and the skull. An area of intraparenchymal haemorrhage also seen. In addition, mass effect causes a midline shift to left.

• They can cross suture lines but they do not cross the tentorium or falx.
• Can be acute or chronic

Subarachnoid haemorrhage:

A non contrasted axial computed tomography scan shows the blood as areas of increased density near the base of the brain shows blood in Texaco star pattern formed blood radiating from suprasellar cistern into the sylvian fissures and anterior interhemispheric fissure.

• Most often accompanied by severe sudden onset headache.
• Can really be visualised in acute stage, when blood is radiographically dense (whiter) than the CSF.

Intracereberal haemorrhage:

Non contrast computed tomography shows a large area of fresh blood appearing white in the region of right thalamus. Blood is denser than CSF so settles dependently.

This settling is not seen with subarachnoid or interparenchymal blood.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the contraceptive shown in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Female condom

The given image shows a female condom. It consists of a pouch made of polyurethane which is 17 cm in length with a flexible ring at each end. The inner ring at the closed end is smaller than the outer ring.

The inner ring is inserted at the apex of the vagina and the outer ring remains outside. It covers the cervix, the entire vagina, and external genitalia. Hence, it provides protection against HIV and STDs. It has a failure rate of 5–15 per 100 woman-years, which is higher than that of a male condom.

It can be fitted by the patient hours before intercourse, and easily removed soon after. It covers the cervix, vagina, and external genitalia and is protective against sexually transmitted diseases. It can also be worn in the puerperal period, unlike the cervical diaphragm.

The female condom should not be used along with a male condom because if worn together they may slip, tear, or become displaced.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: The confusion assessment test is used in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Delirium

The confusion assessment test is used in the detection of delirium.

Delirium is reported to occur in a wide range of mechanically ventilated ICU patients and can be detected by the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM)-ICU or the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist.

These tools are used to ask patients to answer simple questions and perform simple tasks and can be used readily at the bedside.
