questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The enzyme that is common for both glycolysis and gluconeogenesis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phosphoglycerate kinase

The enzyme phosphoglycerate kinase is common for both glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. Phosphoglycerate kinase catalyzes the conversion of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate, which is a reversible step involved in both the processes.

Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are processes that are reverse of each other. All the reversible steps of these two processes are catalyzed by the same enzymes, therefore are common to both.

The irreversible steps of glycolysis are catalyzed by the following enzymes:

• Hexokinase
• Phosphofructokinase
• Pyruvate kinase

The irreversible steps of gluconeogenesis are catalyzed by the following enzymes:

• Pyruvate carboxylase
• Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase
• Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
• Glucose-6-phosphatase
questions.learning: Phosphoglycerate kinase — The enzyme phosphoglycerate kinase is common for both glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. Phosphoglycerate kinase catalyzes the conversion of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate, which is a reversible step involved in both…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Most likely to present with unilateral hydronephrosis?
questions.explanation: Hydronephrosis, the dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces, can be unilateral or bilateral depending on the site of obstruction. Obstructions occurring "at or below" the level of the bladder neck will typically cause "bilateral" hydronephrosis because they affect the common drainage pathway for both kidneys. Phimosis (Option A), Posterior Urethral Valves (Option B), and Urethral Strictures (Option C) are all distal obstructions that lead to bladder distension and bilateral reflux or backup into both ureters and kidneys. A retrocaval ureter (Option D), also known as a circumcaval ureter, is a rare congenital anomaly where the right ureter passes behind the inferior vena cava. This leads to extrinsic compression and "unilateral" (right-sided) obstruction and hydronephrosis. Other causes of unilateral hydronephrosis include ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction or a stone trapped in one ureter. Therefore, among the choices provided, only the retrocaval ureter is a purely unilateral obstructive lesion
questions.learning: Hydronephrosis, the dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces, can be unilateral or bilateral depending on the site of obstruction. Obstructions occurring "at or below" the level of the bladder neck will typically cause "bilateral" hydronephrosis because…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: All of the following increases gastric acid secretion except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serotonin

All of the above increase gastric acid secretion except serotonin.

Serotonin is localized in the enterochromaffin cells of the gastrointestinal (GI) mucosa and within neurons of the GI tract. Serotonin inhibits gastric acid secretion. It stimulates the production and release of gastric and colonic mucus. Serotonin acts as an enteric neurotransmitter and increases intestinal motility.

The main factors that stimulate gastric secretion are acetylcholine, gastrin, and histamine. Parasympathetic stimulation releases Ach which stimulates the secretion of

• pepsinogen by peptic cells
• hydrochloric acid by parietal cells
• mucus by mucous cells.

Both gastrin and histamine strongly stimulate acid secretion by parietal cells but have little effect on other cells.

The stomach mucosa has two important types of tubular glands:

• The oxyntic (gastric) glands secrete hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen, intrinsic factor, and mucus.
• The pyloric glands secrete mainly mucus for protection of the pyloric mucosa from the stomach acid. They also secrete the hormone gastrin.

Note- Serotonin released from the small intestine triggers vomiting by stimulation of 5HT3 receptors. Therefore, 5HT3 antagonists like ondansetron are used as antiemetics.
questions.learning: Serotonin All of the above increase gastric acid secretion except serotonin. Serotonin is localized in the enterochromaffin cells of the gastrointestinal (GI) mucosa and within neurons of the GI tract.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following insulins has a cloudy preparation and requires resuspension prior to injection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lente

Cloudy insulin preparations contain insulin crystals or protamine, which settle on standing and therefore must be gently resuspended (rolled between the palms) before injection to ensure uniform dosing.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• A. Lente ✓

• An intermediate-acting insulin containing zinc-insulin crystals.
• It is a cloudy suspension and requires resuspension before administration.

• B. Glargine ✗

• A long-acting insulin analogue.
• It is a clear solution and should not be mixed or resuspended.

• C. Detemir ✗

• A long-acting insulin analogue.
• It is a clear solution and does not require mixing.

• D. Degludec ✗

• An ultra-long-acting insulin analogue.
• It is also a clear solution.
questions.learning: Lente Cloudy insulin preparations contain insulin crystals or protamine, which settle on standing and therefore must be gently resuspended (rolled between the palms) before injection to ensure uniform dosing.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the formula for sensitivity?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity is a measure of a diagnostic test's ability to correctly identify individuals who truly have the disease (the true positive rate). It is calculated by dividing the number of true positives (TP) by the total number of diseased individuals, which includes true positives and false negatives (FN). Option A represents the Positive Predictive Value (PPV), which measures the probability that a person with a positive test actually has the disease. Option C is the formula for Specificity, measuring the ability to correctly identify healthy individuals (TN / [TN + FP]). Option D does not correspond to a standard epidemiologic measure. High sensitivity is vital for screening tests to ensure as many cases as possible are detected, minimizing the risk of missing diseased individuals due to false negatives
questions.learning: Sensitivity is a measure of a diagnostic test's ability to correctly identify individuals who truly have the disease (the true positive rate). It is calculated by dividing the number of true positives (TP) by the total number of diseased individuals, which…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Not seen in decompression sickness
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hemodilution

Hemodilution is not seen in decompression sickness. Instead, hemoconcentration is seen in decompression sickness.

Hemodilution refers to the dilution of blood, usually due to excessive fluid intake or other medical conditions, but it is not a feature of decompression sickness.

Decompression sickness (DCS) is a condition that occurs when a person ascends too quickly after being exposed to high-pressure environments (such as deep-sea diving), causing nitrogen bubbles to form in the bloodstream and tissues.

Other options

Option A: Vision changes or loss can occur in DCS due to gas bubbles affecting the optic nerve or retinal circulation, leading to temporary or permanent vision impairment.

Option B: Gas bubbles in DCS can also affect the auditory system, leading to hearing loss or tinnitus, a common feature of the condition.

Option D: Decompression sickness can lead to coagulopathy, which refers to abnormal blood clotting due to the formation of nitrogen bubbles that disrupt the vascular system, potentially causing bleeding or clotting disorders.
questions.learning: Hemodilution Hemodilution is not seen in decompression sickness. Instead, hemoconcentration is seen in decompression sickness.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with bronchial asthma on long-term inhaled corticosteroid therapy presents with whitish plaques over the tonsils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral Candidiasis

Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are a common cause of oropharyngeal candidiasis (oral thrush) due to local immunosuppression, allowing overgrowth of Candida albicans. Patients typically present with white, curd-like plaques over the oral mucosa, tongue, or tonsils that can be scraped off, leaving an erythematous base. The risk can be minimized by using a spacer and rinsing the mouth after each inhalation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Oral candidiasis: ✔ Correct. Characterized by scrapable white plaques, commonly associated with ICS use, HIV infection, diabetes, and prolonged antibiotic therapy.
• B. Aphthous ulcer: Presents as painful, shallow ulcers with a yellow base and erythematous halo, not white plaques.
• C. Leukoplakia: A non-scrapable white patch, considered a premalignant lesion, commonly associated with tobacco use.
• D. Lichen planus: Presents with lacy white reticular lesions (Wickham striae) or erosive lesions, not removable plaques.

| White Oral Lesion | Characteristic Feature

| ----------------- | ----------------------

| Oral candidiasis | Scrapable white plaques, erythematous base; ICS, HIV, diabetes

| Leukoplakia | Non-scrapable white patch, premalignant

| Oral lichen planus | Lacy white Wickham striae

| Aphthous ulcer | Painful ulcer with yellow base, not a white plaque
questions.learning: Oral Candidiasis Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are a common cause of oropharyngeal candidiasis (oral thrush) due to local immunosuppression, allowing overgrowth of Candida albicans.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden chest pain and dyspnea, and pulmonary embolism is suspected. Which imaging modality is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: For a patient with suspected acute Pulmonary Embolism (PE), CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is currently the gold-standard and most definitive imaging modality (Option B). CTPA allows for the direct visualization of emboli within the pulmonary arterial system with high sensitivity and specificity. Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scans (Option C) are used primarily when CT is contraindicated (e.g., in severe renal failure), but they are less definitive. Doppler echocardiography (Option A) can show signs of right heart strain but cannot confirm the presence of a clot itself. MR pulmonary angiography (Option D) is less validated and more time-consuming than CTPA. Therefore, because of its rapid availability, high accuracy, and ability to provide alternative diagnoses, CTPA remains the definitive diagnostic tool of choice in modern emergency departments. Finding a filling defect on CTPA is sufficient to initiate therapeutic anticoagulation
questions.learning: For a patient with suspected acute Pulmonary Embolism (PE), CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is currently the gold-standard and most definitive imaging modality (Option B).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for fetal heart acceleration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carotid body chemoreceptors

Amongst the given options, the best answer for the site responsible for Fetal heart acceleration is Carotid body chemoreceptors>Aortic baroreceptors>Autonomic brain stem regulation.

Though the brainstem is critical to mediating this reflex, the primary stimulus for initiating the changes in the heart rate is initiated by the carotid chemo and baro receptors, especially the chemoreceptor which is highly sensitive to the changes in O2 levels in the blood. It plays a permissive role on fetal heart rate acceleration.

Arterial chemoreceptors in the carotid arteries>aortic arch, respond to low pH levels and decreased oxygen saturation. These chemoreceptors detect instances of significant fall in blood oxygen levels, setting off the peripheral chemoreflex and heightening both parasympathetic and sympathetic neural activities. The activation of the parasympathetic branch leads to a swift decline in Fetal Heart Rate (FHR), a clinical manifestation identified as intrapartum decelerations. Concurrently, the sympathetic branch prompts significant peripheral vasoconstriction across a range of vascular territories, which results in the elevation of arterial blood pressure, ensuring continuous perfusion to essential organs.

The permissive action on the FHR acceleration comes in instances of alleviated hypoxemia, detected by the chemoreceptors in the carotid body and aortic arch, suppressing the peripheral chemoreflex, leading to a reduction in parasympathetic and sympathetic neural activities. Deactivation of the parasympathetic branch results in a swift increase in Fetal Heart Rate (FHR), typically seen clinically as an increase in intrapartum accelerations.
questions.learning: Carotid body chemoreceptors Amongst the given options, the best answer for the site responsible for Fetal heart acceleration is Carotid body chemoreceptors>Aortic baroreceptors>Autonomic brain stem regulation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 27-year-old male patient suffers trauma to his eye with vegetative matter. He now presents with a corneal ulcer, alongside hypopyon and satellite lesions. He reports mild pain with photophobia and redness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fungal keratitis

The given clinical scenario most likely describes fungal keratitis with ulceration.

A fungal corneal ulcer is usually caused by trauma with vegetative or organic matter. Signs are more pronounced than symptoms. The corneal ulcer appears dry.

Causative organisms:

* Aspergillus

* Fusarium

* Candida albicans

Signs of a fungal ulcer:

* Irregular margins of the ulcer.

* Presence of satellite lesions surrounding the ulcer.

* An immune ring (Wesseley) may be seen around the ulcer due to the deposition of the immune complexes.

* Slough is usually dry, with feathery borders surrounded by a yellow line of demarcation.

* Hypopyon may be present or absent. If present, it is thick, and immobile due to the direct invasion of the fungal hyphae into the anterior chamber.

Treatment:

* Topical drugs: These include topical natamycin, voriconazole or amphotericin B drops which are effective against Aspergillus and Fusarium. Nystatin is effective against Candida.

* Systemic drugs: Severe ulcers with hypopyon, perforation or suspected endophthalmitis might warrant the use of oral antifungal agents such as ketoconazole or voriconazole.
questions.learning: Fungal keratitis — The given clinical scenario most likely describes fungal keratitis with ulceration. A fungal corneal ulcer is usually caused by trauma with vegetative or organic matter.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
If the contractility of the heart is decreased, which of the following is seen

ESV: End-systolic volume

EDV: End-diastolic volume
options: End diastolic volume and pressure curve shifts to left without change in slope
Slope changes in ESV pressure curve
End systolic volume and pressure curve shifts to left without change in slope
Slope changes in EDV and pressure curve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Slope changes in ESV pressure curve

If the contractility of the heart is decreased, slope changes in the ESV pressure curve are seen.

To answer this question, we will first understand the volume-pressure diagram and the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR) during cardiac cycle.

Volume-pressure diagram during the cardiac cycle

The volume pressure diagram plots the changes in the pressure and volume in the left ventricle that occurs during the cardiac cycle. The x-axis shows the changes in ventricular volume, while the y-axis shows the changes in ventricular pressure.

It has the following phases.

Phase I- This phase is called the period of filling and extends between points A and B. Point A is at the end of systole when the ventricular volume is about 50 mL. This volume is called end-systolic volume. The pressure at this point is about 2 to 3 mm Hg. These volume and pressure go on increasing as the blood from the atrium flows to the ventricle during diastole. At the end of diastole, marked by point B, the ventricle will have a volume of around 120 mL. This volume is called end-diastolic volume. The pressure is slightly raised to 5-7mm Hg.

Phase II- It is the phase of isovolumetric contraction, and extends between points B and C. At the end of diastole (point B), a slight increase in the ventricular pressure closes the mitral valve, and contraction starts. The ventricle contracts while both mitral and aortic valves are closed. Therefore, the pressure within the ventricle slowly rises without any changes in the volume.

Phase III- It is the phase of ejection and extends between point C and point D. Point C is the place where the aortic valve opens. The pressure within the left ventricle rises slowly during isovolumetric contraction until it is sufficient to open the aortic valve. Once the aortic valve opens, blood within the left ventricle is ejected into the aorta. This decreases the volume of the left ventricle, while increasing the pressure within the ventricle.

Phase IV- It is the period of isovolumetric relaxation. It extends between points D and A. At the end of the ejection (Point D), the aortic valve closes. However, the ventricular relaxation continues despite closed aortic and mitral valves. Therefore, the ventricular pressure continues to fall while the volume remains the same. The ventricle returns to its starting point, with about 50 ml of blood left in the ventricle and pressure of about 2 to 3 mm Hg

End-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR)

ESPVR is the maximum pressure that can be developed by the ventricle at the end-systolic volume. It is determined by the line intersecting the upper left corners of the loops. This line can be extended down to the x-axis. The slope of this line is called as ESPVR slope.

Now coming to the question, when the contractility of the heart is decreased, the force of ejection decreases leading to decreased stroke volume, and increased end-systolic volume. Therefore, the volume-pressure diagram shifts to the right. If the diagram shifts to the right, then ESPVR also changes, leading to a change in the slope of the ESPVR curve.

Other options:

Options A and D- End diastolic volume and pressure curve (EDPVR) mainly assesses the compliance of the ventricle, rather than contractility. The slope of this curve increases when the compliance decreases, and vice versa.

Option C- ESPVR shifts to right with change in slope.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with a lump in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. Histopathological examination of the mass showed signet ring appearance. What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Colloidal carcinoma

The given clinical scenario and histopathological findings are suggestive of colloid/mucinous carcinoma of the breast.

Colloidal carcinoma is an invasive breast carcinoma, which shows intra and extracellular mucin deposition. In intracellular type, nuclei are pushed to the peripherally to form signet ring appearance.

Extracellular type shows tumor cells with faint nuclei arranged in clusters floating in pools/lakes of mucin on histopathological examination.

Other options:

Option B: Papillary carcinoma consists of true papillae with a leaf-like arrangement of fibrovascular tissue, lined by the tumor cells.

Option C: Medullary carcinoma of the breast shows sheets of highly pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates and pushing border.

Option D: Phyllodes tumor shows the presence of nodules of proliferating stroma covered by epithelium (leaf-like architecture).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which neuromuscular blocking agent undergoes Hofmann elimination?
questions.explanation: Atracurium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that is unique because it undergoes Hofmann elimination. Hofmann elimination is a spontaneous, non-enzymatic chemical degradation that occurs at physiological temperature and pH. Because this process is independent of kidney and liver function, atracurium (and its isomer cisatracurium) is the drug of choice for inducing muscle relaxation in patients with renal or hepatic failure. Pancuronium (Option A), Rocuronium (Option B), and Vecuronium (Option C) are primarily cleared by the liver or kidneys; their duration of action is significantly prolonged in patients with organ dysfunction, increasing the risk of prolonged paralysis. A byproduct of atracurium's degradation is laudanosine, which can theoretically cross the blood-brain barrier and cause seizures at very high concentrations. Cisatracurium is often preferred as it produces less laudanosine and does not cause histamine release. Understanding these specific metabolic pathways is fundamental for choosing safe anesthetic agents for medically complex surgical patients
questions.learning: Atracurium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that is unique because it undergoes Hofmann elimination. Hofmann elimination is a spontaneous, non-enzymatic chemical degradation that occurs at physiological temperature and pH.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient underwent gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma. Which of the following vitamins needs to be supplemented in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B12

A patient who has undergone gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma needs to be supplemented with vitamin B12.

Vitamin B12 absorption is a complex process that relies on several factors. Intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein secreted by the parietal cells in the stomach, is essential for this process. Gastric acid and pepsin release vitamin B12 from dietary proteins, allowing it to bind with cobalophilin in the saliva. In the jejunum, cobalophilin is broken down, freeing vitamin B12 to bind with intrinsic factor. This complex is then absorbed in the distal ileum through specific receptors.  Following gastrectomy, the production of intrinsic factor is impaired due to the removal of gastric tissue, making vitamin B12 absorption difficult. Therefore, vitamin B12 supplementation is necessary after gastrectomy to prevent deficiency.

Other complications of gastrectomy include:

• Nutritional deficiencies- Iron deficiency anemia (most common), Vitamin B12 deficiency, and osteoporosis
• Dumping syndrome: early and late
• Diarrhea
• Duodenal stump leak/blow out
• Bile reflux gastritis and esophagitis
• Gall stones
• Roux syndrome
questions.learning: Vitamin B12 — A patient who has undergone gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma needs to be supplemented with vitamin B12. Vitamin B12 absorption is a complex process that relies on several factors.

Modified Mallampati classification:

• Class II: Soft palate and fauces seen, tip of uvula not visible.
• Class III: Soft palate, base of uvula visible.
• Class IV: Soft palate not visible at all. Only hard palate visible.

Classes 3 and 4 are difficult intubation situations.
Initially, the Mallampatti scoring system (1985) had only 3 classes. This was modified by Samsoon and Young to include class 4. Later class 0 was also added.

questions.text: Analyzing the statements given about cystic masses of the neck, identify the false statement:

Thyroglossal cyst moves upwards on swallowing and tongue protrusion
Fluctuation is positive in branchial cysts
questions.explanation: The statement claiming that a Type 3 branchial fistula opens on the cricopharyngeus is false (Option A). Anatomically, a second branchial fistula opens into the tonsillar fossa, while a third branchial fistula (and fourth) has its internal orifice located in the pyriform fossa of the larynx. The cricopharyngeus is a muscle of the esophagus and is not the standard site for these embryological remnants. All other statements are true: Cystic hygroma is a lymphatic malformation filled with clear lymph (Option B). A Thyroglossal cyst is unique because it is attached to the hyoid bone, meaning it moves upwards with both swallowing and tongue protrusion (Option C). A branchial cyst is a fluid-filled lesion, so the clinical fluctuation test is positive (Option D). Therefore, based on the specific anatomical tracts of branchial anomalies, the description of the internal opening in Option A is the definitive error

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which substance serves as a mediator in chronic inflammation?
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation is characterized by a long duration, tissue destruction, and attempts at healing through fibrosis. TGF-beta (Transforming Growth Factor-beta) is a critical anti-inflammatory cytokine and a central mediator in chronic inflammation. It plays a dual role: it suppresses the inflammatory response by inhibiting lymphocyte activity, while simultaneously acting as the most potent inducer of fibrosis by stimulating fibroblast migration and collagen synthesis. IL-1 (Option A) and TNF-alpha (Option B) are classic mediators of acute inflammation, responsible for initiating the vascular response, fever, and acute-phase reactant production. While they can be present in chronic inflammation (as in autoimmune diseases), TGF-beta is specifically characteristic of the chronic phase's reparative and fibrotic processes. The persistence of TGF-beta can lead to pathological scarring in organs, such as liver cirrhosis or pulmonary fibrosis. Understanding these mediators is essential for developing therapies to control chronic inflammatory diseases and prevent permanent organ damage resulting from excessive fibrotic remodeling
questions.learning: Chronic inflammation is characterized by a long duration, tissue destruction, and attempts at healing through fibrosis. TGF-beta (Transforming Growth Factor-beta) is a critical anti-inflammatory cytokine and a central mediator in chronic inflammation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman with no other comorbid conditions develops preeclampsia. She enquires about the cause of her condition. The doctor explains that it is due to the failure of the invasion of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spiral artery by extravillous trophoblasts

Preeclampsia occurs due to the failure of the invasion of extravillous trophoblasts into the spiral artery.

The spiral artery supplies blood to the endometrium. In normal pregnancy, there is an invasion of the extravillous trophoblasts (specifically, endovascular trophoblasts) into the walls of the spiral arteries. In the first wave of invasion (10–12 weeks), endovascular trophoblasts invade up to decidual segments. In the second wave (16–18 weeks), they invade up to the myometrial segments.

This vascular remodeling process replaces the endothelial lining and the muscular arterial wall with endovascular trophoblasts. This results in the distension of the spiral arterioles, thereby transforming them into a low resistance, low pressure, and high flow system.

In preeclampsia, the failure of the second wave of endovascular trophoblastic invasion into uterine vessels leads to decreased placental perfusion.

The images below show the sequential branching of the uterine artery and the vascular remodeling in preeclampsia respectively,

Other contributory etiological factors include genetic factors and maladaptive responses to fetal antigens and cardiovascular changes in pregnancy.

The basic pathology in preeclampsia is endothelial dysfunction leading to decreased nitric oxide production and vascular spasm. This leads to ischemic changes that result in necrosis, hemorrhage, and end-organ damage.

Changes leading to vasospasm and endothelial dysfunction include:

• Reduced vasodilatory prostaglandin PGI2 and increased vasoconstrictor thromboxane (TXA2)
• Reduced angiotensinase activity and increased sensitivity of vessels to angiotensin II, which is a vasopressor
• Increased production of endothelin 1, a potent vasoconstrictor
• Increased inflammatory mediators (tumor necrosis factor- α, interleukins) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) causing endothelial injury
• Increased antiangiogenic factors like soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase I (SFlt-1) and soluble endoglin (sEng)

The definitive treatment of pre-eclampsia is the termination of pregnancy at ≥37 weeks.
questions.learning: Spiral artery by extravillous trophoblasts Preeclampsia occurs due to the failure of the invasion of extravillous trophoblasts into the spiral artery.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old child from a malaria-endemic area presents with fever, altered sensorium, seizures, and coma, without any focal neurological deficits on examination. A peripheral blood smear shows Plasmodium falciparum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of fever, seizures, and unarousable coma in the presence of Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia is the classic definition of cerebral malaria. This is the most severe neurological complication of malaria and is a major cause of death in children in endemic regions. The diagnosis is clinical, supported by the absence of other obvious causes of encephalopathy (such as meningitis). Tubercular (Option A), Viral (Option B), and Fungal (Option D) meningitis are important differentials for fever and coma, but they typically require a longer subacute history or specific CSF findings. Furthermore, the confirmed presence of P. falciparum on a blood smear in a symptomatic child strongly points toward malaria as the primary cause. Cerebral malaria is a medical emergency requiring immediate intravenous artesunate to reduce parasite load and supportive care to manage intracranial pressure and seizures
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of fever, seizures, and unarousable coma in the presence of Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia is the classic definition of cerebral malaria.

questions.text: A tympanometry graph is displayed below. The arrow points to a sharp peak at pressure = 0 daPa. What type of tympanogram does the arrow represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type As

The given tympanograph is a type As tympanogram.

Tympanometry: It is used in evaluating the status of the middle ear and the functioning of the eustachian tube. Results of tympanometry are plotted in the form of a tympanogram with:

* Compliance on the Y axis (ease of mobility of TM)

* Middle ear pressure on the X axis (regulated by eustachian tube)

Principle: When a sound wave strikes the tympanic membrane, some of the sound energy is absorbed while the rest is reflected. A stiffer tympanic membrane would reflect more sound energy than a compliant one.

Tympanometry has also been used to evaluate the function of the eustachian tube in cases of intact or perforated tympanic membranes. A pressure of -200 or +200 mm H₂O is created in the middle ear, and the person is asked to swallow 5 times in 20 seconds. The ability to equilibrate the pressure indicates normal tubal function. It is also used in evaluating the patency of the grommet inserted in the tympanic membrane for treating serous otitis media.

By charting the compliance of the tympano-ossicular system against various pressure changes, different types of graphs called tympanograms are obtained. They are as follows:

Pearl PF1978: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)

A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its frequency can be increased or decreased by 5Hz.

The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram.

Normal thresholds:

* For AC: 15 dB

* For BC: 25 dB

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the cell seen in the image below?
questions.explanation: The cell shown is a Reed–Sternberg (RS) cell, which is the diagnostic hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma. RS cells are large, abnormal B-lymphocytes, typically binucleated or bilobed, with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli that give the characteristic “owl-eye” appearance. Faggot cells (Option A) are seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) and contain multiple Auer rods bundled together, giving a stick-like or “faggot” appearance. Mott cells (Option C) are plasma cells filled with Russell bodies, appearing as multiple round, grape-like cytoplasmic inclusions due to accumulated immunoglobulins, commonly seen in plasma cell dyscrasias. Sézary–Lutzner cells (Option D) are atypical T-lymphocytes with cerebriform (brain-like) nuclei, characteristic of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides/Sézary syndrome). Thus, the distinctive morphology of a large binucleated cell with owl-eye nucleoli confirms the diagnosis of a Reed–Sternberg cell, which is essential for distinguishing Hodgkin lymphoma from non-Hodgkin lymphomas

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the grade of tympanic membrane retraction shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Grade 2

The given image shows retraction in both pars tensa and pars flaccida. It is grade 2 retraction as the pars flaccida retraction is in contact with the neck of malleus while that in parts tensa is in contact with the incus.

Tympanic membrane can be divided into two parts. Pars tensa makes up most of the tympanic membrane. It is peripherally thickened to form annulus tympanicus (a fibrocartilaginous ring). It contains the cone of light. Pars flaccida (Shrapnell's membrane), is slightly pinkish and is located above the lateral process of malleus.

Tympanic membrane retraction can be either in the pars tensa or pars flaccida.

Tos classification is used to grade the retraction in pars flaccida or attic retraction

• Stage 1: The par flaccida is dimpled but not in touch with the malleus.
• Stage 2: The tympanic membrane is in contact with the neck of malleus and the entire extent of retraction can be visualized.
• Stage 3: The retraction is not visible fully, and there may be partial erosion of bony attic wall.
• Stage 4: The retraction is definite erosion of the bony attic wall and the full extent of retraction is not visible.

Due to difficulty in distinguishing the latter two, they are grouped as stage 3/4.

Sade classification is used to grade the retraction in pars tensa

• Stage 1: The tympanic membrane is retracted but not in touch with the incus
• Stage 2: The tympanic membrane is in contact with the long process of the incus
• Stage 3: Middle ear atelectasis - the tympanic membrane is in contact with the promontory, but not adherent. It can be raised from the promontory with suction
• Stage 4: Adhesive otitis media - the tympanic membrane is adherent to the promontory

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient has a blood glucose level of 200 mg/dL and GFR of 90 ml/min. What is the amount of glucose excreted if the transport maximum of the patient is as shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 30 mg/min

The amount of glucose excreted in the above scenario is 30 mg/min.

Calculation:

Step 1: Calculate total filtered glucose:

In this question,

• GFR = 90 ml/min
• Plasma glucose concentration = 200 mg/dL= 2 mg/ml (1 dL=100 ml).
• Total filtered glucose = GFR X Plasma glucose concentration.

= 90 ml/min X 2 mg/ml
= 180 mg/min.

Step 2: Check transport maximum:

In the above question transport maximum is 150 mg/min.

Step 3: Calculate the excretion:

Excretion = Total filtered glucose - Total reabsorbed glucose (Transport Maximum)

= 180-150 mg/min
= 30 mg/min

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old patient presents with long- standing projectile vomiting accompanied by significant weight loss. Based on this clinical scenario, which metabolic abnormality is most likely to be present?
options: Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hyponatremia
Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypernatremia
Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypercalcemia
Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic acidosis with hyponatremia
questions.explanation: Chronic projectile vomiting, classically seen in gastric outlet obstruction, leads to massive loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) along with potassium (K⁺) and sodium (Na⁺). The loss of hydrogen ions (H⁺) and chloride ions (Cl⁻) directly produces hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. To compensate for volume depletion, the kidneys activate the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS). This causes sodium reabsorption in exchange for increased urinary excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions, resulting in paradoxical aciduria and worsening hypokalemia. Prolonged vomiting also leads to hyponatremia (Option A) due to direct sodium loss and dilution from ADH-mediated water retention. Hypernatremia (Option B) and hypercalcemia (Option C) are not typical features. Metabolic acidosis (Option D) occurs with diarrhea due to loss of bicarbonate, not with vomiting. Definitive management includes surgical correction of the obstruction along with aggressive fluid resuscitation using isotonic saline and potassium replacement
questions.learning: Chronic projectile vomiting, classically seen in gastric outlet obstruction, leads to massive loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) along with potassium (K⁺) and sodium (Na⁺).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Major contributor for amniotic fluid post 20 weeks is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fetal urine

Fetal urine is the major contributor to amniotic fluid post 20 weeks.

Amniotic fluid is present in the amniotic cavity which is the space between the epiblast (ectoderm) and trophoblast. The volume of the amniotic fluid increases with pregnancy and reaches a maximum at term. It is contributed by:

• Early pregnancy - ultrafiltrate of maternal plasma (option D).
• Second trimester - the extracellular fluid that diffuses through the fetal skin (option B) and thus reflects the composition of fetal plasma.
• After 20 weeks - keratinization of fetal skin prevents diffusion across the skin. Hence, fetal urine forms amniotic fluid.

Note: Fetal kidneys start producing urine at 12 weeks (8–11 weeks), and by 18 weeks, they produce 7 to 14 mL per day.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. The radiological image shows the following findings. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Orbital blowout fracture

The given CT image shows the characteristic "hanging drop sign" indicating a blowout fracture of the orbital wall.

Hanging drop/tear-drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow-out" fracture, which represents the orbital contents herniating through the floor of the orbit into the maxillary antrum.

Blow-out orbital fractures are caused by trauma to the orbit by a large, rounded object, e.g cricket ball, a human fist, etc. This force can cause the displacement of the eyeball backwards and an increase in intraorbital pressure. This leads to fracturing at the weakest point of the orbital wall (orbital floor and sometimes medial wall). Clinical signs are periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis and subconjunctival haemorrhage (later stages).

Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10-14 days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotic

Indications for surgery in a "blow-out" fracture are as follows:

* Diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma

* A fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum

* Incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in globe retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze

* Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

The most useful projection for detecting an orbital floor fracture is the Water’s view.

Other options:

Option B: Zygomatic fracture Involves zygomatic bone (cheekbone), producing “flattened cheek” and step deformity at the infraorbital rim.

Option C:  Maxillary fracture Involves alveolar process / maxillary sinus walls. Here, the fracture is confined to the orbital floor.

Option D: Le-fort 1 fracture is a horizontal fracture of the maxilla, separating the upper alveolar part (upper teeth + palate) from the rest of the face.

Pearl PF1981: Le-Fort's classification of Maxillary Fracture

Le-Fort I is a transverse fracture of the maxilla

* Fracture line passes through the lower part of nasal septum, maxillary antra and the pterygoid plates

* It separates palate from the rest of the face leading to floating teeth or palate

* Also called Guerin’s fracture.

Le-Fort II is a pyramidal fracture

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, lacrimal bone, floor of the orbit, upper part of the maxillary sinus and pterygoid plates

* X-ray or CT appears like hanging maxilla

* It is associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

Le-Fort III is craniofacial dysjunction i.e., facial skeleton completely disconnected from its cranial attachment

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, ethmo-frontal junction, superior orbital fissure, lateral wall of the orbit, fronto-zygomatic and temporo-zygomatic sutures and the upper part of pterygoid plates

* It is also associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

questions.text: The maximum dose of PGF2 alpha in postpartum hemorrhage is? (NEET PG 2019)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 mg

Prostaglandin F2 alpha (PGF2α), also known as carboprost, is used for the treatment of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) due to uterine atony. The therapeutic regimen and maximum dosage are crucial for effective management and patient safety.

• Dose and Administration: The approved dose for treating uterine atony with PGF2α is 0.25 mg administered intramuscularly (IM).
• Maximum Dose: The maximum cumulative dose is 2 mg. This is achieved by administering a total of 8 doses of 0.25 mg each.
• Dosing Interval: These doses can be repeated at intervals of 15 to 90 minutes, depending on the clinical response and the patient's condition.

Contraindications

• Bronchial Asthma: PGF2α can cause bronchoconstriction, which makes it contraindicated in patients with bronchial asthma.
• Suspected Amniotic Fluid Embolism: Due to its potential to cause pulmonary airway and vascular constriction, it is also contraindicated in cases of suspected amniotic fluid embolism.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following are incorrectly paired?
options: CCK - I cells, Duodenum and jejunum
Motilin - M cells, Duodenum and Jejunum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Motilin - M cells, Duodenum and Jejunum

Motilin is secreted by the Mo cells(not M cells) in the stomach, small intestine, and colon

Motilin is a gastrointestinal hormones that is secreted by enterochromaffin cells and Mo cells in the stomach, small intestine, and colon. It mediates its action via G-protein-coupled receptors on enteric neurons in the duodenum and colon. It produces contraction of smooth muscle in the stomach and intestines in the period between meals.

M cells are microfold cells are located in the epithelium covering mucosa-associated lymphoid tissues of the small intestine such as the Peyer's patches (PPs). Their function is to transport luminal antigens to the underlying lymphoid follicles to initiate an immune response.

Gastrin is secreted by G cells of the antrum, duodenum, and jejunum. It stimulates gastric acid secretion and mucosal growth.

Secretin is secreted by the S cells of the duodenum. Its primary function is to promote the secretion of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice by the ductal cells of the pancreas and duodenum. This secretion is poor in enzymes.

Cholecystokinin (CCK) is secreted by I cells of the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. It stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, pancreatic bicarbonate secretion, gallbladder contraction, and growth of the exocrine pancreas. It also inhibits gastric emptying.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Image shown below depicts a condition in the children which is an accurate statement?
questions.explanation: The image depicts Kwashiorkor, a form of severe acute malnutrition primarily caused by a severe deficiency in dietary protein despite some caloric intake. The characteristic clinical finding is "edema" (swelling), which leads to the protuberant, "pot-belly" appearance seen in the children. This occurs because low plasma protein (hypoalbuminemia) causes fluid to leak into the interstitial spaces and the abdominal cavity. Marasmus (Options C and D) is caused by a global deficiency of all calories (protein and carbohydrates); it presents with an "old man" appearance, severe muscle wasting, and a "baggy pants" appearance of the skin, but no edema or pot-belly. Therefore, while both are forms of protein-energy malnutrition, the specific protuberant abdomen caused by edema is the hallmark of Kwashiorkor. Treatment involves slow, therapeutic refeeding with high-protein formulas and management of concurrent infections
questions.learning: The image depicts Kwashiorkor, a form of severe acute malnutrition primarily caused by a severe deficiency in dietary protein despite some caloric intake.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with a history of tuberculosis presents with abdominal distension and pedal edema. On examination, his neck veins are prominent, and a chest X-ray is provided. Which of the following findings is most likely to be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation—history of tuberculosis, abdominal distension, pedal edema, and raised JVP—along with chest X-ray findings suggests cardiac tamponade due to tuberculous pericardial effusion. A key diagnostic feature of cardiac tamponade is pulsus paradoxus, defined as an exaggerated fall in systolic blood pressure (>10 mmHg) during inspiration. The option given (SBP falls from 80 to 60 mmHg) clearly represents this phenomenon. Pathophysiology : In tamponade, fluid accumulation in the pericardial sac compresses the heart, impairing ventricular filling. During inspiration, increased venous return to the right heart further compromises left ventricular filling, causing a marked drop in systolic BP. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Pulsus bisferiens: Seen in aortic regurgitation/HOCM, not tamponade (B) Kussmaul breathing: Seen in constrictive pericarditis, not tamponade (D) Fine crepitations: Suggest pulmonary edema, not a key feature here Thus, the most likely finding is pulsus paradoxus → option (C)
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation—history of tuberculosis, abdominal distension, pedal edema, and raised JVP—along with chest X-ray findings suggests cardiac tamponade due to tuberculous pericardial effusion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) used in preoperative staging of gastro-oesophageal tumours is to detect:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Distant metastatic disease

Positron Emission Tomography (PET-CT) is used in the preoperative staging of gastro-esophageal cancers primarily to detect occult distant metastases, thereby avoiding unnecessary surgery in patients with advanced disease.

Why not the other options?

• B. Extension into stomach: Best assessed by endoscopy and CT/endoscopic ultrasound (EUS).
• C. Local spread: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is the investigation of choice for T staging.
• D. Lymph node status: EUS ± FNA and CT are superior for regional nodal assessment.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman with schizophrenia presents to the gynecology department after a sexual assault and is uncertain about continuing the pregnancy. According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Amendment Act, 2020, up to what gestational age is termination of pregnancy legally permitted for mentally ill rape survivors?
questions.explanation: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 (based on the 2020 bill), significantly expanded the legal window for abortion in India for certain vulnerable categories of women. Specifically, the upper gestational limit for MTP was increased from 20 to 24 weeks for survivors of sexual assault, rape, or incest, as well as for women with mental illness or physical disabilities. For a mentally ill rape victim, as described in the scenario, the 24-week limit applies. Option A (20 weeks) was the previous legal limit. Option B (22 weeks) and Option D (28 weeks) do not correspond to the specific legal thresholds defined in the act. Termination beyond 24 weeks is generally only permitted in cases of substantial fetal abnormalities as determined by a Medical Board. Therefore, the 24-week threshold is the correct legal standard for this patient

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 63-year-old female presented to the OPD with abdominal pain and a tense and tender swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. What is the most likely diagnosis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Strangulated femoral hernia

The above clinical scenario of a tense and tender swelling present lateral and below the pubic tubercle is suggestive of a femoral hernia. The femoral hernia traverses the femoral canal, which lies medial to the femoral vein.

A femoral hernia occurs in both males and females, but it is more common in females. It will pass through the femoral ring proximally to enter the femoral canal. The femoral canal is bound by the femoral vein laterally, the inguinal ligament anteriorly, and the pelvic bone with iliopectineal ligament (Cooper's) and lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's) medially. Lacunar ligament has a sharp unyielding edge that prevents the reduction of the femoral hernia. The incidence of strangulation in femoral hernias is high because of the narrowness of the neck of the sac and the rigidity of the femoral ring.

All patients with unexplained bowel obstruction should be examined properly for a femoral hernia. Surgery is the only treatment for femoral hernia, and these patients should be treated on priority because of the high risk of strangulation. The surgical approaches which are used are:

• Low approach (Lockwood): suitable when there is no risk of strangulation; bowel can't be inspected and resected in this approach
• Inguinal approach (Lotheissen)
• High approach (McEvedy): suitable for emergency situations when the risk of bowel strangulation is high
• Laparoscopic approach: both TEP and TAPP approaches can be used; the laparoscopic approach is recommended in women.

Other Options:

Option B: Inguinal hernia is above and medial to the pubic tubercle. Another structure that is useful in differentiating between inguinal and femoral hernia is inguinal ligament. An inguinal hernia leaves the abdominal cavity just above the inguinal ligament and a femoral hernia leaves just below the inguinal ligament.

Option C: In case of Intussusception, patients present with cramping abdominal pain, palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass, vomiting, and passage of red currant jelly stools.

Option D: Adhesions can lead to intestinal obstruction, but there won't be any swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle,.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents with complaints of greenish-frothy vaginal discharge for 1 month. On examination vulvovaginal erythema is noticed. On saline microscopy, motile organisms are seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trichomoniasis

The clinical vignette and microscopic findings are suggestive of trichomoniasis.

The clinical features include vaginal discharge which is profuse, thin, slightly green in color, and frothy. It may be associated with vaginal irritation, dysuria, and increased frequency. Cervical inflammation with punctate hemorrhagic spots known as the strawberry cervix is typically seen in trichomoniasis, caused by Trichomonas vaginalis. It is a sexually transmitted infection. Motile trichomonads are seen on wet mount examination.

The below image shows the strawberry cervix seen in trichomoniasis.

Other options:

Option B: Bacterial vaginosis is caused by an alteration in the normal vaginal flora and presents a malodorous grey-white discharge. It is diagnosed using Amsel's criteria, where at least three of the four following criteria should be present to confirm the diagnosis:

* Homogenous vaginal discharge

* Vaginal pH > 4.5

* Amine-like odor on adding KOH (Whiff test positive)

* Clue cells (>20% of cells)

Option C: Chlamydial cervicitis may present with severe abdominal pain with high fever, dyspareunia, prolonged menstrual cycles, and intermenstrual bleeding can be elicited. On examination, cervicitis with a yellow, cloudy, mucoid discharge can be seen from the os. The cervix tends to bleed easily when scraped.

Option D: Candidiasis is caused by infection with Candida albicans and presents with pruritus, burning, and dysuria with vulvar erythema, edema, and excoriations. A curdy white discharge will be present.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All the following viral vaccines are types of Live vaccines except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatitis B vaccine

Viral vaccines can be live attenuated or inactivated/recombinant.

Live attenuated viral vaccines:

• Measles vaccine
• Rotavirus vaccine
• Varicella vaccine

Non-live (inactivated/recombinant) vaccine:

• Hepatitis B vaccine → recombinant subunit vaccine (HBsAg produced using yeast)

Key points:

• Live vaccines produce strong, long-lasting immunity
• They are contraindicated in immunocompromised individuals
• Recombinant vaccines are safer but may require booster doses

questions.text: A pregnant woman with cardiac disease is on warfarin therapy. When will the final switch to heparin be advised?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 36 weeks

The final switch to heparin in a pregnant women is advised at 36 weeks of pregnancy and is continued till 7 days postpartum.

This switch is made from warfarin to heparin at 36 weeks, as warfarin is a strong anticoagulant which can cause post partum hemorrhage in the mother at the time of labour and can also cross the placenta into the fetal blood and can increase the risk of intracranial hemorrhage in the fetus

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the factors would suggest a risk for a patient with TIA developing stroke in the future according to ABCD2 scoring?
options: SBP >130 mm Hg and DBP > 80 mm Hg
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diabetes

According to the ABCD2 scoring system, which is commonly used to assess the short-term risk of stroke following a transient ischemic attack (TIA), diabetes would suggest a higher risk factor.

Age more than 60 years, SBP more than 140 or DBP more than 90 mmHg, and duration of TIA of 10-59 minutes or more than 60 minutes are other criteria included in the ABCD2 scoring system.

TIA is defined as episodes of stroke symptoms that last for only a brief period of time (<24 hours). The ABCD2 scoring system is most frequently used to calculate the short-term risk of stroke after TIA.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old female patient presents with the complaint of a palpable painless mass in the left breast. On examination, the mass was highly mobile, measured 3x3 cm, and was rubbery in consistency. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fibroadenoma

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of fibroadenoma of breast. It presents as painless, palpable lump and is rubbery in consistency.

Fibroadenoma is one of the aberrations of normal development and involution of the breast (ANDI). The most common age group affected is 15-25 years (early reproductive period) with a peak incidence in the second decade.

Fibroadenomas can be classified into 2 types:

* Without complex features - classified as a non-proliferative condition

* With complex features -

* Associated with cysts > 0.3 cm, sclerosing adenosis, epithelial calcifications, or papillary apocrine change

* Classified as proliferative changes without atypia

Fibroadenomas are benign tumours, although neoplasia may develop in the epithelial elements within them. Cancer in a newly discovered fibroadenoma is exceedingly rare; 50% of neoplasias that involve fibroadenomas are LCIS, 35% are invasive carcinomas, and 15% are intraductal carcinoma.

It arises from hyperplasia of a single lobule and presents as a well-circumscribed, smooth, firm, non-tender, freely mobile mass (mouse in the breast). It is a biphasic tumor consisting of fibroblastic stroma and epithelium-lined gland. Popcorn calcification is seen in mammography.

Excision is not advised unless there is suspicious histology on fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC). Giant fibroadenomas are >5 cm in size, common in adolescent girls, and require excision by submammary incision.

The ultrasound image depicts a well-circumscribed oval mass with uniform hypoechogenicity.
questions.learning: Fibroadenoma — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of fibroadenoma of breast. It presents as painless, palpable lump and is rubbery in consistency.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby presents with a characteristic skin lesion, as shown in the image below. Identifying this finding is important for appropriate management and prognosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a Port Wine Stain (Nevus Flammeus), a permanent capillary malformation. It is characterized by its large size, flat surface (macular), and distinct, non-fading reddish-purple color that often grows proportionately with the child. Unlike other birthmarks, it does not regress spontaneously. A Naevus simplex (Option C), often called a "stork bite," is smaller, pinker, and typically fades within the first two years of life. Capillary (strawberry) hemangiomas (Option D) and cavernous hemangiomas (Option B) are raised, vascular tumors that usually appear shortly after birth and eventually undergo involution. Critically, a Port Wine Stain in the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (as seen in the image) requires screening for Sturge-Weber syndrome, which can involve glaucoma and intracranial calcifications. Therefore, based on the flat, permanent appearance, Port Wine Stain is the correct diagnosis

questions.text: An asymptomatic patient presents with a reducible hernia below the inguinal ligament. Which of the following is the most appropriate management to consider? (NEET PG 2016)
options: Watchful waiting and follow-up if symptomatic
Surgical repair on the next elective list
Emergency surgical repair with exploration of the bowel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Surgical repair on the next elective list

A femoral hernia occurs below the inguinal ligament through the femoral ring. While this patient's hernia is currently asymptomatic and reducible, femoral hernias have rigid boundaries (femoral vein laterally, inguinal ligament superiorly, pubic arc inferiorly, and lacunar ligament medially), creating a high risk for strangulation. Femoral hernias warrant prompt elective surgical intervention regardless of symptoms, as they have a significantly higher risk of complications compared to other hernias.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In a lesion at the sensory decussations, which nuclei are affected? 1. Lateral vestibular nucleus 2. Nucleus gracilis 3. Spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve 4. Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus 5. Hypoglossal nucleus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3, 4, 5

The sensory decussation occurs in the caudal (closed) medulla, where the internal arcuate fibers arising from the gracile and cuneate nuclei cross to form the medial lemniscus. A lesion at this level affects nuclei located in the caudal medulla but spares structures situated more rostrally.

Nuclei affected at the level of sensory decussation:

• Nucleus gracilis ✓
• Spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve ✓
• Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus ✓
• Hypoglossal nucleus ✓

Thus, the correct combination is 2, 3, 4, 5.

Why not the other options?

• 1. Lateral vestibular nucleus: Located in the rostral medulla/caudal pons, not at the level of the sensory decussation.
• Options A, B, and D either omit affected nuclei or incorrectly include the lateral vestibular nucleus.
questions.learning: 2, 3, 4, 5 The sensory decussation occurs in the caudal (closed) medulla, where the internal arcuate fibers arising from the gracile and cuneate nuclei cross to form the medial lemniscus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhoea presents to the gynaecology OPD for evaluation. She has normal secondary sexual characters. Her karyotype is 46,XX and ultrasonography reveals normal ovaries and tubes but absent uterus. What is her clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome

• The patient has the classical features:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Normal breast development and secondary sexual characteristics
• 46,XX karyotype
• Normal ovaries and fallopian tubes
• Absent uterus on ultrasonography
• agenesis or hypoplasia of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS):

• Karyotype: 46,XY
• Testes present, absent uterus, sparse/absent pubic and axillary hair.

• B. Turner syndrome:

• Karyotype: 45,X
• Streak ovaries, absent secondary sexual characteristics, uterus present but infantile.

• D. Primary ovarian failure: Characterized by elevated FSH, absent ovarian function, and poor secondary sexual development if occurring before puberty. The uterus is present.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common cause of shock in severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) is:
options: Hypovolemic shock resulting from third space loss
Septic shock resulting from infected pancreatic necrosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypovolemic shock resulting from third space loss

In severe acute pancreatitis (SAP), the most common cause of shock in the early phase is hypovolemic shock due to massive third-space fluid loss, vomiting, reduced oral intake, and increased capillary permeability. This leads to intravascular volume depletion and hypotension.

Why not the other options?

• B. Septic shock resulting from infected pancreatic necrosis: Occurs later (usually after 1–2 weeks) due to infected necrosis.
• C. Cardiogenic shock resulting from SIRS: SIRS causes vasodilation rather than primary cardiogenic shock.
• D. Abdominal compartment syndrome: A serious complication but not the commonest cause of shock.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A farmer presents to you with a cauliflower-shaped mass on the foot, which developed after a minor injury. Microscopy shows copper penny bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chromoblastomycosis

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical vignette is chromoblastomycosis.

Chromomycosis is a term used to describe various conditions caused by pigmented (dematiaceous) fungi. Chromoblastomycosis, the most common chromomycosis, is more commonly seen in tropical areas among agricultural workers and woodcutters who walk barefoot. Traumatic implantation is the mode of infection.

Patients present with warty cauliflower-like cutaneous nodules on the feet and lower legs. Species of the fungal genus Fonsecaea are implicated as the causative agents. Diagnosis is made by the demonstration of sclerotic bodies (copper-penny bodies) in tissue sections. Sclerotic bodies appear as round or irregular, dark brown bodies with septae.

It can be managed with itraconazole (100–200 mg daily) or terbinafine (250 mg daily). For small lesions, surgical excision is the therapy of choice.

Other options:

Option B - Blastomycosis is an infection caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis. It causes a chronic infection with granulomatous and suppurative lesions, which starts in the lungs but may disseminate to other organs. Symptoms of an acute lower respiratory tract infection with pulmonary infiltrates are the most common clinical presentations. Microscopic examination of stained specimens shows broad-based budding yeast cells.

Option C - Sporotrichosis caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii, is commonly seen in gardeners followed by minor trauma. Patients present with skin nodules or lymph node ulceration. Microscopy shows asteroid bodies. It can be seen as an oval, basophilic structure with eosinophilic radiation.

Option D - Phaeohyphomycosis caused by dematiaceous fungi is frequently encountered in immunodeficient individuals. Clinical manifestations include brain abscesses, intramuscular abscesses, and cysts. On microscopy, the fungi appear as distorted hyphal strands. In contrast to chromoblastomycosis, sclerotic bodies are not found.
questions.learning: Chromoblastomycosis — The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical vignette is chromoblastomycosis. Chromomycosis is a term used to describe various conditions caused by pigmented (dematiaceous) fungi.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the gun that caused the wound and the range of the shot.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pistol, near shot

The given image showing a gunshot entry wound with powder burn around the wound is likely due to a near-shot injury by a pistol.

A near-shot injury is one when the range of flame is within 60 cm.

The features of a near-shot wound are a circular entry wound with the size same as that of the bullet. The edges are lacerated, inverted, and surrounded by a narrow zone of abrasion. There are no signs of burning or singeing. Powder tattooing around the entry wounds is another important feature.

Other options:

Option A: In an intermediate range which is up to 7 feet, the edge of the wound is abraded and the appearance is referred to as a rat hole. There is no burning and the tattooing is appreciable till 3-4 feet and then starts disappearing.

Option B: In shotgun injuries due to a close-range i.e between contact and 3 feet, the entry wound is circular or elliptical with features of the scorching, singing, and less dense tattooing.

Option D: In a close shot pistol injury,  the range of flame is within 5-8 cm with a circular entry wound. Other features such as burning, singeing, blackening and tattooing of skin are seen in and around the entry wound.
questions.learning: Pistol, near shot — The given image showing a gunshot entry wound with powder burn around the wound is likely due to a near-shot injury by a pistol. A near-shot injury is one when the range of flame is within 60 cm.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the correct sequence of the auditory pathways: A.Superior Olivary nucleus B. Cochlear Nucleus C. Inferior Colliculi D. Lateral lemniscus E. Medial geniculate ganglion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. BADCE

Cochlear nucleus (B), superior olivary nucleus (A), lateral lemniscus (D), inferior colliculi (C), and medial geniculate ganglion (E) represent the correct sequence of the auditory pathway.

The correct sequence of structures involved in the auditory pathway from the periphery to the center is

1. Vestibulocochlear nerve
2. Cochlear Nucleus
3. Superior olivary nucleus
4. Lateral lemniscus
5. Inferior colliculus
6. Medial geniculate body
7. Auditory cortex

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The image below shows the cross-section of the trachea. Identify the structure marked.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trachealis muscle

The structure marked in the image shows the trachealis muscle.

The trachea is a tube-like structure that allows air to pass between the larynx and the bronchi.

The trachealis muscle is a smooth muscle located at the posterior wall of the trachea. It connects the ends of the C-shaped tracheal cartilage rings and completes the posterior part of the tracheal wall.

The histological section of the trachea shows the following structures:

* Respiratory epithelium

* Basement membrane

* Submucosal glands (both serous and mucous parts)

* Perichondrium

* Tracheal cartilage

* Trachealis muscle (smooth muscle).

The histological image below is that of the trachea as identified by the presence of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lining, the serous and mucous glands, and hyaline cartilage.
questions.learning: Trachealis muscle — The structure marked in the image shows the trachealis muscle. The trachea is a tube-like structure that allows air to pass between the larynx and the bronchi.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident, and a whole-body CT scan is planned as part of trauma assessment. The standard whole-body CT protocol includes all of the following except which one?
questions.explanation: The whole-body CT protocol, often called a "pan-scan," is a rapid screening tool for major trauma to identify life-threatening internal injuries. Standard protocols include CT of the Head (Option D) and Cervical Spine (Option B) to rule out intracranial hemorrhage and spinal instability, as well as CT of the Chest, Abdomen (Option A), and Pelvis to check for visceral injury or internal bleeding. CT of the limbs (Option C) is NOT part of the standard whole-body trauma protocol. Injuries to the extremities are typically assessed via physical examination and targeted conventional X-rays once the patient is hemodynamically stabilized. Scanning all limbs in the primary pan-scan would significantly increase the radiation dose and scan time without necessarily altering immediate life-saving interventions. Therefore, while essential for managing fractures later, CT limbs are excluded from the initial "whole-body" trauma assessment to focus on the brain, spine, and torso

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient with respiratory volume of 500 mL. The intraplueral pressure measured -4 before inspiration and -8 at the end of inspiration. The pulmonary compliance of the patient is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 125 ml/cm H2O

Pulmonary compliance of this patient is 125 mL/cm of H2O.

Compliance is developed due to the tendency for tissue to resume its original position after an applied force has been removed.

After an expiration during quiet breathing, the lungs have a tendency to collapse and the chest wall has a tendency to expand. The interaction between the recoil of the lungs and recoil of the chest can be measured through a spirometer and a curve of airway pressure plotted against volume is the pressure-volume curve of the total respiratory system (Ptr).

Compliance of the lung and chest wall is measured as the slope of the Ptr curve, or, as a change in lung volume per unit change in airway pressure (ΔV/ΔP).

Compliance = Change in lung volume / Change in pressure

Compliance = 500/4

Compliance = 125 ml/cm H20
questions.learning: 125 ml/cm H2O Pulmonary compliance of this patient is 125 mL/cm of H2O. Compliance is developed due to the tendency for tissue to resume its original position after an applied force has been removed.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
Match the following E.coli with their respective pathogenesis.

E. coli
Mechanism of action

1. ETEC
A. Produces a heat-stable toxin and causes activation of guanylyl cyclase

2. EIEC
B. Invades intestinal mucosal cells

3. EHEC
C. Produces a toxin against vascular endothelium cells

4. EPEC
D. Adheres to the mucosal surface and causes effacement of microvilli
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A-1,B-2,C-3,D-4

The correctly matched pairs are as follows:

E. coli
Mechanism of action

1. ETEC
A. Produce a heat-stable toxin and cause activation of guanylyl cyclase

2. EIEC
B. Invades intestinal mucosal cells

3. EHEC
C. Produces a toxin against vascular endothelium cells

4. EPEC
D. Adhere to the mucosal surface and cause effacement of microvilli

The various strains of Escherichia coli are:

• Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is the most common organism that causes diarrhea in travelers. It produces the following toxins:

• LT (heat-labile toxin)- acts by ↑cAMP
• ST (heat-stable toxin)- two types of ST are known, ST-A (ST-I) and ST-B (ST-II)

• ST-A is soluble in methanol and acts by ↑cGMP in the intestine.
• ST-B is insoluble in methanol, and the mode of action is not known.

• Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) invade interstitial epithelial cells in the intestine and cause a condition resembling shigellosis. This ability is determined by a plasmid, detection of which can also be a diagnostic test. Sereny's test was employed to diagnose EIEC but it is not in use anymore.
• Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) produces verocytotoxin, which targets vascular endothelium. It causes hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome.
• Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) causes infantile diarrhea in developing countries. It adheres to the mucosal surface of small intestine using EAF and LEE and causes effacement of microvilli. This leads to attachment and effacement lesions of intestinal cells.
• Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC) produces the stacked brick pattern of adherence on hep-2 cells. EAEC has been associated with persistent diarrhea. Intestinal colonization of EAEC is mediated by AAF (aggregative adherence fimbriae). EAEC produces EAST-1 toxin (enteroaggregative heat-stable toxin) which is considered to be a major virulence factor.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35- year old woman presented to the clinic with the symptoms of hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus. Further examination reveals conductive hearing loss with Rinne test negative. A reddish mass is seen behind the tympanic membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glomus tumor

This clinical scenario is suggestive of a glomus tumor.

Glomus tumor is the most common benign middle ear neoplasm. It is seen frequently in middle-aged females. The tumor consists of paraganglionic cells from the neural crest. Glomus tumor is an extremely vascular benign tumor.

There are two types of glomus tumors: glomus jugulare and glomus tympanicum. Glomus jugulare arises from the dome of the jugular bulb and invades the hypotympanum. Glomus tympanicum arises from the promontory of the middle ear.

Clinical features include conductive hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus- earliest symptoms. Otoscopy examination shows a red reflex through an intact tympanic membrane as a "rising sun" appearance since the tumor arises from the floor of the middle ear. Paralysis of the 9th to 12th cranial nerves can also occur. An audible bruit over the mastoid is heard on auscultation in all the stages of the tumor.

Other options:

Option A: Acute otitis media presents with throbbing earache and a red and bulging tympanic membrane with loss of landmarks on examination. Tuning fork tests reveal a conductive type of hearing loss.

Option B: Chronic otitis media presents with mucoid or mucopurulent ear discharge, the conductive type of hearing loss, and central perforation of the tympanic membrane. Middle ear mucosa can be seen through the perforation.

Option D: Serous otitis media presents with hearing loss, delayed and defective speech, and mild earaches associated with upper respiratory tract infections. Otoscopy reveals a dull, opaque, and retracted tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex, a thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus, fluid levels, and air bubbles behind the tympanic membrane.
