questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is associated with the clinical condition shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malignant melanoma

The given image showing a black, heterogeneous, hairy palpable lesion in a child is suggestive of congenital melanocytic nevus. Malignant melanoma is more commonly associated with a congenital melanocytic nevus.

Congenital melanocytic nevi (CMN) are benign, pigmented, melanocytic nevi present at birth. They are most commonly brown, black, purplish, or red, usually a palpable lesion with heterogeneous color and texture. CMN often have thick hair at birth, which grows at a significantly greater rate than the surrounding scalp hair.

Congenital melanocytic nevi can be classified based on size: small (<1.5 cm), medium (1.5-19.9 cm), and large or giant (>20 cm). Larger CMN have a higher risk of developing malignant melanoma. Management of CMN depends on the size and location of the lesion. Smaller nevi may be observed, while larger nevi or those at a higher risk for complications may require surgical excision, particularly if there is a concern for malignant transformation. Complications of CMN include neurological abnormalities (intraparenchymal melanosis is the commonest finding), malignant melanoma, and other tumors like rhabdomyosarcoma.

The lifetime risk of malignant transformation in large or giant CMN ranges from 5% to 10%. Regular follow-up and monitoring for changes in size, color, or texture are essential for early detection of potential complications.

Note: More than 50% of patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome have glaucoma as an ocular complication. The image given below shows port-wine staining in a child with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
questions.learning: Malignant melanoma — The given image showing a black, heterogeneous, hairy palpable lesion in a child is suggestive of congenital melanocytic nevus. Malignant melanoma is more commonly associated with a congenital melanocytic nevus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis for the ocular lesion observed in a 21-year-old male patient?
questions.explanation: The image displays follicular conjunctivitis, which is characteristic of infections caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (Serotypes D-K). In adults, this is known as "Inclusion Conjunctivitis" and is typically acquired from genital secretions. It features large, pale follicles most prominent in the lower tarsal conjunctiva. Option B (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) causes hyperacute, severe purulent conjunctivitis with massive lid swelling. Option C (Haemophilus influenzae) typically causes acute bacterial conjunctivitis in children, characterized by crusting and redness. Option D (Vitamin A deficiency) causes xerosis and Bitot's spots rather than follicles. Chlamydial infection can also cause Trachoma (Serotypes A-C), the leading infectious cause of blindness, which features follicles on the upper tarsal conjunctiva. Treatment for inclusion conjunctivitis involves oral azithromycin or doxycycline, and it is essential to treat sexual partners simultaneously to prevent reinfection and systemic complications
questions.learning: The image displays follicular conjunctivitis, which is characteristic of infections caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (Serotypes D-K). In adults, this is known as "Inclusion Conjunctivitis" and is typically acquired from genital secretions.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young male presents with a painless swelling in the right testis, which he noticed two months ago. On examination, the swelling is firm and non-tender, with no transillumination and the contralateral testis appears normal. An ultrasound reveals a hypoechoic mass in the right testis. Further imaging shows enlargement of the para-aortic and pre-aortic lymph nodes. Tumor markers, including AFP, β-hCG, and LDH, are elevated. The physician suspects testicular cancer. What is the next appropriate step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High inguinal orchidectomy

The clinical features and the raised AFP, β-hCG, and LDH levels are suggestive of testicular cancer and the next best step in management is high inguinal orchidectomy.

Clinical features of testicular carcinoma:

* Painless testicular lump is the most common presenting feature.

* Epididymo-orchitis.

* Severe pain and acute enlargement of the testis because of haemorrhage into the tumour.

* Intra-abdominal spread may cause abdominal or lumbar pain.

* Lung metastases are usually silent but they can cause chest pain, dyspnoea and haemoptysis in the later stages of the disease.

Although testicular cancers often spread to the retroperitoneal lymph nodes, including the pre-aortic nodes. A biopsy of the scrotal mass or the lymph nodes is generally not the first step.

A high inguinal approach is crucial because it allows for removal of the testicle along with the spermatic cord, minimizing the risk of further spread. This is the standard initial management for suspected testicular cancer. After removal of the affected testis, metastatic workup should be done with CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.

Early-stage tumors don't require additional treatment after orchidectomy, while late-stage tumours are given combination chemotherapy with bleomycin, etoposide, and cis-platinum (BEP chemotherapy). They are highly sensitive to combination chemotherapy with BEP. So chemotherapy is given to high-risk cases and low-risk cases with a good prognosis are managed by surveillance protocols.

Other Options:

Option A: Lymph node biopsies, while sometimes necessary, are usually performed after a diagnosis of testicular cancer is established to assess the extent of spread.

Option B: Scrotal biopsies for testicular mass risk seeding the scrotal skin with cancer cells, potentially worsening the prognosis.

Option D: Repeating hormone markers while potentially useful for monitoring the disease after a diagnosis is made is not the priority when a suspicious scrotal mass and concerning lymphadenopathy are present.

III. Sex cord stromal tumors

* Leydig cell tumor

* Sertoli cell tumor

* Granulosa cell tumor

* Fibroma–thecoma

IV. Tumor containing both germ-cell and sex cord-stromal elements

* Gonadoblastoma

V. Hematolymphoid tumors

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A forensic expert receives a summons from the district court to record evidence in a criminal case, but two days earlier, he had already received a summons for a civil case in the same court. What is the appropriate course of action for him?
options: Attend the court for which the summons came first.
Attend the court for the criminal case.
questions.explanation: When a witness receives conflicting summons (subpoenas) for the same day, legal protocol dictates a specific order of priority. Criminal cases always take precedence over civil cases due to their public importance and the urgency of justice in criminal law. The forensic expert is legally mandated to attend the criminal court and must formally notify the civil court of the conflict, requesting a rescheduled date. Regarding the distractors, informing both and waiting (Option A) is insufficient as it risks contempt of court for non-attendance. The order of receipt (Option B) does not determine priority; only the nature and level of the court do. Ignoring both (Option D) is a serious legal offense that can result in fines, imprisonment, or arrest warrants. If both summons were for the same type of case, the expert would attend the higher court first, or if at the same level, the one received first
questions.learning: When a witness receives conflicting summons (subpoenas) for the same day, legal protocol dictates a specific order of priority. Criminal cases always take precedence over civil cases due to their public importance and the urgency of justice in criminal law.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A previously healthy 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of chest pain on exertion. She takes no medications. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Cardiac stress ECG shows inducible ST-segment depressions in the precordial leads that coincide with the patient's report of chest pain and resolve upon cessation of exercise. Pharmacotherapy with verapamil is initiated. This drug is most likely to have which of the following sets of effects?
options: End diastolic volume (EDV) increase, BP decrease, Contractility decrease, HR decrease
End diastolic volume (EDV) decrease, BP decrease, Contractility decrease, HR decrease
End diastolic volume (EDV) increase, BP no change, Contractility increase, HR decrease
End diastolic volume (EDV) decrease, BP increase, Contractility decrease, HR no change
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. End diastolic volume (EDV) increase, BP decrease, Contractility decrease, HR decrease

Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine Ca²⁺ channel blocker. It causes negative inotropy (↓ contractility) and negative chronotropy/dromotropy (↓ HR, ↓ AV conduction). It also causes arteriolar vasodilation → ↓ BP. Because HR falls, diastolic filling time increases, so EDV tends to increase.

• EDV decrease – More typical with venodilators (nitrates) or reduced filling.
• Contractility increase – Opposite of verapamil.
• BP no change / BP increase – Not expected with verapamil’s vasodilation.
questions.learning: End diastolic volume (EDV) increase, BP decrease, Contractility decrease, HR decrease Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine Ca²⁺ channel blocker. It causes negative inotropy (↓ contractility) and negative chronotropy/dromotropy (↓ HR, ↓ AV conduction).

questions.text: A schoolboy presented with the following finding. He has a history of trauma to his upper arm in the past. Which nerve is most likely to be injured in this condition?

There is paralysis of the triceps, and weakness of the wrist and hand.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Five days after surgery requiring prolonged immobilization, a patient develops severe pain in one leg. On examination, Homan’s sign is positive. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT) is a common postoperative complication, particularly in patients who undergo prolonged immobilization, satisfying Virchow's triad of stasis. Homan's sign is a clinical test where the patient experiences calf pain upon passive dorsiflexion of the foot. While it is historically associated with DVT, its sensitivity and specificity are relatively low. Urinary sepsis (Option B) presents with fever, chills, and urinary symptoms, not localized leg pain. Peripheral vascular disease (Option C) typically causes chronic exertional pain (claudication) rather than acute postoperative swelling and pain. Lymphangitis (Option D) is an inflammation of the lymphatic channels, usually appearing as red streaks on the skin with associated lymphadenopathy. For a postoperative patient with leg pain and a positive Homan's sign, DVT must be the working diagnosis until ruled out by a Doppler ultrasound. Prophylaxis with anticoagulants and early mobilization are standard practices to prevent the potentially fatal sequel of DVT: pulmonary embolism
questions.learning: Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT) is a common postoperative complication, particularly in patients who undergo prolonged immobilization, satisfying Virchow's triad of stasis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with increased frequency of micturition, incomplete bladder emptying, and frequent urinary tract infections. What is the diagnosis based on the image shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bladder stones

The clinical scenario along with the X-ray gives the diagnosis of bladder stones. The tip of a catheter can also be seen in the Xray.

Primary bladder stone:

* Develops in sterile urine in the absence of any known functional, anatomic, or infectious factors and does not necessarily imply that stones have formed de novo in the bladder.

* Most common in children younger than 10 years of age

* Most vesical calculi are mixed

* Ammonium acid urate, calcium oxalate, uric acid, and calcium phosphate are the most common components of primary bladder calculi

Secondary bladder stone: Forms during infection, due to bladder outflow obstruction, impaired bladder emptying, or the presence of a foreign body.

Types:

* Calcium oxalate stones

* Uric acid stones - occur in patients with gout but are also observed in patients with ileostomies or with bladder outlet obstruction

* Cystine stones - in cystinuria

* Triple phosphate stones - occur in urine infected with urea-splitting organisms
questions.learning: Bladder stones — The clinical scenario along with the X-ray gives the diagnosis of bladder stones. The tip of a catheter can also be seen in the Xray.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with fatigue, loss of appetite, constipation, recurrent kidney stone–related urinary symptoms, and polyuria, along with a history of psychiatric illness, raising suspicion of hyperparathyroidism. Which investigation would be most helpful in confirming this diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient presents with multi-system symptoms of hypercalcemia: fatigue, constipation, and renal stones ("Stones, Groans, and Psychic Moans"), strongly suggesting Primary Hyperparathyroidism. This condition is most commonly caused by a benign parathyroid adenoma. Once the diagnosis is biochemically established (elevated PTH and Calcium), imaging is required to localize the abnormal gland for surgery. The Tc-99m Sestamibi scan (Option A) is the gold standard functional imaging prioritized for this purpose. It is highly effective at detecting overactive parathyroid tissue due to its high mitochondrial content, which retains the tracer longer than normal thyroid tissue. USG neck (Option B) is an excellent structural adjunct but may miss ectopic glands. CT neck (Option C) and PET scan (Option D) are much less sensitive or specific as initial localization tools compared to Sestamibi. Therefore, the Sestamibi scan is the most beneficial diagnostic imaging step for pre-operative planning. **************
questions.learning: This patient presents with multi-system symptoms of hypercalcemia: fatigue, constipation, and renal stones ("Stones, Groans, and Psychic Moans"), strongly suggesting Primary Hyperparathyroidism.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Amsel's criteria is used in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bacterial vaginosis

Amsel's criteria is used in bacterial vaginosis.

According to Amsel's criteria, the discharge has the following characteristics.

* White milky non-viscous discharge, adherent to the vaginal wall

* The pH of the discharge is more than 4.5

* Fishy odor when mixed with 10% KOH. This is called the Whiff test.

* Presence of clue cells-the epithelial cells have a fuzzy border due to the adherence of bacteria.

* Decrease in the number of lactobacilli and increase in the number of Gardnerella and other bacteria.

It is treated with 500 mg of metronidazole twice daily for 7 days.

Shown below is the Gram-stained smear of vaginal discharge of a patient diagnosed with bacterial vaginosis. It reveals vaginal epithelial cells that have a fuzzy border due to the adherence of bacteria. These are called clue cells.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man is unemployed because he is unable to walk after an accident. His unemployment is classified as a _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Handicap

The patient here being unemployed can be classified as handicap, according to the concept given below.

Disease → Impairment → Disability → Handicap

* Impairment is any loss or abnormality in normal structure or function.

* Disability is the inability to carry out normal actions due to impairment.

* Handicap is experiencing disadvantages due to disability and inability to discharge obligations normally.

In the given example:

* Accident: Disease (or disorder)

* Loss of foot: Impairment (extrinsic or intrinsic)

* Cannot walk: Disability (objectified)

* Unemployed: Handicap (socialized)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient is started on lithium therapy. Which of the following side effects should the patient be asked to watch out for to monitor for toxicity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vertigo and Diarrhoea

Vertigo and diarrhoea are known side-effects of lithium therapy. Lithium therapy can cause side effects at both therapeutic and toxic levels.

Known significant side effects of lithium therapy include

• Polyuria-polydipsia
• Dry mouth
• Leukocytosis Headache
• Hand tremors
• Confusion
• Decreased memory
• Muscle weakness
• Hyperreflexia
• Muscle twitch
• Vertigo
• ECG changes
• Nausea & vomiting
• Diarrhoea

Other options:

No evidence of significant association with sore throat, fever or breathlessness has been documented with lithium therapy

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with chronic joint pain and morning stiffness lasting about 30 minutes. Examination reveals Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes, and X-ray findings show joint space narrowing with osteophyte formation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical profile of an elderly patient with chronic pain in weight-bearing joints, short-lived morning stiffness (less than 30 minutes), and characteristic Heberden's nodes (at the DIP joints) and Bouchard's nodes (at the PIP joints) is diagnostic of Osteoarthritis (OA). The radiographic findings—narrowed joint spaces and osteophytes (bone spurs)—are the "classic" indicators of OA. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (Option C) typically presents with prolonged morning stiffness (more than 1 hour), involves different hand joints (MCP and PIP), and shows periarticular osteopenia rather than osteophytes. Osteoporosis (Option A) is a systemic loss of bone density that is usually painless until a fracture occurs. Bone tumors (Option D) would present as a localized mass or focal destructive lesion rather than symmetrical joint wear. OA is a degenerative "wear and tear" disease. Therefore, based on the specific nodes and radiographic spurs, Osteoarthritis is the only viable diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical profile of an elderly patient with chronic pain in weight-bearing joints, short-lived morning stiffness (less than 30 minutes), and characteristic Heberden's nodes (at the DIP joints) and Bouchard's nodes (at the PIP joints) is diagnostic of…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the type of ANA staining pattern shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Centromeric

The given picture shows discrete and large speckles in the resting cells, and the alignment of the speckles in the chromosome region in the dividing cells. This is suggestive of centromeric pattern of ANA staining. Centromeric pattern is seen in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome).

The main patterns of ANA staining are as follows:

Homogenous pattern refers to diffuse staining of the nucleus in the resting cells. There is also staining of the chromosome region in the dividing cells. The usual antibodies which show this pattern are anti-histone antibodies and anti-dsDNA antibodies. This type of pattern is also seen in chronic autoimmune hepatitis and juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Homogenous staining is shown in the image below.

Fine speckled pattern refers to hundreds of dots present throughout the nucleus. However, there is no staining of the chromosome region of the dividing cells as shown in the image below. This pattern is shown by anti-SS-A/Ro and anti-SS-B/La antibodies.

Coarse speckled pattern refers to hundreds of dots present in the nucleus, but generally larger than the dots seen in fine speckled pattern. There is no staining of nucleoli or dividing chromosomes. This type of pattern is seen in anti-Sm and anti-U1 RNP antibodies.

Dense fine speckled pattern shows the speckles distributed throughout the nucleoli. This pattern differs from the fine and coarse speckled patterns in that the speckles are associated with the chromosomes in the dividing cells. This type of pattern is not associated with systemic rheumatic disease.
questions.learning: Centromeric — The given picture shows discrete and large speckles in the resting cells, and the alignment of the speckles in the chromosome region in the dividing cells.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which congenital abnormality or teratogenic effect is most commonly associated with the use of lithium during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Lithium is a commonly used mood stabilizer that is known to cross the placenta and exert specific teratogenic effects, particularly during the first trimester of pregnancy. The most famous and well-documented association is with cardiac defects (Option A), specifically Ebstein’s anomaly. This rare malformation involve the apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets, leading to "atrialization" of the right ventricle and potential heart failure. While the absolute risk is lower than once thought, it remains significantly higher than in the general population. Facial defects (Option B), CNS defects (Option C), and urogenital defects (Option D) are associated with other teratogens (like phenytoin or valproic acid) but are not the hallmark toxicity of lithium. Therefore, for any pregnant patient requiring lithium, detailed fetal echocardiography is recommended at 18–20 weeks to screen for these cardiac malformations
questions.learning: Lithium is a commonly used mood stabilizer that is known to cross the placenta and exert specific teratogenic effects, particularly during the first trimester of pregnancy.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following fine motor milestones will appear ahead of others?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Copies a circle

Fine motor development follows a predictable sequence, progressing from simple imitation (copying) to independent drawing, and from simpler shapes to more complex figures. Copying a circle is achieved earlier than drawing or copying a cross and is an important developmental milestone.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Copies a cross: Usually achieved at 4 years.
• C. Draws a circle: Drawing a circle independently is a more advanced skill than copying one.
• D. Draws a cross: An independent drawing task that develops later than copying a circle.
questions.learning: Copies a circle Fine motor development follows a predictable sequence, progressing from simple imitation (copying) to independent drawing, and from simpler shapes to more complex figures.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Post-exposure Measles vaccine should be given ?
questions.explanation: Measles is a highly contagious viral infection. For susceptible individuals who have been exposed to the virus, the measles vaccine can prevent or modify the disease if administered promptly. The recommended window for post-exposure vaccination is within 72 hours (3 days) of exposure. Administration within this timeframe provides active immunity that can overtake the natural infection's incubation period. If the 3-day window has passed, immunoglobulin (IG) can be given up to 6 days after exposure to provide passive immunity. Options A, C, and D do not match the clinically established "golden period" for post-exposure prophylaxis with the vaccine. This intervention is crucial during outbreaks to protect unimmunized contacts. Therefore, the 3-day rule is the standard epidemiological practice for post-exposure measles control
questions.learning: Measles is a highly contagious viral infection. For susceptible individuals who have been exposed to the virus, the measles vaccine can prevent or modify the disease if administered promptly.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a hernia medial to the inferior epigastric artery. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management for the same?
options: Direct hernia and Lichtenstein mesh repair
Indirect hernia and Lichtenstein mesh repair
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Direct hernia and Lichtenstein mesh repair

The given clinical scenario of a hernia medial to the inferior epigastric artery is suggestive of a direct hernia, for which Lichtenstein mesh repair is the appropriate surgical method for its management.

The contents of a direct hernia protrude outward, forward, and medial to the inferior epigastric artery and the deep inguinal ring. Whereas, the contents of an indirect hernia protrude lateral to the inferior epigastric artery. The sac of an indirect inguinal hernia passes from the deep inguinal ring obliquely towards the superficial inguinal ring and then to the scrotum.

A direct hernia protrudes through the Hesselbach triangle, which is a zone of weakness for direct hernias.

A Lichtenstein mesh repair is currently one of the most frequently used methods for treating an inguinal hernia. It is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. It is an anterior tension-free mesh repair that reduces the chances of recurrence of a hernia. A piece of prosthetic nonabsorbable mesh is used to bridge the defect in this repair.

Other surgical methods used for the repair of an inguinal hernia are:

• Bassini repair - It is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. In this method, a mesh is not used. It is associated with a high recurrence and is not used frequently now. It is used only in cases of hernial strangulation and peritonitis where the use of a mesh is not preferred. It is performed by suturing the transversus abdominis and internal oblique musculoaponeurotic arches/conjoined tendon to the inguinal ligament.
• Shouldice repair - It is a multilayered repair, where the posterior wall of the inguinal canal is strengthened by continuous sutures. It involves double-breasting of the transversalis fascia. It is associated with a very low recurrence rate.
• Gilbert repair (plug and patch repair) - It is an extension of Lichtenstein’s original mesh repair and has now become the most commonly performed primary anterior inguinal hernia repair. In this technique, a cone-shaped plug of polypropylene mesh is used. It is deployed like an upside-down umbrella when inserted into the internal inguinal ring to occlude the hernia
• McVay repair (Cooper's ligament repair) is used for the correction of direct inguinal hernia, large indirect hernia, recurrent hernia, femoral hernias (particularly suited for strangulated femoral hernias). In this method, the transversus abdominis aponeurosis is approximated to Cooper's ligament.
• Stoppa-Rives repair - It is used for the repair of large, recurrent, or bilateral hernias. In this method, a sub-umbilical midline incision is given to place a large mesh into the preperitoneal space.
• Herniotomy - It is used to treat inguinal hernia in a child which occurs due to the presence of a patent processus vaginalis. Therefore in herniotomy, the repair of the inguinal ring is not done.
questions.learning: Direct hernia and Lichtenstein mesh repair — The given clinical scenario of a hernia medial to the inferior epigastric artery is suggestive of a direct hernia, for which Lichtenstein mesh repair is the appropriate surgical method for its management.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are adverse effects of loop-acting and thiazide diuretics? 1. Metabolic acidosis 2. Hypovolemia 3. Hyponatremia 4. Hypokalemia Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) and thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide) commonly cause volume depletion (hypovolemia), hyponatremia, and hypokalemia due to increased renal loss of sodium and potassium. They also produce metabolic alkalosis (not acidosis) because of increased hydrogen ion loss.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Metabolic acidosis ❌: They cause metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis.
• 2. Hypovolemia ✔️: Due to excessive diuresis.
• 3. Hyponatremia ✔️: Common, especially with thiazides.
• 4. Hypokalemia ✔️: Due to increased distal potassium excretion.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) and thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide) commonly cause volume depletion (hypovolemia), hyponatremia, and hypokalemia due to increased renal loss of sodium and potassium.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is brought in to the casualty with maxillofacial trauma after an RTA. He is unconscious with a dropping SpO2. The ER doctor decides to intubate him. What is the preferred method of securing airway for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tracheostomy

Patients with severe maxillofacial trauma are very likely to experience severe airway compromise or obstruction. Hence to maintain airway competency, intubation is necessary and in the above case, the presence of facial trauma, tracheostomy is ideal.

Tracheostomy involves making an opening and placing a stoma in the anterior wall of the trachea.

Functions:

* Provides an alternative pathway for breathing by bypassing the obstruction.

* Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing dead space by 30-50% and reducing airway resistance

* Uses a cuff to protect the airways from secretions and blood

* Allows suction of secretions in the setting of the impaired cough reflex.

* Allows positive pressure respiration

* Allows administration of anesthesia

Indications:

* Respiratory obstruction due to

* Infections (laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, epiglottitis, diphtheria)

* Trauma due to external injury, mandibular or maxillofacial fractures

* Neoplasms

* Foreign bodies or edema

* Bilateral abductor paralysis

* Congenital anomalies

* Retained secretions

* Inability to cough due to coma, spasm, or paralysis of respiratory muscles

* Aspiration of pharyngeal secretions

* Painful cough

* Respiratory insufficiency due to emphysema, chronic bronchitis

Other options:

Option A and B: Mask ventilation and LMA are not enough as the patient has severe airway compromise.

Option D:  Nasotracheal intubation is contraindicated in the presence of facial trauma because there may be an undiscovered fracture at the base of the skull. The tube could be forced through it and into the brain.
questions.learning: Tracheostomy Patients with severe maxillofacial trauma are very likely to experience severe airway compromise or obstruction. Hence to maintain airway competency, intubation is necessary and in the above case, the presence of facial trauma, tracheostomy is…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Sympathetic ophthalmia is seen after ____________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Penetrating trauma

Sympathetic ophthalmia is seen after a penetrating trauma.

Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis seen after a penetrating trauma or less frequently, following intraocular surgery, usually multiple vitreoretinal procedures. Patients present between 2 weeks and 3 months after initial injury.

The earliest symptom is blurred near vision in the sympathizing (uninjured) eye. The earliest sign is a retrolental flare in the sympathizing eye. Anterior uveitis develops in both eyes. The fundus shows multifocal choroidal infiltrates in the mid-periphery. Sub-retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) infiltrates corresponding to Dalen–Fuchs nodules (image)(a granuloma situated between Bruch membrane and the RPE) are also present.

Steroids are the basis of treatment. High-dose oral prednisolone is given for several months. Immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, cyclosporine, and methotrexate can be used in resistant cases or as steroid-sparing agents. Enucleation of a severely injured eye with no visual potential within 2 weeks of injury prevents the occurrence of sympathetic ophthalmia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A newborn had hypoplasia of the mandibles and zygomatic bones, malformed external ears, and slanted palpebral fissures. Abnormality in the development of which of the following pharyngeal arches will most likely lead to the given condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pharyngeal arch 1

Treacher Collins syndrome that results from abnormal development of the 1st pharyngeal arch (mandibular arch).

First arch syndromes are congenital defects caused due to the failure of the neural crest cells to migrate into the 1st pharyngeal arch.

* Treacher-Collins syndrome (mandibulo-facial dysostosis) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder seen in 1/50,000 live births. It is characterized by

* Craniofacial bone defects involving the mandible (causing micrognathia), maxilla, and zygomatic arches

* Ear defects involving the external ear, atresia of auditory canals, and abnormalities of the middle ear ossicles, leading to bilateral conductive hearing loss

* Eye defects such as down-slanting palpebral fissures and lower eyelid colobomas

* Pierre Robin sequence (or Robin sequence) is a deformity seen in 1/8500 births. It may be caused due to genetic defects or due to environmental factors. It can also be seen in oligohydramnios, when the chin gets compressed against the chest in utero.

* It is characterized by a triad of micrognathia, glossoptosis (posteriorly placed tongue), and cleft palate.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with low-grade fever and cough. Based on the provided chest X-ray, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The Chest X-ray demonstrates numerous tiny, uniform, 1-2 mm nodules scattered symmetrically throughout both lung fields, resembling millet seeds. This is the classic radiological presentation of Miliary Tuberculosis, a form of disseminated TB resulting from hematogenous spread of the bacilli. Lung cancer (Option A) typically presents as one or more larger, irregular masses. ARDS (Option C) shows diffuse "white-out" or bilateral alveolar infiltrates rather than discrete miliary nodules. Aspergilloma (Option D) is a solid ball of fungus that typically resides in a pre-existing cavity. Miliary TB can be a life-threatening emergency, particularly in young adults or immuno compromised individuals, and may involve multiple organ systems including the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Diagnosis is often difficult and may require high-resolution CT (HRCT) or sputum/tissue cultures. Prompt initiation of standard four-drug antitubercular therapy (ATT) is essential

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not associated with post-transcriptional modification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glycosylation

Post-transcriptional modifications occur after RNA is synthesized from DNA and are essential for converting pre-mRNA into mature mRNA. The major modifications include:

• 5′ Capping: Addition of a 7-methylguanosine cap at the 5′ end, which protects mRNA from degradation and helps in ribosome binding.
• Endonuclease cleavage and splicing: Removal of introns and joining of exons to form mature mRNA.
• Methylation: Certain bases in RNA may be methylated during RNA processing.

Glycosylation is not a post-transcriptional modification. It is a post-translational modification of proteins that occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, where carbohydrate groups are added to proteins.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Heavy metal chelators are all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oxime

Heavy metal chelators are agents that bind toxic metals and form stable complexes that can be excreted from the body, thereby reducing metal toxicity.

Examples include:

• Penicillamine – used in copper poisoning and Wilson disease.
• BAL (Dimercaprol) – used in arsenic, mercury, and gold poisoning.
• Trientine – another copper chelator used in Wilson disease.

Oximes (e.g., pralidoxime) are not heavy-metal chelators. They are used in organophosphate poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase by removing the phosphate group from the inhibited enzyme.
questions.learning: Oxime Heavy metal chelators are agents that bind toxic metals and form stable complexes that can be excreted from the body, thereby reducing metal toxicity.

questions.text: Which among the following is a subcutaneous fungal agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sporothrix schenckii

Sporothrix schenckii is a subcutaneous fungal agent. The other three mentioned are systemic mycoses.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A teenage patient presented with a history of dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. On ultrasonography, a transverse vaginal septum was seen. What is the most common complication that can be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endometriosis

The most common complication that can be seen in this patient is endometriosis.

Transverse vaginal septum leads to obstructed flow of menstrual blood. This may lead to retrograde menstruation, which increases the likelihood of the development of endometriosis, according to Sampson's theory of endometriosis.

Transverse vaginal septum occurs as a result of the failure of Müllerian duct fusion or failure of vaginal plate canalization. It may be obstructive or non-obstructive. The commonest site of a transverse septum is the junction between the upper and middle third of the vagina.

Patients with an obstructive or imperforate vaginal septum present with symptoms similar to the imperforate hymen. Symptoms include amenorrhoea, cyclical abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, and a palpable pelvic mass. The vagina may appear shortened and the cervix may not be identifiable. Secondary sexual characteristics appear normal. The diagnosis can be confirmed with ultrasound or MRI.

There is an increased risk of endometriosis. Other complications such as pyomucocolpos, pyometra, and pyosalpinges can also develop in infants with obstructive vaginal septums.

Treatment is by manual dilatation of the perforation or surgical excision of the septum.

Other options:

Option B: Tubo-ovarian abscess develops in pelvic inflammatory disease.

Option C: Dermoid cysts are cystic ovarian tumors that are often associated with mucinous cystadenomas.

Option D: Theca lutein cysts are found in association with hydatidiform moles, choriocarcinoma, and gonadotropin or clomiphene citrate therapy. They regress with the management of the mole and choriocarcinoma and discontinuation of gonadotropin therapy.
questions.learning: Endometriosis — The most common complication that can be seen in this patient is endometriosis. Transverse vaginal septum leads to obstructed flow of menstrual blood.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents to the ophthalmology OPD with a history of progressive diminution of vision in his left eye for the past few months. There is no history of ocular trauma or previous ocular surgery. On examination, both pupils are equal in size at rest, and the anterior segment examination is unremarkable. Visual acuity is reduced in the left eye compared with the right eye. As part of the neuro-ophthalmological examination, the examiner performs the pupillary light examination demonstrated in the accompanying video, alternately moving a bright light between the two eyes. Based on the pupillary response demonstrated in the video, which of the following is the most likely underlying pathology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left optic nerve lesion

• The video demonstrates a left Marcus Gunn pupil (left relative afferent pupillary defect/RAPD) on the swinging flashlight test.
• When the light is moved from the normal right eye to the affected left eye, both pupils appear to dilate because the afferent light stimulus reaching the brain is reduced.
• Marcus Gunn pupil = RAPD = afferent pathway defect, classically due to an optic nerve lesion (e.g., optic neuritis) or severe asymmetric retinal disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with weight gain, thinning of hair, and dry skin. The clinical features are suggestive of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Which of the following antibodies is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody

Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. An elevated TSH and the presence of thyroid peroxidase antibodies usually confirm the diagnosis.

It is an autoimmune disease (associated with HLA DR-3 and HLA-B8) that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual and progressive thyroid failure. The most commonly associated antibody is anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody (Anti-TPO), which targets the enzyme thyroid peroxidase, essential for thyroid hormone synthesis.

Clinical features of Hashimoto's thyroiditis are as follows:

* More common in women (10 to 20 times)

* Diffusely enlarged, painless, lobulated gland

* Patients usually present with hypothyroidism (due to alteration in thyroid function by infiltration of lymphocytes and resultant fibrosis)

* Hashitoxicosis: initial transient phase of thyrotoxicosis

Laboratory investigations show,

* Elevated TSH

* Low T3 and T4

* Presence of thyroid autoantibodies-

* Anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO)

* Antithyroglobulin (Anti-Tg)

* Thyrotropin Receptor Antibody (Anti-TSH-R)

* Anti sodium/iodide symporter (Anti-NIS)

The management of Hashimoto's thyroiditis is as follows:

* Thyroid hormone replacement therapy

Surgery may be required if there is a suspicion of malignancy or goiters causing compressive symptoms.

Note: All the other options (Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI), TSH receptor antibodies (TSHR-Ab), Long-acting thyroid stimulator) are antibodies that are primarily associated with Graves’ disease, leading to hyperthyroidism

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old female patient presented for her first complete eye examination after a school vision screening found unequal visual acuity. Her parents have not noted any eye problems. Visual acuity in the right eye was 20/20 and the left eye is 20/80. The rest of the examination including Fundus exam was unremarkable, What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Amblyopia

The most probable diagnosis from the given scenario is Amblyopia.

Amblyopia is an uncorrectable decrease in vision in one or both eyes with no apparent structural abnormality seen to explain it. It is a diagnosis of exclusion. Generally, a difference of two lines or more on an eye chart test of visual acuity between the two eyes or a best-corrected vision of 20/30 or worse would be defined as amblyopia. For example, our patient has 20/20 vision with the right eye and only 20/80 with the left and the left eye even after best-corrected vision couldn't achieve <20/30 vision, the left eye is said to be amblyopic.

Clinical features:

* Decreased contrast sensitivity

* Diminution of vision

* Sunglass effect- brightness is less compared to the normal eye

* Crowding phenomenon- slipping of images

Treatment of choice:

* Occlusion of the normal eye (4 to 6 hours/day) using patches.

* Penalization: Blurring of vision using atropine.

Prism correction is not the right treatment as the child doesn't have strabismus.

Other options:

Option A: Brain lesion does not cause difference in visual acuity in both eyes.

Option B: Retinoblastoma can be identified by fundoscopy.

Option C: Congenital cataract presents with loss of red reflex immediately after birth.
questions.learning: Amblyopia — The most probable diagnosis from the given scenario is Amblyopia. Amblyopia is an uncorrectable decrease in vision in one or both eyes with no apparent structural abnormality seen to explain it.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: You are an intern posted in the ICU. While taking a blood sample for ABG, which of the following steps would you not do?
options: Normal ph can't rule out acid base disorder
Add 0.5 ml Heparin to the syringe before taking blood
If modified Allens test is negative, alternate site is chosen
Radial artery is the preferred site
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Add 0.5 ml Heparin to the syringe before taking blood

0.5 ml of Heparin is not added to the syringe before taking blood.

Very little heparin is needed in the sample to prevent clotting; 0.05 to 0.10 ml of a dilute solution will help prevent coagulation of 1 ml of blood without affecting its pH. This is achieved by drawing 0.5 ml into the syringe and flushing it out. The residue that remains adherent to the syringe is sufficient for the procedure.

Heparin must be added to the syringe as an anticoagulant. Because the pH of heparin is near 7.0, and the Po2 and Pco2 of the heparin solution are near room air values, excess heparin can alter ABG measurements. After flushing the syringe with heparin, a sufficient amount usually remains in the dead space of the syringe and needle for anticoagulation without distortion of the ABG determination.

Note:

• Modified Allen's test positive indicates that the collateral blood flow is normal
• Modified Allen's test negative indicates that the collateral blood flow is abnormal and an alternate site must be chosen.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A girl develops eye pain after returning from a picnic and reports poor hygiene while handling her contact lenses. What is the most likely cause of her condition?
questions.explanation: Improper contact lens hygiene, particularly combined with exposure to contaminated water (picnic/outdoor setting), is a primary risk factor for Acanthamoeba keratitis. This free-living protozoan can invade the cornea, causing severe pain out of proportion to clinical signs, redness, and photophobia. A classic advanced sign is a ring-shaped stromal infiltrate. Plasmodium (Option B) causes malaria and does not affect the eye in this manner. While Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option C) is a common bacterial cause of contact lens keratitis, the clinical context of outdoor water exposure often points toward protozoal causes in exams. Herpes simplex (Option D) causes dendritic ulcers and is not specifically linked to contact lens hygiene. Therefore, Acanthamoeba is the most likely cause
questions.learning: Improper contact lens hygiene, particularly combined with exposure to contaminated water (picnic/outdoor setting), is a primary risk factor for Acanthamoeba keratitis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Weber-Fechner law relates magnitude of sensation to ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Log of Intensity of stimulus

Weber-Fechner Law states that the magnitude of sensation felt is proportionate to the log of the intensity of the stimulus.

Other Laws in Physiology:

• Doctrine of specific nerve energies - When the nerve pathways from a particular sense organ are stimulated, the sensation evoked is that for which the receptor is specialized no matter how or where along the pathway the activity is initiated.
• Law of projection - No matter where a particular sensory pathway is stimulated along its course to the cortex, the conscious sensation produced is referred to the location of the receptor. This principle is called the law of projection.
questions.learning: Log of Intensity of stimulus Weber-Fechner Law states that the magnitude of sensation felt is proportionate to the log of the intensity of the stimulus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male patient presented with a sudden onset of scrotal pain and discharge. Based on the image below, what is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fournier's gangrene

The given scenario of an elderly male patient with sudden-onset scrotal pain and discharge, with the image showing a blackish discoloration of the scrotum, is likely to be Fournier's gangrene.

Fournier's gangrene is an uncommon polymicrobial infection involving the perineal soft tissue, external genitalia, and perianal region. There is subcutaneous tissue inflammation leading to obliterative arteritis and gangrene. It typically follows minor injuries or procedures in the perineal area, urethral dilatation, and injection for hemorrhoids are some of the etiological factors.

Clinically, sudden scrotal pain with associated prostration, pallor, and pyrexia can be seen. Other features such as crepitus and foul-smelling exudate can be present.

Emergency surgical debridement is needed after initial measures like fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics are undertaken. Urinary diversion and other supportive measures are useful in the management of the condition.

Other options:

Option A: Torsion of testis is a surgical emergency typically seen in the age group of 10-25 years. It is characterized by sudden groin and lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Examination findings reveal a swollen, tender scrotum and testis with a twisted tender cord above it and loss of cremasteric reflex.

Option B: Acute epididymo-orchitis is an infection of the epididymis and testis. It is seen in sexually-active young men. In older men, it is seen following a urinary tract infection, secondary to an indwelling catheter. The features include groin ache, fever, swollen and painful epididymis and testis.

Option C: Scrotal carcinoma is a rare carcinoma that is seen in workers exposed to oil, coal products, and aromatic hydrocarbons. It starts as a wart or ulcer in the scrotum and can extend to the testis.
questions.learning: Fournier's gangrene — The given scenario of an elderly male patient with sudden-onset scrotal pain and discharge, with the image showing a blackish discoloration of the scrotum, is likely to be Fournier's gangrene.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A woman with a history of infertility is currently receiving HMG treatment. Based on the ultrasound findings provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided ultrasound image shows ovaries that are massively enlarged with multiple large, thin-walled cystic follicles bilaterally. In the clinical context of a woman undergoing infertility treatment with HMG (Human Menopausal Gonadotropins), this appearance is pathognomonic for Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) . OHSS is a potentially life-threatening iatrogenic complication of ovulation induction, characterized by increased capillary permeability leading to fluid shifts into the third space (ascites, pleural effusion). Theca lutein cysts (Option B) present similarly but are usually associated with molar pregnancies rather than infertility drugs. PCOD (Option C) would show much smaller, peripheral "string of pearls" follicles rather than these massive cysts. Therefore, the combination of recent HMG use and the characteristic "multicystic" ovarian enlargement confirms OHSS. Management involves intensive fluid and electrolyte monitoring and prevention of further gonadotropin exposure
questions.learning: The provided ultrasound image shows ovaries that are massively enlarged with multiple large, thin-walled cystic follicles bilaterally. In the clinical context of a woman undergoing infertility treatment with HMG (Human Menopausal Gonadotropins), this…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with unilateral throbbing headache accompanied by photophobia, nausea, and vomiting, with symptomatic relief following the use of sumatriptan. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of unilateral, throbbing pain with sensory sensitivities like photophobia and gastrointestinal symptoms like nausea/vomiting is the classic presentation of a migraine headache. The patient’s specific response to sumatriptan further confirms this diagnosis. Sumatriptan is a selective 5-HT receptor agonist that acts as a vasoconstrictor to reverse the cerebral vasodilation that occurs during the headache phase. Tension headaches (Option B) are typically bilateral, feel like a "band" of pressure, and lack systemic symptoms. Cluster headaches (Option C) feature severe peri-orbital pain with autonomic signs like eye watering and nasal congestion. Sinus headaches (Option D) are associated with facial pressure and nasal discharge, not photophobia. Migraines can occur with or without an aura—neurologic disturbances like scintillating scotomas that often precede the pain
questions.learning: The combination of unilateral, throbbing pain with sensory sensitivities like photophobia and gastrointestinal symptoms like nausea/vomiting is the classic presentation of a migraine headache.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscle causes opening of laryngeal inlet?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroepiglotticus

The laryngeal inlet (aditus of the larynx) is the opening that connects the pharynx to the larynx. Its size is regulated by specific intrinsic laryngeal muscles that either widen or narrow the inlet during breathing and swallowing.

Muscle Responsible for Opening the Laryngeal Inlet: Thyroepiglotticus muscle

• It is an extension of the thyroarytenoid muscle.
• Action: Pulls the epiglottis anteriorly and upward, thereby widening (opening) the laryngeal inlet.
• Helps facilitate air passage during respiration.

Other Muscles:

• Vocalis → Fine adjustment of vocal cord tension for phonation.
• Cricoarytenoid muscles → Mainly control abduction or adduction of vocal cords, not the laryngeal inlet directly.
• Thyroarytenoid → Relaxes vocal cords and narrows the laryngeal vestibule.
questions.learning: Thyroepiglotticus — The laryngeal inlet (aditus of the larynx) is the opening that connects the pharynx to the larynx. Its size is regulated by specific intrinsic laryngeal muscles that either widen or narrow the inlet during breathing and swallowing.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 49-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of watery diarrhea, dehydration, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria. Which of the following neuroendocrine tumors can be responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. VIPoma

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of VIPoma.

Vasoactive intestinal peptide-secreting tumors (VIPomas) are neuroendocrine tumors that secrete excessive amounts of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). The condition is known as Verner–Morrison syndrome or WDHA syndrome.

WDHA stands for:

* WD - Watery Diarrhea

* H – Hypokalemia

* A – Achlorhydria

Diagnosis can be made by the demonstration of an elevated plasma VIP level and the history of large-volume diarrhea.

Treatment includes correction of dehydration, hypokalemia, and electrolyte losses with fluid and electrolyte replacement. Long-acting somatostatin analogs such as octreotide and lanreotide are the drug of choice.

Pearl PF0939: Pancreatic Endocrine Neoplasms

Endocrine neoplasm

Syndrome

Glucagonoma

Mild diabetes mellitus, a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema), and anemia

Insulinoma

Clinically significant hypoglycemia

Gastrinoma

Peptic ulceration often unresponsive to therapy and in unusual locations such as the jejunum

Somatostatinoma

Diabetes mellitus, cholelithiasis, steatorrhea, and hypochlorhydria

VIPoma

Watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria, or WDHA syndrome

Pancreatic polypeptide-secreting endocrine tumors

Present as mass lesions as even high plasma levels of this hormone fail to cause symptoms

* Islet hyperplasia (previously known as nesidioblastosis) is seen in maternal diabetes, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome , and rare mutations in the β-cell K+-channel protein or sulfonylurea receptor.

* In maternal diabetes, the fetal islets respond to hyperglycemia by increasing their size and number. In the postnatal period, these hyperactive islets may be responsible for serious episodes of hypoglycemia.
questions.learning: VIPoma — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of VIPoma. Vasoactive intestinal peptide-secreting tumors (VIPomas) are neuroendocrine tumors that secrete excessive amounts of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which opportunistic pathogen demonstrates a "crushed ping pong ball appearance" on Gomori methenamine stain?
questions.explanation: The opportunistic pathogen Pneumocystis jirovecii is identified by its characteristic "crushed ping pong ball" appearance when viewed under a Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain. This morphology is also described as a helmet, hat, or cup-and-saucer appearance. It typically causes life-threatening interstitial pneumonia in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with HIV whose CD4 counts are below 200. Histoplasma capsulatum (Option A) appears as tiny intracellular oval yeasts within macrophages, not as crushed spheres. Cryptococcus neoformans (Option B) presents as round to oval yeasts with a thick polysaccharide capsule that creates a clear halo on India ink. Aspergillus fumigatus (Option D) is characterized by septate hyphae with acute-angle branching rather than rounded cysts. Consequently, the distinct cystic morphology on silver stain is pathognomonic for Pneumocystis jirovecii. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole remains the cornerstone for prevention and treatment in susceptible populations
questions.learning: The opportunistic pathogen Pneumocystis jirovecii is identified by its characteristic "crushed ping pong ball" appearance when viewed under a Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Glasgow coma scale is a type of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ordinal scale data

Glasgow coma scale is a type of ordinal data as the GCS score can be graded as mild, moderate, and severe based on the order of severity.
questions.learning: Ordinal scale data Glasgow coma scale is a type of ordinal data as the GCS score can be graded as mild, moderate, and severe based on the order of severity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which physiological process operates through a mechanism similar to that of cervical dilation and fetal expulsion during uterine contractions?
questions.explanation: Cervical dilation and uterine contractions during labor are governed by a positive feedback loop known as the Ferguson reflex. As the fetal head stretches the cervix, more oxytocin is released, which in turn causes stronger contractions and further stretching. The physiological process that shares this exact positive feedback mechanism is milk ejection by oxytocin (Option A). Suckling at the breast sends signals to the brain that trigger oxytocin release; the resulting milk ejection encourages the baby to continue suckling, which further stimulates oxytocin release until the breast is emptied. Water retention by ADH (Option B) is a negative feedback loop designed to restore homeostasis. FSH secretion (Option C) is also primarily controlled by negative feedback from estrogen/inhibin. Therefore, the two core "oxytocin-driven" reproductive processes represent the classic examples of positive feedback in human physiology
questions.learning: Cervical dilation and uterine contractions during labor are governed by a positive feedback loop known as the Ferguson reflex. As the fetal head stretches the cervix, more oxytocin is released, which in turn causes stronger contractions and further stretching.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Biosafety level for culture of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. BSL III

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is handled in Biosafety Level III (BSL-III) laboratories.

• MTB is transmitted via airborne droplet nuclei, requiring strict airborne precautions
• BSL-III is designed for pathogens that can cause serious or potentially lethal disease via inhalation
• Laboratory features include:

• Negative pressure rooms
• HEPA-filtered exhaust air
• Controlled access
• Work within biosafety cabinets

Comparison:

• BSL I: non-pathogenic organisms
• BSL II: moderate-risk pathogens (e.g., Staphylococcus, Salmonella)
• BSL III: airborne pathogens (e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
• BSL IV: highly dangerous agents with no treatment (e.g., Ebola virus)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with vomiting and diarrhea occurring about 20 minutes after meals following a Billroth II gastrectomy. What is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this condition?
options: Conversion of Billroth II to Billroth I procedure
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing Early Dumping Syndrome, a common complication following gastric surgeries like a Billroth II gastrectomy. It results from the rapid delivery of hyperosmolar food into the small intestine, leading to fluid shifts and vasomotor symptoms. The most appropriate initial management involves dietary modification, specifically eating small, frequent meals and avoiding large amounts of simple carbohydrates. Patients should also be advised to separate solid food and liquid intake (avoiding drinking with meals). A low-fat diet (Option A) is not the primary focus for dumping. Insulin (Option C) would worsen the hypoglycemia seen in late dumping. Surgical conversion (Option D) is a last resort reserved only for severe cases refractory to all medical and dietary management. Most patients achieve significant symptomatic relief by simply changing their eating habits to slow the transit of food into the jejunum. These dietary adjustments are the cornerstone of post-gastrectomy care

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with hoarseness of Voice. On examination an ulcero-proliferative Mass is seen on Right Vocal Cord, Cord was however mobile. There is no lymph node involvement and no metastasis. Which of the following is the best treatment modality for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Radiotherapy

The patient with superficial exophytic lesions will be advised for radiotherapy.

Cases that do well with radiotherapy:

* Cancer of the vocal cord without impairment of its mobility

* Superficial exophytic lesions

Radiotherapy does not give good results in:

* Lesions with fixed cords

* Subglottic extension

* Cartilage invasion

* Nodal metastases

These lesions require surgery. Cartilage invasion is a contraindication to radiotherapy.

Laryngeal carcinoma is more common in males.

Laryngeal cancer

* Male: Female ratio is 10:1

* Risk factors: Smoking tobacco and alcohol

* 90-95% are squamous

* Most common site: Glottis followed by supraglottis and subglottis.
