questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient complains of decreased distant vision but now he does not use spectacles for near vision. The image of his ocular examination is given below. What is this type of refractive error called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Index myopia

The most likely diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the image is index myopia seen in nuclear senile cataracts.

Index myopia occurs due to an increase in the refractive index of the crystalline lens due to nuclear sclerosis. Nuclear sclerosis is an ageing process in which the lens becomes hard and inelastic resulting in an increase in the refractive index, causing progressive myopia (decreased distant vision). A patient with presbyopia may be able to read again, without the aid of spectacles. This improvement in vision is termed second sight.

Other options:

Option B: Axial myopia is the most common type of myopia resulting due to an increase in the anteroposterior length of the eyeball.

Option C: Curvatural myopia results due to increased curvature of the cornea, lens, or both.

Option D: Positional myopia results due to anterior placement of the crystalline lens in the eye.
questions.learning: Index myopia — The most likely diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the image is index myopia seen in nuclear senile cataracts. Index myopia occurs due to an increase in the refractive index of the crystalline lens due to nuclear sclerosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the content present in the contraceptive shown below?
questions.explanation: The image displays a vaginal contraceptive sponge (such as Today Sponge). These devices are impregnated with a spermicide, and the most common and standard active ingredient used is Nonoxynol-9. Nonoxynol-9 works by disrupting the cell membrane of the spermatozoa, rendering them immobile and unable to fertilize the egg. Menfegol (Option B) and Octoxynol-8 (Option C) are also spermicides, but they are significantly less common in commercial sponge formulations compared to Nonoxynol-9. The sponge provides triple protection by acting as a mechanical barrier over the cervix, absorbing semen, and releasing spermicide over a 24-hour period. While convenient and available over-the-counter, it is less effective than hormonal or intrauterine methods. Clinicians must counsel users that Nonoxynol-9 does not protect against STIs and may even increase the risk of HIV transmission due to localized mucosal irritation
questions.learning: The image displays a vaginal contraceptive sponge (such as Today Sponge). These devices are impregnated with a spermicide, and the most common and standard active ingredient used is Nonoxynol-9.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with complaints of numbness over the mandibular region. Injury to which of the following nerves best explains this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inferior alveolar nerve

The inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, provides sensory innervation to the mandibular teeth and, through its terminal mental nerve, supplies sensation to the chin, lower lip, and skin over the mandibular region. Injury to this nerve causes numbness of the lower lip, chin, and mandibular area.

Why not the other options?

• A. Auriculotemporal nerve: Supplies sensation to the temporal region, external ear, and TMJ.
• B. Masseteric nerve: A motor nerve supplying the masseter muscle.
• D. Lingual nerve: Provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and floor of the mouth, not the skin over the mandible.
questions.learning: Inferior alveolar nerve — The inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, provides sensory innervation to the mandibular teeth and, through its terminal mental nerve, supplies sensation to the chin, lower lip,…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a population with a mean blood glucose level of 105 mg/dL and a standard deviation of 10 mg/dL, assuming a normal distribution, what range of blood glucose values would be expected to include approximately 95% of individuals?
questions.explanation: In a normal distribution (Gaussian distribution), approximately 95% of all data points fall within ±2 standard deviations (SD) from the mean (more precisely ±1.96 SD). Given a mean of 105 mg/dL and an SD of 10 mg/dL, the calculation for the 95% range is: Mean ± (2 × SD) = 105 ± (2 × 10) = 105 ± 20. This results in a range of 85 to 125 mg/dL. Option B (101–110) covers a much narrower range of only ±0.5 SD. Option C (90–125) is an asymmetric range and does not follow the empirical rule. Option D (95–115) represents only ±1 SD from the mean, which accounts for approximately 68% of the population rather than 95%. Therefore, 85–125 mg/dL is the statistically correct range for a 95% confidence interval
questions.learning: In a normal distribution (Gaussian distribution), approximately 95% of all data points fall within ±2 standard deviations (SD) from the mean (more precisely ±1.96 SD).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an indication for expectant management in unruptured ectopic gestation?
options: Initial serum beta hCG level < 200 mIU/mL
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gestational sac size >4 cm

Gestational sac > 4cm is an indication for surgical management of ectopic pregnancy.

Management of ectopic pregnancy:

Expectant management is where only observation is done hoping for spontaneous resolution.

Indications:

* Asymptomatic

* No evidence of bleeding or rupture on TVS

* Initial serum hCG level <200 mIU/mL

* Gestational sac size less than 4 cm

* No fetal heartbeat on TVS

Medical management with intramuscular methotrexate injection, which can be done in single-dose or multidose protocols. The dose for single-dose therapy is 50 mg/m2.

Indications

* Low initial serum beta-hCG level

* Small gestational sac size- 4cm

* Absent fetal cardiac activity

* Hemodynamically stable

Surgical management of ectopic pregnancy includes laparoscopic salpingostomy/ salpingectomy and microsurgical laparotomy.

Indications

* Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met

* Significant pain and hemoperitoneum

* Gestational sac ≥4cm

* Fetal cardiac activity present

* Beta-hCG >5000 mIU/mL

* Failure of expectant or medical management
questions.learning: Gestational sac size >4 cm Gestational sac > 4cm is an indication for surgical management of ectopic pregnancy. Management of ectopic pregnancy: Expectant management is where only observation is done hoping for spontaneous resolution.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures of brachial plexus do not give branches?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Divisions

The divisions in the brachial plexus do not give any branches.

However, the roots, trunks, and cords of the brachial plexus give out direct branches.
questions.learning: Divisions — The divisions in the brachial plexus do not give any branches. However, the roots, trunks, and cords of the brachial plexus give out direct branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Primary follicles arrest in which phase of prophase 1?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diplotene

The correct answer is Diplotene.

Primary oocytes remain arrested in the diplotene (dictyate) stage of prophase I from fetal life until puberty.

This arrest is maintained by oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI) and meiosis resumes only at ovulation.

Leptotene, zygotene, and pachytene are earlier phases of prophase I that do not show physiological arrest.
questions.learning: Diplotene — The correct answer is Diplotene. Primary oocytes remain arrested in the diplotene (dictyate) stage of prophase I from fetal life until puberty.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Sudden painful loss of vision in one eye is due to the lesion at?
questions.explanation: Sudden, painful loss of vision in one eye is the classic clinical presentation of Optic Neuritis, an inflammatory lesion of the optic nerve. This is most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis. The pain is typically retro-orbital and is significantly worsened by eye movements. Lesions at the Optic chiasma (Option B) typically result in bitemporal hemianopia—a painless, bilateral visual field defect. Lesions of the Optic tract (Option C) or the Visual cortex (Option D) cause homonymous hemianopia affecting the field of vision in both eyes, and these are almost always painless. Other causes of sudden vision loss, like Central Retinal Artery Occlusion or Retinal Detachment, are characteristically painless. Therefore, the combination of sudden onset, lateralization to one eye, and localized pain points specifically to an optic nerve pathology. Immediate ophthalmological and neurological evaluation is required, often involving MRI of the brain and orbits to assess for demyelinating disease
questions.learning: Sudden, painful loss of vision in one eye is the classic clinical presentation of Optic Neuritis, an inflammatory lesion of the optic nerve. This is most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Among the following, what is the most common symptom of adult obsessive-compulsive disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pathological doubt

Among the above options, pathological doubt is the common symptom of adult OCD. Pathological doubt is the second most common pattern of adult obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), only after obsession of contamination.

Pathological doubt is an obsession with doubt, followed by a compulsion to check. The obsession often implies some danger of violence e.g., forgetting to turn off the stove or not locking a door. The checking may involve multiple trips back into the house to check the stove. These patients have obsessional self-doubt and always feel guilty about having forgotten or committed something.

The frequency of presenting patterns of OCD :

Obsession of contamination > Pathological doubt > Intrusive thoughts> Symmetry
questions.learning: Pathological doubt Among the above options, pathological doubt is the common symptom of adult OCD. Pathological doubt is the second most common pattern of adult obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), only after obsession of contamination.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 55 year old female complains of lower backache. The radiographic image of her lumbosacral spine is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Osteoporosis

The radiographic image of an elderly female's lumbosacral spine shows ballooning of disc spaces, resulting in the characteristic biconcave appearance of vertebral bodies known as the 'codfish' appearance, typically seen in osteoporosis.

Osteoporosis is a common metabolic bone disease characterised by a diffuse reduction in bone density due to a decrease in bone mass.

Risk factors for osteoporosis include:

• Increasing age
• Female sex
• Alcohol
• Smoking
• Previous history of fragility fractures
• Family history of hip fracture
• Low body mass index- less than 18.5 kg/m2
• Excessive usage of glucocorticoids

Osteoporosis presents with fractures that occur without any trauma or as a result of low-impact trauma. The commonly associated fractures are fractures of the distal part of the radius (Colle's fracture), fractures of the hip, and fractures of the vertebrae. In severe cases, the fracture of vertebrae can cause kyphosis.

Radiological findings:

• A decreased vertical height of the vertebra due to collapse
• Ground glass appearance - especially in bones like pelvis
• Codfish appearance - it occurs due to bulging of the disc into the adjacent vertebral bodies so that it becomes biconcave.

DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of osteoporosis. T-score less than -2.5 in the lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip indicates osteoporosis.
questions.learning: Osteoporosis — The radiographic image of an elderly female's lumbosacral spine shows ballooning of disc spaces, resulting in the characteristic biconcave appearance of vertebral bodies known as the 'codfish' appearance, typically seen in osteoporosis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following will lead to a decrease in diastolic BP?
options: Systemic infusion of smooth muscle relaxant
Systemic infusion of beta-1 adrenergic agonist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loss of lumbar sympathetic outflow

Loss of lumbar sympathetic outflow will lead to a decrease in diastolic blood pressure (DBP).

Loss or blockade of the lumbar sympathetic chain (spinal anaesthesia) causes dilation of capacitance (venous) vessels. This leads to a decrease in diastolic blood pressure and subsequent orthostatic lightheadedness or syncope.

Vasodilation is more marked on the venous than on the arterial side of the circulation, resulting in blood pooling in the venous capacitance vessels. This reduction in circulating blood volume is well tolerated at low levels of spinal anaesthesia in healthy patients. With an increasing level of block, this effect becomes more marked, and venous return becomes gravity-dependent. If venous return decreases too much, cardiac output and organ perfusion decline sharply.

Other options:

Option A: Systemic infusion of alpha-adrenergic blocker will minimally decrease diastolic BP, not significantly like in loss of lumbar sympathetic outflow.

Option C: Systemic infusion of smooth muscle relaxants like Sildenafil, which is a PDE 5 inhibitor (increases cGMP), does not cause a decrease in DBP.

Option D: Systemic infusion of beta-1 adrenergic agonist increases systolic BP and heart rate.
questions.learning: Loss of lumbar sympathetic outflow Loss of lumbar sympathetic outflow will lead to a decrease in diastolic blood pressure (DBP). Loss or blockade of the lumbar sympathetic chain (spinal anaesthesia) causes dilation of capacitance (venous) vessels.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy fell from the bed and developed swelling in the nose and difficulty in breathing. Examination revealed smooth rounded swellings on either side of the septum, through both the nares. On palpation, it was soft and fluctuant. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Incision and drainage

This clinical vignette is strongly suggestive of a septal hematoma. The most appropriate next step in management would be incision and drainage of the hematoma.

Septal hematoma is caused due to collection of blood in between the perichondrium or periosteum and the cartilage of the nasal septum. It may be caused due to trauma, septal surgery, or spontaneously as in bleeding disorders.

Clinically, patients may present with bilateral nasal obstruction, pain, pressure over the nasal bridge, or a frontal headache. On examination, bilateral hematomas will be seen as purplish or reddish smooth swelling on either side of the septum. Palpation will reveal a soft, fluctuant swelling.

All septal hematomas must be drained to prevent the formation of septal abscess or organization of the hematoma by fibrosis leading to a permanently thickened septum. Drainage of the hematoma should be done either through aspiration with a wide gauge needle or through an incision made over the mucosa at the point of greatest fluctuation. It must be followed by nasal packing. Patients should thereafter be started on systemic antibiotics.

Given below are a clinical image and a illustrated image of septal hematoma.

Pearl PF1620: Septal Haematoma

* Septal hematoma is a collection of blood under the perichondrium or periosteum of the nasal septum

* Causes: Trauma, septal surgery and bleeding disorders

* Clinical features: Bilateral nasal obstruction (most common presenting feature), frontal headache

* Treatment:

* Aspiration of small hematomas

* Incision and drainage of large hematomas followed by nasal packing

* Systemic antibiotics to prevent abscess formation

* Complications: Septal abscess, depression of dorsum, permanently thickened septum
questions.learning: Incision and drainage — This clinical vignette is strongly suggestive of a septal hematoma. The most appropriate next step in management would be incision and drainage of the hematoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of these is incorrect about management of hepatoma?
options: Milan criteria is applicable for single tumor up to 5 cm or three tumors each less than 3 cm
A FLR (future liver remnant) of at least 40% normal liver is a pre-requisite for resection
Colorectal metastasis to liver can be excised
Percutaneous ablation is used for hepatomas
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A FLR (future liver remnant) of at least 40% normal liver is a pre-requisite for resection

Management of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC/hepatoma) depends on tumor burden, liver function, and the feasibility of curative therapy (resection, transplantation, ablation). Key concepts:

• Milan criteria define eligibility for liver transplantation in HCC: single tumor ≤5 cm OR up to 3 tumors each ≤3 cm, with no vascular invasion or metastasis.
• Percutaneous ablation (RFA/MWA) is a curative option for small HCC (typically ≤3 cm, selected up to 5 cm).
• Liver metastasis from colorectal cancer is often resectable, and metastasectomy can be curative in selected patients.

Future Liver Remnant (FLR) requirement

The amount of liver that must remain after resection depends on baseline liver quality:

• Normal liver: FLR ≥ 20–25%
• Steatosis/chemotherapy-injured liver: FLR ≥ 30%
• Cirrhotic liver: FLR ≥ 40%

Thus, saying FLR must be at least 40% in normal liver is incorrect (40% is required for cirrhosis, not normal liver).
questions.learning: A FLR (future liver remnant) of at least 40% normal liver is a pre-requisite for resection Management of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC/hepatoma) depends on tumor burden, liver function, and the feasibility of curative therapy (resection, transplantation,…

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with supraspinatus tendinitis. At what degree of shoulder abduction is pain most likely to occur in this condition?
questions.explanation: Supraspinatus tendinitis is a common cause of shoulder pain. The hallmark clinical finding is the "Painful Arc" sign. A patient with this condition typically experiences maximal pain during mid-range shoulder abduction, specifically between 60 and 120 degrees (Option B) . This occurs because the inflamed supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa are compressed against the acromion as the humerus rotates upward through this specific range. Pain from 0-60 degrees (Option A) is less common and may suggest other pathologies. Pain after 120 degrees (Option C) often diminishes as the greater tuberosity cleared the acromion, or it may indicate an AC joint issue. Because the subacromial space is most narrow during the middle of the abduction arc, the 60-120 degree range is the definitive clinical hallmark for subacromial impingement and supraspinatus tendinitis. This is a fundamental concept in orthopedic physical examination of the shoulder
questions.learning: Supraspinatus tendinitis is a common cause of shoulder pain. The hallmark clinical finding is the "Painful Arc" sign.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a painful, red, granular lesion on the vulva along with bilateral lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A painful red granular lesion on the vulva with bilateral painful lymphadenopathy (often forming fluctuant buboes) is the classic presentation of chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. The hallmark of this infection is that the ulcer is markedly tender, unlike syphilis. Regarding the distractors, Gonorrhea (Option B) causes urethritis or pelvic inflammatory disease but not primary genital ulcers. Granuloma Inguinale (Option C) presents with painless, beefy-red ulcers that expand slowly and, notably, lacks lymphadenopathy. Lymphogranuloma Venereum (Option D) typically features an initial painless ulcer that heals quickly, followed later by painful inguinal swelling (the "groove sign"). Because the primary lesion itself is painful and accompanied by immediate nodal involvement, chancroid is the most likely diagnosis. Therefore, H. ducreyi is the causative agent in this clinical scenario
questions.learning: A painful red granular lesion on the vulva with bilateral painful lymphadenopathy (often forming fluctuant buboes) is the classic presentation of chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which element is essential for the conversion of prothrombin into thrombin?
questions.explanation: The coagulation cascade involves a series of enzymatic steps that lead to the formation of a blood clot. One of the final stages is the conversion of prothrombin (Factor II) to thrombin (Factor IIa) by the prothrombinase complex. This complex consists of activated Factor X, Factor V, phospholipids, and ionized Calcium (Option A), which is known as Factor IV in the clotting system. Calcium is essential because it allows the clotting factors to bind to the negatively charged phospholipid surfaces of activated platelets. Without ionized calcium, blood will not clot, which is why anticoagulants like EDTA or citrate work by chelating (binding) calcium. Magnesium (Option B), potassium (Option C), and sodium (Option D) are essential electrolytes for other bodily functions but do not serve as a specific cofactor in the blood clotting cascade. Therefore, calcium is the critical element required for thrombin generation
questions.learning: The coagulation cascade involves a series of enzymatic steps that lead to the formation of a blood clot. One of the final stages is the conversion of prothrombin (Factor II) to thrombin (Factor IIa) by the prothrombinase complex.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient came to the OPD with complaints of vomiting and diarrhoea along with skin eruptions. He gives the history of similar episodes in the past. After switching to gluten free diet his symptoms resolved. Which marker is useful in diagnosing this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anti tissue transglutaminase antibody

The given scenario of vomiting, diarrhoea, skin eruptions and resolving symptoms with gluten free diet along with crypt hperplasia, villous atrophy and intra epithelial lymphocyte as seen in histopathology are suggestive of celiac disease. Anti tissue transglutaminase antibody will help in diagnosing this condition.

Small intestinal adenocarcinoma is also associated with celiac disease.

Celiac disease or celiac sprue or gluten-sensitive enteropathy is triggered by the ingestion of gluten, which is the major storage protein of wheat and similar grains. It usually affects the 2nd part of the duodenum or proximal jejunum.

Antibodies associated with celiac disease are:

• Anti-gliadin antibodies
• Anti tissue transglutaminase antibodies
• Anti endomysial antibodies

MARSH's score is used to assess celiac disease histologically.

Dermatitis herpetiformis occurs in about 10% of patients with celiac disease.

Other options :

Option A : Serological markers that are usually positive in patients with Crohn's disease include the anti–Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody (ASCA).

Option B : Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)-associated vasculitis is categorized into 3 distinct forms:  Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA; formerly Wegener granulomatosis), Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, formerly called Churg–Strauss syndrome (CSS).

Option D : Anti-parietal cell antibody is positive in patients with Pernicious anemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An elderly male who is a known smoker presented with chronic cough, significant weight loss, and fatigue. Serum calcium level is raised. A lung biopsy was done, and it showed large atypical cells with hyperchromasia. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Squamous cell carcinoma

The most probable diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

Squamous cell carcinoma is most commonly found in men and is strongly associated with smoking. It predominantly arises in the central or hilar region. Histologically, it is characterized by the presence of keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.

Hypercalcemia is one of the most common paraneoplastic syndromes associated with squamous cell cancer (SCC) of the lung. Increased levels of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTH-rP) are the most likely mechanism of his hypercalcemia. The symptoms could include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, constipation, lethargy, polyuria, polydipsia, and dehydration.

The image given below shows keratin pearls seen in squamous cell carcinomas.

Other options:

Option A: Large cell neuroendocrine tumor - These tumors are a subtype of large cell carcinoma and show neuroendocrine features on immunohistochemistry. They are aggressive and can be associated with paraneoplastic syndromes, but they do not commonly cause hypercalcemia.

Option B: Small cell carcinoma - This is a highly aggressive neuroendocrine tumor strongly associated with smoking. It frequently presents with paraneoplastic syndromes, including SIADH and ectopic ACTH production, but hypercalcemia is less common. Histologically, it is characterized by small cells with scant cytoplasm, ill-defined cell borders, and finely granular nuclear chromatin.

Option C: Adenocarcinoma - This is the most common type of lung cancer and is more common in non-smokers and women. It usually arises in the peripheral lung tissue and is associated with glandular differentiation or mucin production. Histologically, adenocarcinoma is characterized by glandular or acinar structures and/or intracytoplasmic mucin.
questions.learning: Squamous cell carcinoma — The most probable diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. Squamous cell carcinoma is most commonly found in men and is strongly associated with smoking.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Fluid leaving the proximal convoluted tubule in the absence of antidiuretic hormone is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Isotonic

Fluid leaving the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) in the absence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is isotonic.

The PCT is the site of maximum water reabsorption under normal physiological conditions. It reabsorbs around 60% of the filtered NaCl and water and other nutrients such as glucose and amino acids. Isosmotic reabsorption occurs in the PCT, so the amount of solute and water reabsorbed are coupled and proportional to each other. Here, sodium is reabsorbed along with the water. The large amounts of sodium and water reabsorption are essential in maintaining the ECF volume.

In addition to the isosmotic reabsorption, the water reabsorption in the PCT also occurs through aquaporin-1 which are active water channels. Reabsorption of sodium and water in PCT is not affected by ADH levels. Thus even in the absence of ADH, fluid is isotonic in PCT.
questions.learning: Isotonic Fluid leaving the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) in the absence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is isotonic. The PCT is the site of maximum water reabsorption under normal physiological conditions.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which is the best graft for a femoropopliteal bypass?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Great saphenous vein

The great saphenous vein (GSV) is the best as it lasts longer than polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), dacron, and human umbilical vein as a graft in a femoropopliteal bypass.

The GSV is the conduit of choice for arterial bypass grafts below the inguinal ligament.

For bypass above the inguinal ligament, while both GSV and PTFE grafts have similar patency rates in the first 2 years, the GSV is superior thereafter and hence preferred over PTFE or any other grafts.

The ipsilateral GSV is the conduit of choice for femoropopliteal bypass. When it is not available, contralateral GSV should be used. Other veins are preferred when both ipsilateral and contralateral GSV is not available and they include a small saphenous vein, cephalic vein, and basilic vein.

Non-autogenous grafts are used for patients who lack a suitable venous conduit. The most commonly used prosthetic conduit is PTFE. Recent studies have shown that heparin-bonded PTFE is superior to compared to PTFE without heparin.
questions.learning: Great saphenous vein — The great saphenous vein (GSV) is the best as it lasts longer than polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), dacron, and human umbilical vein as a graft in a femoropopliteal bypass.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with non-pulsatile proptosis that increases when bending down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Orbital varices

This patient with non-pulsatile propotosis that increases on bending down most likely has orbital varices.

Orbital varices:

* They are venous malformations of the orbit caused by vascular dysgenesis.

* Patients usually present with non-pulsatile, intermittent, and reducible proptosis.

* On activities such as forward bending or lowering of the head, turning the head forcefully, hyperextension of the neck, and coughing, the varices fill up, causing proptosis, and then, they regress on shifting to a non-dependent position.

Treatment:

* Small lesions generally do not require treatment

* Surgical excision is technically difficult and often incomplete because the lesions are friable and bleed easily; Specialized techniques such as embolization and carbon dioxide laser surgery may be helpful.

Other options:

Option A: Thyroid eye disease (TED) is the most common cause of both bilateral and unilateral proptosis in an adult in the euthyroid state. The main features of TED include lid retraction, proptosis, periorbital edema, chemosis, and restrictive myopathy.

Option C:  In cavernous sinus thrombosis, proptosis is initially unilateral but soon becomes bilateral due to the spread of infection to the contralateral sinus through the intercavernous communication. Also, cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with high-grade fever with chills, rigor, and headache.

Option D: Orbital cellulitis is the most common cause of unilateral proptosis in children. It refers to the acute infection of the contents of the orbit behind the orbital septum. Features include pain, lid edema, erythema, chemosis, and axial proptosis. Increased pain with movement of eyes and ophthalmoplegia (decreased ocular motility) is a classic symptom.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding the given image?
options: It is associated with facial angiofibroma
They are diagnostic of a neurocutaneous syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is associated with facial angiofibroma

The given image shows discrete tan-colored nodules over the iris called Lisch nodules (pigmented melanocytic hamartomas). They are seen in neurofibromatosis-1 (NF-1). Facial angiofibroma (adenoma sebaceum) is a feature of tuberous sclerosis (TS) and not neurofibromatosis.

The image below shows facial angiofibroma seen in tuberous sclerosis (Bourneville disease).

Lisch nodules are specifically associated with NF-1 and are usually multiple and bilateral. They are best visualized with a slit lamp examination and don’t cause any visual disturbances.

Other important ocular manifestations in NF-1 include eyelid plexiform neurofibroma, which causes S-shaped deformity of the upper lid, with a 'bag of worms' like texture, optic nerve glioma, and spheno-orbital encephalocele due to dysplasia of greater wing of the sphenoid.

NF-1 (von Recklinghausen's disease) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a loss-of-function mutation of the NF-1 gene located on chromosome 17q11.2. NF-1 produces neurofibromin, which acts as a tumor suppressor and a negative regulator of RAS-MAP kinase signaling.

Clinical features of NF-1 include café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules,  neurofibromas, and optic gliomas.
NF-1 is more common than NF2 and typically diagnosed in childhood. NF-2 is rarer but often presents with bilateral acoustic neuroma, juvenile cataract and schwannoma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is true about skeletal muscle contraction?

1. Extracellular Ca2+ is not important for contraction
2. Ca2+ is released from mitochondria
3. Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
4. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels on sarcolemma have no role in EC coupling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 only

During the contraction of the skeletal muscle, the Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Only statement 3 is correct.

Excitation contraction coupling refers to the process by which the membrane depolarization of the muscle fibre (excitation) leads to the contraction of the muscle.

The steps of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle are as follows:

• Motor-neuron discharge causes the release of acetylcholine at the motor endplate, which binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
• This causes increased Na+ and K+ conductance in the endplate membrane, leading to the generation of end-plate potential, which is a local potential.
• When the local endplate potential reaches a threshold for the muscle fibre, and an action potential is generated.
• The generated action potential passes inward through the T tubules, leading to the spread of depolarisation.
• The depolarization of the muscle fibre causes the release of Ca2+ from terminal cisterns of sarcoplasmic reticulum and diffusion to thick and thin filaments.
• The calcium released, binds to troponin C, uncovering myosin-binding sites on actin.
• The formation of cross-linkages between actin and myosin and sliding of thin on thick filaments causes contraction of the skeletal muscle.

Steps in relaxation:

• The cytoplasmic calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, by the action of SERCA (sarcoplasmic endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase).
• Once the calcium concentration is lowered, the interaction between actin and myosin ceases, and the muscle relaxes.

Other options:

Statement 1: Incorrect - Extracellular calcium levels play an important role in muscle contraction. When there is a decrease in extracellular calcium as in hypocalcemia, the voltage-gated sodium channels are activated, which causes sodium influx. The increased intracellular sodium concentration causes sustained depolarization, which may lead to tetany.

Statement 2: Incorrect - Ca2+ is not released from mitochondria. It is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Statement 4: Voltage-gated calcium channels on T-tubules (part of sarcolemma) are activated by a depolarizing stimulus, which causes the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The increased calcium concentration will eventually lead to muscle contraction.
questions.learning: 3 only During the contraction of the skeletal muscle, the Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Excitation contraction coupling refers to the process by which the membrane depolarization of the muscle fibre (excitation) leads to the contraction…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about congenital CMV?
options: 40-50 % of the cases are symptomatic at birth
Optimum sample for PCR is blood/ urine/ saliva sample within 2-3 weeks of birth
If asymptomatic at birth, then there is a higher risk of developing SNHL later
Most common congenital infection after congenital syphilis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Optimum sample for PCR is blood/ urine/ saliva sample within 2-3 weeks of birth

The correct statement regarding CMV infection is optimum sample for PCR is blood/ urine/ saliva sample within 2-3 weeks of birth

CMV is the most common congenital infection (Option D). The clinical manifestations are hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly. One of the long-term sequelae is sensorineural hearing loss. Neuroimaging shows intracranial periventricular calcifications. Other manifestations include IUGR, hydrops, microcephaly, pneumonitis, chorioretinitis, seizures, abnormal dentition, and hypocalcified enamel.

Only 10% of the infected babies are symptomatic (Option A). Asymptomatic neonates have lesser chances of having late sequelae i.e. sensorineural hearing loss. About half of the symptomatic infants develop long-term sequelae which include sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), vision loss, seizure disorders, mental retardation, and developmental delay. However, in asymptomatic infants, only about 13.5% develop long-term sequelae which is commonly SNHL (option C).

Diagnosis can be made by the presence of IgM antibodies in the fetal blood. Isolation of the virus from the urine or blood by PCR is more sensitive. The investigation of choice is PCR or viral culture. It should be done within the first three weeks of life. After this period, it is difficult to distinguish between a congenital and an acquired infection. Since not all affected infants are viremic at birth, urine and/or saliva are more reliable samples than blood (Option B).

There is no definitive treatment for congenital CMV infection. Treatment with ganciclovir is indicated only in patients with progressive neurologic disease and deafness. Below is the image showing the blueberry muffin baby.

questions.text: A woman post-emergency LSCS for preeclampsia with fetal distress. Which is the best drug for thromboprophylaxis postpartum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. LMWH

Pregnancy and postpartum are hypercoagulable states due to physiological changes that prepare the body to prevent bleeding.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient came to the hospital with complaint of abdominal pain. Routine investigations were unremarkable. On observation, the urine turned black on standing. Which of the following enzymes is likely to be defective in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Homogentisate oxidase

Urine turning black on exposure to air is suggestive of alkaptonuria which occurs due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase enzyme.

Alkaptonuria is a disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate. The defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of homogentisate, which is then excreted in the urine. The excreted homogentisate gets oxidized when exposed to the air and causes the urine to turn black.

In some cases, the excessive homogentisate may get oxidized to benzoquinone acetate, which binds to the connective tissue. This leads to arthritis and pigmentation of the connective tissue, a condition called ochronosis.

Other options:

Option B: Xanthine oxidase deficiency results in hypouricemia, xanthinuria, and xanthine lithiasis.

Option C: Defects in phenylalanine hydroxylase can lead to phenylketonuria characterised by hyperreflexia, seizures, hypopigmentation, low IQ, hyperactivity, and tremors.

Option D: Defects in dihydroorotate dehydrogenase are rarely seen in clinical practice. Miller syndrome is associated with this defect.
questions.learning: Homogentisate oxidase Urine turning black on exposure to air is suggestive of alkaptonuria which occurs due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase enzyme.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A person had a dog bite. Vaccination is up to date for both the dog and the man. The person's history is significant for having undergone splenectomy five years ago. What is the best management in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amoxiclav

Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Amoxiclav) is the drug of choice in this patient.

Antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated in:

• High-risk animal bites: cat bites in any location and hand bites by any animals, including humans. Cat and human bites have a higher risk of infection versus dog bites. Moreover, hand bites have a risk of developing an infection in the closed spaces of the hand.
• High-risk patients: comorbidities such as diabetes, liver disease, and absence of functional spleen. Patients without a functional spleen are at an increased risk for overwhelming sepsis primarily due to Capnocytophaga species.

Pasteurella species is the most common isolate from cat and dog bites. Streptococci, S. aureus and Eikenella corrodens are found in human bites. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the first-line drug of choice for prophylaxis. In patients with penicillin allergy, clindamycin plus doxycycline/co-trimoxazole/fluoroquinolone can be used.
questions.learning: Amoxiclav Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Amoxiclav) is the drug of choice in this patient. Antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated in: • High-risk animal bites: cat bites in any location and hand bites by any animals, including humans.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old nulligravid woman presents for evaluation of infertility. She has been unable to conceive for 14 months. One year ago, she stopped taking oral contraceptive pills, which she had used since age 17. Her husband’s semen analysis is normal. Four years ago, she had an episode of pelvic tenderness and vaginal discharge that resolved without treatment. Her menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. Prior to marriage, she was sexually active with three male partners and used condoms inconsistently. She is 169 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 31.6 kg/m². Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s infertility?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Loss of ciliary action

Tubal factor infertility commonly results from prior pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) due to sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

PID causes inflammation and scarring of the fallopian tubes, which leads to:

• Damage to the ciliated epithelial cells of the tube

• Loss of normal ciliary movement required to transport the ovum toward the uterus

• Tubal obstruction or impaired ovum transport, resulting in infertility or ectopic pregnancy

Why other options are less likely:

• Insulin resistance → associated with PCOS, usually with irregular cycles

• Ectopic endometrial tissue → endometriosis, typically causes pelvic pain/dysmenorrhea

• Primary ovarian insufficiency → amenorrhea with elevated FSH
questions.learning: Loss of ciliary action Tubal factor infertility commonly results from prior pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) due to sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A tall male presents with absent pubic and axillary hair, poorly developed genitalia, and markedly elevated levels of LH and FSH. Karyotype analysis reveals an XXY chromosomal pattern. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The 47,XXY karyotype is pathognomonic for Klinefelter's syndrome, the most common sex chromosome disorder in males. The extra X chromosome interferes with testicular development, leading to primary testicular failure (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). This explains the elevated LH and FSH levels (lack of negative feedback) and the underdeveloped genitalia with poor secondary sexual characteristics. Affected individuals are characteristically tall with long limbs. Vanishing testis syndrome (Option A) involves the prenatal loss of testes in a 46,XY male. Noonan syndrome (Option C) is an autosomal dominant condition often called "male Turner syndrome," typically associated with short stature and heart defects. Adrenal hyperplasia (Option D) usually presents with virilization or salt-wasting, not a tall stature with underdeveloped male features. Testosterone replacement therapy is used to manage symptoms and improve bone density, although infertility is usually permanent
questions.learning: The 47,XXY karyotype is pathognomonic for Klinefelter's syndrome, the most common sex chromosome disorder in males. The extra X chromosome interferes with testicular development, leading to primary testicular failure (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presented with seizures which subsided with injection Midazolam. Blood investigations and lumbar puncture studies were normal. MRI is done and the image is given below. What is the next best investigation of choice for further assessment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MR spectroscopy

The given clinical history of a child along with an MRI showing a ring-enhancing intraaxial lesion of the brain could likely be a tuberculoma or neurocysticercosis and MR spectroscopy would be the next best investigation for further assessment.

Magnetic Resonance (MR) spectroscopy is a non-invasive test based on the principle of magnetic resonance used to analyse the metabolite distribution within the brain tissue. It contains N-acetyl aspartate (NAA), a neuronal viability signal; choline (a component of cell membranes and a marker of cellular turnover); creatine (present in metabolically active tissues); lipids (released with cell membrane disruption); and lactate (a hallmark of anaerobic metabolism).

The image below shows a normal MR spectroscopy.

In tuberculoma, MR spectroscopy has reduced NAA owing to the destruction of the normal brain parenchyma and increased levels of lactate or lipids. In neurocysticercosis, there is reduced NAA and creatine and elevated lactate, alanine, succinate, and choline levels.

Other options:

Option B- Ocular B- scan is done to rule out diseases in the posterior segment in the presence of media opacities which is not significant for this case.

Option C- CBNAAT of CSF will not be the next investigation as the lumbar puncture analysis was normal.

Option D- PET-CT is done to assess the stage of cancer and is hence not required in this case.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Patients with which of the following conditions are more susceptible to infections caused by catalase-positive organisms:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic granulomatous disease

Susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms is a hallmark of Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD).

• Defect in NADPH oxidase → impaired respiratory burst
• Phagocytes cannot generate reactive oxygen species to kill ingested microbes

Catalase-positive organisms degrade their own hydrogen peroxide using catalase. Phagocytes cannot utilize microbial H₂O₂ → failure of intracellular killing

Common organisms:

• Staphylococcus aureus
• Serratia marcescens
• Aspergillus species
• Nocardia

Differentiation:

• Hyper IgM → defective class switching
• Job syndrome → impaired neutrophil chemotaxis, recurrent staph infections but not specifically catalase-positive pattern

Chediak-Higashi → lysosomal trafficking defect

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following vaccines produces seroconversion more rapidly than the incubation period of the disease it is meant to prevent?
questions.explanation: In public health and immunology, certain vaccines can be used for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) because the immune system can mount a protective response faster than the virus can complete its incubation period. Measles (Option B) is the classic example of this. The incubation period for measles is approximately 10-14 days, whereas the live-attenuated measles vaccine induces protective antibodies within 3-5 days of administration. Therefore, if a susceptible individual is vaccinated within 72 hours of exposure, the infection can often be prevented or significantly modified. Coronavirus (Option A), Polio (Option C), and Mumps (Option D) have varying incubation periods and seroconversion rates, but they are not the standard examples used to illustrate this specific epidemiological concept as effectively as measles. This property makes measles vaccination a critical emergency response tool during outbreaks in refugee camps or schools. Susceptible contacts of a measles case should always be prioritized for immediate vaccination
questions.learning: In public health and immunology, certain vaccines can be used for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) because the immune system can mount a protective response faster than the virus can complete its incubation period.

Pearl PF0981: National Strategic Plan for Malaria Elimination 2017 - 2022

* The National Strategic Plan (NSP) for Malaria Elimination (2017-22) was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare under NVBDCP, which is based on the National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016 – 2030).

* The NSP focuses mainly on the districts which function as the operational units.

Accordingly all the districts are classified into the following four categories

Category of districts
Definition

Category 0: Prevention of re-establishment phase
Includes all districts in which no incidence of malaria was reported in last three years.

Category 1: Elimination phase
District in which annual parasite incidence (API), is less than one per 1000 population.

Category 2: Pre elimination phase
Districts with API in between one and two per 1000 population.

Category 3: Intensified control phase
Districts having API more than two.

The above classification is more operational than the classification mentioned in the NFME which is state focussed.

The goals of NSP strategy are phased elimination of malaria in India. The National Framework for Malaria Elimination (NFME) in India has set 2030 as goal for eliminating malaria, and the goals of NSP in consonance with overall goals.

The goals of NSP 2017 – 2022 are:

* Eliminate malaria in category 1 (API < 1) districts by 2020, and category 2 (API 1 - 2) districts by 2022.

* Reduce transmission in category 3 districts to stabilize API at less than 1 by 2022

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The appearance of USG at saphenofemoral junction, showing common femoral vein, common femoral artery and the great saphenous vein is called as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mickey mouse sign

The normal anatomy of the femoral vessels and great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction on USG is called the mickey mouse sign.

The given images below show the mickey mouse sign (FV- femoral vein; FA- femoral artery; GSV- great saphenous vein).

Other options:

Option B: String sign (of Kantor) on barium studies appears as a thin, thread-like stream of contrast passing through the stenosed bowel segment, particularly in Crohn's disease.

Option C: Tillaux sign is said to be positive if the mass/swelling is mobile perpendicular to the mesentery attachment line. Tillaux’s sign is seen in a mesenteric cyst.

Option D: Stemmer's sign is the inability to tent the skin at the base of the toes due to skin thickening, as seen in lymphedema.
questions.learning: Mickey mouse sign — The normal anatomy of the femoral vessels and great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction on USG is called the mickey mouse sign.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-day old male neonate who has not yet passed meconium developed abdominal distension. There is no history of fever. On rectal examination, forceful expulsion of stool was observed. A barium enema is performed and the findings are shown in the image below. Which of the following is the gold standard for the diagnosis of the above condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rectal biopsy

The clinical scenario of a newborn presenting with failure to pass meconium, abdominal distension, forceful expulsion of stools on rectal examination, and barium enema showing dilated right colon with a transition zone in the mid-descending colon is suggestive of Hirschsprung's disease. The gold standard for the diagnosis of Hirschprung's disease is a rectal biopsy.

Hirschsprung disease or congenital aganglionic colon is characterized by the absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus and submucosal (Meissner) plexus of the distal intestinal segment. This is because of the premature arrest of normal migration of neural crest cells from the cecum to the rectum.

They are predominantly seen in boys and are associated with Down syndrome. Most cases present during the neonatal period with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and failure to pass meconium. Later they may also have poor feeding and severe constipation. Forceful expulsion of stools is observed on rectal examination as the stools accumulate in the distal colon.

A barium enema is obtained on all suspected cases. This demonstrates the location of the transition zone between the dilated ganglionic colon and the distal aganglionic rectal segment.  In older children, anorectal manometry shows a high internal sphincter pressure due to the absence of normal inhibitory reflex.

Rectal biopsy is the gold standard investigation shows the following:

* Absent ganglia

* Hypertrophied nerve trunks

* Positive immunostaining for acetylcholinesterase

* Calretinin immunostaining (superior to acetylcholinesterase staining)

The definitive surgeries are the Swenson procedure, Duhamel procedure, and Soave's procedure

The most common cause of death in uncorrected Hirschprung's disease is enterocolitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician with abdominal pain and melena. She also complains of progressive fatigue and a 5 kg (11 Ib) weight loss over the last 2 months. She has a strong family history of colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancer. Colonoscopy shows a protuberant, friable mass in the ascending colon, and biopsy is diagnostic for colon adenocarcinoma. Genetic analysis confirms a mutation consistent with Lynch syndrome. Which of the following is most likely responsible for the development of colon cancer in this patient?
options: Insertion of abnormal bases into DNA
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nucleotide mismatches that escape repair

Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer) is caused by mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2. These genes normally correct base–base mismatches and insertion–deletion errors that occur during DNA replication.

Pathogenesis:

Defective mismatch repair leads to accumulation of unrepaired nucleotide mismatches, particularly in repetitive DNA sequences called microsatellites.

This results in microsatellite instability (MSI), which promotes mutations in genes controlling cell growth and apoptosis, leading to early-onset colorectal cancer and other malignancies.
questions.learning: Nucleotide mismatches that escape repair Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer) is caused by mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What type of gait will be seen following a fracture in this region?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High stepping

In the above scenario, the structure marked in the given image is the neck of the fibula. Injury at this site causes failure of dorsiflexion (foot drop) due to injury to the common fibular nerve (also known as common peroneal nerve). Foot drop leads to high stepping gait.

The common peroneal nerve supplies the extensors and evertors of the foot. Injury to the common peroneal nerve results in foot drop. So the patient attempts to lift the leg high enough during walking so that the foot does not drag on the floor. This is known as a high-stepping gait.

The common fibular is derived from the dorsal branches of the L4 - L5 and S1 - S2 ventral rami. It innervates the short head of the biceps femoris in the posterior compartment of the thigh and then continues into the lateral and anterior compartments of the leg and onto the foot.

It gives the following branches:

• Sural communicating nerve (cutaneous branch)
• Lateral sural cutaneous nerve (cutaneous branch)
• Superficial fibular nerve
• Deep fibular nerve.

Injury to the common peroneal nerve will lead to:

• Weakness of dorsiflexion of foot or foot drop
• Loss of dorsiflexion
• Loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the leg and dorsum of the foot.
• Wasting of fibular and anterior tibial muscles.

Other Options:

Option A: Waddling gait is seen in developmental dysplasia of the hip and in proximal muscle weakness.

Option C: Wide-stepping gait is a broad-based unstable gait and is indicative of cerebellar dysfunction.

Option D: Stamping of the foot is seen in tarsal tunnel syndrome. Tarsal tunnel syndrome is a condition with pain and sensory disturbance occurring in the medial part of the forefoot, unrelated to weight-bearing. This is due to compression of the posterior tibial nerve behind and below the medial malleolus. Typically the pain worsens at night and gets relieved on walking or stamping the foot.
questions.learning: High stepping — In the above scenario, the structure marked in the given image is the neck of the fibula. Injury at this site causes failure of dorsiflexion (foot drop) due to injury to the common fibular nerve (also known as common peroneal nerve).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A middle-aged man presented to the OPD with dysuria and purulent urethral discharge for the last 3 days. Gram stain of the discharge is shown below. He admits to having unprotected sexual intercourse one week ago. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Tab. Acyclovir 500 mg TDS for 1 week
Tab. Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days
Inj. Benzathaine Penicillin 2.4 MU IM Stat
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tab. Cefixime 400 mg Stat

This clinical scenario along with the microscopic findings of gram‐negative intracellular diplococci indicates infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The treatment of choice for the infection among the given options would be Tab. Cefixime 400 mg Stat.

Gonorrhea is a disease acquired by sexual contact. The first step in infection is the adhesion of gonococci to the urethra or other mucosal surfaces. The incubation period is 2-8 days. The major symptoms include purulent urethral discharge and dysuria.

In males, the disease starts as acute urethritis presenting with purulent discharge. The patients may also have penile lymphangitis when the soft tissue inflammation is extensive. This infection may extend along the urethra to involve the prostate, seminal vesicles, and epididymis.

In females, the initial infection involves the cervix uteri and urethra which may extend to Bartholin glands, endometrium, and fallopian tubes. Pelvic inflammatory disease and salpingitis may lead to sterility. Rarely peritonitis may develop with perihepatic inflammation (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome).

The discharge is collected and subjected to Gram stain, revealing gram‐negative intracellular diplococci within phagocytes. Stuart's transport medium is used. Cultures can be obtained from chocolate agar or Mueller-Hinton agar. Specifically, Thayer-Martin agar is used to isolate N. gonorrhoeae.

Single-agent therapy with ceftriaxone is preferred for the treatment of gonococcal infections.

According to CDC guidelines (2021), treatment of uncomplicated gonococcal infections is as follows:

• Weight <150 kg – Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscular (IM) in a single dose
• Weight ≥150 kg – Ceftriaxone 1 g IM in a single dose

The doses of ceftriaxone are higher than the previous guidelines as the gonococcal minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) are rising worldwide. The British BASHH guidelines also recommend a high dose of 1g. Other cephalosporins like Cefixime can be given orally.

Concurrent chlamydial infection must also be treated unless it has been excluded by molecular testing.

First-line drug administered is

• Oral doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days

As per Suraksha clinic, syndromic management of Urethral discharge is done by Gray kit which contains Tab. Azithromycin 1gm stat and Tab. Cefixime 400mg stat.    Partner treatment is also required.

Other options:

Option A: Acyclovir is given for viral infections. It has no role in gonococcal urethritis

Option B: Doxycycline is given alongside Ceftriaxone or cefixime to concurrently treat chlamydial infection along with gonorrhoea.

Option D: Benzathine Penicillin was once a treatment option for gonorrhoea, but it is no longer recommended due to widespread resistance.
questions.learning: Cefixime 400 mg Stat — This clinical scenario along with the microscopic findings of gram‐negative intracellular diplococci indicates infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In case of a chemical injury to the eye, what is the immediate first step in the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Copious irrigation with saline

Chemical injury to the eye is an absolute ocular emergency, and the immediate first step is copious irrigation with saline (or any clean fluid available).

• Chemicals (especially alkali) penetrate rapidly and cause ongoing tissue damage
• Immediate dilution and removal of the chemical limits severity of injury and improves prognosis

Key management principles:

• Start irrigation immediately (do NOT delay for history or examination)
• Use normal saline, Ringer lactate, or even clean water if nothing else is available
• Continue until ocular surface pH normalizes (≈ 7–7.4)
• Evert eyelids to remove retained particles

Why not others:

• Visual acuity, history, IOP measurement → important but only after irrigation
• Any delay worsens corneal and limbal damage

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding an esophageal foreign body?
options: Most common site of impaction is at level of cricopharyngeus
One of the constrictions of the esopahgus is at the level of the right bronchus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Most common site of impaction is at level of cricopharyngeus

The correct statement with regard to the oesophageal foreign body in the image is that the most common site of impaction is at the level of the cricopharyngeus.

Foreign bodies commonly ingested by children are coins, disk batteries, and small toy items. In adults, it is usually a food bolus (mostly meat) that gets lodged.

The flat surface of a coin is seen on the anteroposterior view (AP view) and the edge is seen on the lateral view. This indicates that it is oriented in the coronal plane, which is seen when it is lodged in the esophagus (and not in the trachea).

Initial symptoms are choking, gagging, and coughing followed by excessive salivation, dysphagia, food refusal, vomiting, or pain in the neck and throat. Respiratory symptoms such as stridor, wheezing, cyanosis, or dyspnea are seen if the esophageal foreign body impinges on the larynx or tracheal wall. Imaging with chest and abdominal X-rays should be performed in AP and lateral positions. Chest CT should always be performed if oesophageal perforation is suspected.

Endoscopic removal of the esophageal foreign body is the procedure of choice. It should be performed

• Immediately in esophageal obstruction, disk batteries, and sharp pointed objects.
• Within 12-24 hours in non-pointed objects, pointed objects in the stomach, and coins in the esophagus.
• Non-urgent removal in objects in stomach >2.5cm in diameter, and disk battery in the stomach (up to 48h)

Other options:

Option A: If a foreign body becomes lodged in the esophagus and causes perforation, it can lead to mediastinitis, a potentially life-threatening infection of the mediastinum.

Option C: Esophageal foreign bodies are more commonly seen in children, although they do occur in adults, particularly in those with underlying esophageal abnormalities (e.g., strictures or motility disorders).

Option D: The esophagus has several natural constrictions, including at the cricopharyngeus (C6 level), at the aortic arch, at the level of the left main bronchus and at the diaphragmatic hiatus.
questions.learning: Most common site of impaction is at level of cricopharyngeus The correct statement with regard to the oesophageal foreign body in the image is that the most common site of impaction is at the level of the cricopharyngeus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with pelvic fracture and membranous urethral rupture. What should be the initial management?
options: A suprapubic catheter should be inserted as soon as possible
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A suprapubic catheter should be inserted as soon as possible

The initial management should be insertion of suprapubic catheter.

A suprapubic catheter should be inserted as soon as practicable. The distended bladder may be palpable making suprapubic catheterization straightforward, but often the bruising and swelling associated with the fracture makes this difficult and ultrasound guidance is required.

Passing a catheter blindly per urethra may convert a partial tear into a complete tear and it may also lead to false passages.

A retrograde urethrogram should also be done as soon as possible to see the extent of the rupture.
questions.learning: A suprapubic catheter should be inserted as soon as possible The initial management should be insertion of suprapubic catheter. A suprapubic catheter should be inserted as soon as practicable.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An MRCP image is shown below. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Choledocholithiasis

The given MRCP image shows multiple round filling defects within the common bile duct indicative of choledocholithiasis.

Choledocholithiasis or common bile duct stones are classified based on their point of origin. Choledocholithiasis is mostly clinically silent but may present with biliary colic and even obstructive jaundice. Management of choledocholithiasis includes ERCP +/- sphincterotomy followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

MRCP uses the fluid which is present in the biliary and pancreatic ducts as a contrast agent and does not require external contrast material administered into the ductal system. It is a non-invasive investigation for evaluating extrahepatic, intrahepatic bile duct, and pancreatic duct. No interventions are performed under MRCP.

MRCP uses T2 weighted  MRI and it recognizes slow-flowing or stationary fluid within ducts, which appear brighter relative to adjacent solid tissues. MRCP can be used to evaluate various conditions of the pancreaticobiliary ductal system, examples include:

• Congenital anomalies of the cystic and hepatic ducts
• Post-surgical biliary anatomy
• Pancreas divisum
• Anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction
• Choledocholithiasis
• Biliary structures
• Chronic pancreatitis
• Pancreatic cystic lesions
• Trauma to the biliary system

MRCP in benign strictures would typically show smooth elongated tapering of the bile duct, while malignancy-associated strictures typically show abrupt shouldering.
questions.learning: Choledocholithiasis — The given MRCP image shows multiple round filling defects within the common bile duct indicative of choledocholithiasis. Choledocholithiasis or common bile duct stones are classified based on their point of origin.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus developed the following rhythm. His blood pressure was 90/40 mm Hg and he had a feeble pulse. What is the next step of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. DC cardioversion

The clinical scenario suggests supraventricular tachycardia with hemodynamic instability and the next step of management is DC cardioversion (50-100J).

If the patient was hemodyamically stable, initial treatment would be vagal maneuvers (Valsalva maneuver) in awake patients. This is because vagal maneuvers alone can terminate approximately 20% to 25% of reentry supraventricular tachycardias (SVTs).

If this is unsuccessful, then iv adenosine 6 mg is given. If necessary another dose of adenosine 12 mg may be administered after 1-2 minutes.

If the drug is administered via a central venous catheter, then these doses are reduced to 3 mg and 6 mg respectively.
questions.learning: DC cardioversion — The clinical scenario suggests supraventricular tachycardia with hemodynamic instability and the next step of management is DC cardioversion (50-100J).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which additional drug can be added for a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) who is already using inhaled salmeterol but reports no clinical improvement on follow-up?
questions.explanation: In the management of stable COPD, therapy is escalated by combining different classes of bronchodilators. The patient is already taking Salmeterol, a Long-Acting Beta-Agonist (LABA). The most appropriate and standard "next step" is to add an anticholinergic agent, such as Ipratropium (a short-acting muscarinic antagonist) or Tiotropium (a LAMA). These drugs provide synergistic bronchodilation by blocking parasympathetic-mediated airway constriction. Theophylline (Option A) is a second or third-line oral bronchodilator with a narrow therapeutic window. Azithromycin (Option B) is used for its anti-inflammatory properties in frequent exacerbators but is not a primary bronchodilator. Oral glucocorticoids (Option C) are reserved for acute exacerbations rather than daily maintenance therapy due to significant systemic side effects. Therefore, adding an inhaled muscarinic antagonist like Ipratropium to the existing LABA is the definitive clinical strategy to improve pulmonary function
questions.learning: In the management of stable COPD, therapy is escalated by combining different classes of bronchodilators. The patient is already taking Salmeterol, a Long-Acting Beta-Agonist (LABA).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man is found to have a rectal mass on digital rectal examination, despite having no history of altered bowel habits. If rectal carcinoma is suspected, what is the most appropriate next step in the evaluation or management of this patient?
questions.explanation: In a patient with a rectal mass detected on digital rectal examination, the next step is to confirm the diagnosis and evaluate the entire colon. A full colonoscopy allows direct visualization of the rectal lesion and enables biopsy for histopathological confirmation, which is essential before planning treatment. Importantly, colonoscopy also helps detect synchronous lesions elsewhere in the colon, which are present in a small but significant number of patients with colorectal cancer. Although rigid sigmoidoscopy can visualize and biopsy a rectal lesion, it is limited to the distal bowel and may miss proximal pathology. Therefore, it is not sufficient as a complete evaluation. A CT scan of the abdomen is used for staging after diagnosis, not for initial confirmation. A barium enema is largely outdated and has been replaced by endoscopic techniques. Thus, the most appropriate next step is full colonoscopy with biopsy, as it provides both diagnostic confirmation and complete colonic assessment

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the Maha Kumbh mela, what was the primary purpose of Mobile medical vans having multiple surveillance units for fever, diarrhoea and respiratory illnesses?
options: To reduce number of health workers and professionals
For immediate quarantine measures of symptomatic individuals
To diagnose with lab tests and give potential warning for early outbreaks of fever, diarrhoea, respiratory infections
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. To diagnose with lab tests and give potential warning for early outbreaks of fever, diarrhoea, respiratory infections

During mass gatherings like the Maha Kumbh Mela, mobile medical vans with surveillance units function as early warning systems. Such mass gatherings create a high risk for communicable disease outbreaks due to overcrowding, poor sanitation, shared water sources, high person-to-person contact & rapid movement of people.

They enable rapid diagnosis, syndromic surveillance, and real-time data collection for fever, diarrhoeal, and respiratory illnesses, allowing early detection of outbreaks and timely public health response. In India, surveillance is mainly conducted under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP).
questions.learning: To diagnose with lab tests and give potential warning for early outbreaks of fever, diarrhoea, respiratory infections During mass gatherings like the Maha Kumbh Mela, mobile medical vans with surveillance units function as early warning systems.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A tuberculosis patient on anti-tubercular treatment presents with a tingling sensation and paresthesia in the lower limbs. He is not a diabetic and occasionally consumes alcohol. Which of the following vitamins must be supplemented to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B6

Vitamin B6 must be supplemented for this patient. The clinical features of tingling sensation and paresthesias in a patient on anti-tubercular treatment are suggestive of the adverse effect of isoniazid.

Isoniazid is the first-line antitubercular drug that inhibits the production of mycolic acid. It is a bactericidal drug against tubercle bacilli.

Adverse effects of isoniazid:

• Peripheral neuritis (paresthesias, numbness, tingling sensation) due to interference with the production of active coenzyme pyridoxal phosphate from pyridoxine. Therefore, pyridoxine 10 mg/day (vitamin B6) is given prophylactically along with isoniazid to prevent neurotoxicity.
• Hepatitis - isoniazid must be stopped at the first sign of hepatotoxicity.
• Rashes
• Anemia
• Arthralgia

Toxicity of isoniazid results in metabolic acidosis and seizures.

Note: Vitamin deficiency in alcoholics includes the following:

• Folate causes megaloblastic anemia. It is treated by supplementation of oral doses of 5-15 mg of folic acid.
• Vitamin B6 results in peripheral neuritis, anemia, and glossitis, and lowers the seizure threshold. It is treated by supplementation of oral doses of 2-5 mg of pyridoxine.
• Thiamine results in Wernicke's encephalopathy. It is treated with 200 mg of intravenous thiamine three times daily, followed by 10 mg/day until complete recovery.
• Vitamin A results in xerophthalmia and night blindness. It is treated with supplementation of oral vitamin A 3000-5000 IU/day.
questions.learning: Vitamin B6 Vitamin B6 must be supplemented for this patient. The clinical features of tingling sensation and paresthesias in a patient on anti-tubercular treatment are suggestive of the adverse effect of isoniazid.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The mechanism by which glucose is absorbed in the intestine is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secondary active transport

Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport.

On the basolateral side, there is active transport of sodium ions out of the cell into the interstitial fluid. This depletes sodium inside the cell. Because of this Na+ concentration difference, more Na+ binds to the SGLT on the luminal side. This increases the affinity of SGLT for glucose and glucose binds to it.

Then, both the Na+ and glucose are transported together to the interior of the cell. Thus, glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport. The energy for glucose transport is provided indirectly, by the active transport of Na+ out of the cell. The glucose moves out of the cell into the blood across the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion mediated via GLUT.
questions.learning: Secondary active transport Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport. On the basolateral side, there is active transport of sodium ions out of the cell into the interstitial fluid.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In alleged history of gunshot injury, there is burning, blackening, tattooing around the wound. The injury is:
