questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The most common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rossenmuller which is marked 3 in the image.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx. The theories for etiology include genetics, infection with Epstein-Barr virus, air pollution, and smoking.

The WHO classification of three types of nasopharyngeal carcinoma includes

* Keratinising

* Nonkeratinising differentiated

* Nonkeratinising undifferentiated

The most common site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rosenmuller. From here, it can spread extensively in any direction locally. It also can spread lymphatically to the cervical, retropharyngeal, or parapharyngeal lymph nodes.

Trotter's triad consists of ipsilateral conductive hearing loss (eustachian tube blockage), trigeminal neuralgia of the mandibular division, and palatal asymmetry due to invasion of levator palatini muscles may be seen. This triad occurs in malignant tumors of the lateral nasopharyngeal wall due to extensive invasion.

Diagnosis is made by high-resolution, contrast-enhanced CT of the neck. The treatment of choice is radiotherapy. Stage I and II can be treated with radiotherapy alone, while higher stages require combination treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

Given below is the labelled diagram showing the fossa of Rossenmuller, eustachian tube, and torus tubaris.
questions.learning: 3 The most common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rossenmuller which is marked 3 in the image. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Melanin is derived from which of the following amino acids?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tyrosine

Melanin is derived from tyrosine.

Products derived from tyrosine:

* Melanin

* Catecholamines e.g epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine

* Thyroxine

Tyrosine is a precursor of melanin, thyroxin, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA).

* Formation of DOPA: Tyrosine is hydroxylated by tyrosinase to form dihydroxy phenylalanine or DOPA. Tyrosinase is a monooxygenase that contains copper.

* Formation of melanin: Tyrosinase acts on DOPA to form dopaquinone, which is then converted to indolequinone. The indolequinone is polymerized to form melanin.

* Formation of catecholamines: Epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. They are produced by the adrenal medulla and sympathetic ganglia.

* Tyrosine is first hydroxylated to dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) by tyrosine hydroxylase.

* DOPA is decarboxylated by DOPA decarboxylase to form dopamine.

* Dopamine is further hydroxylated to norepinephrine or noradrenaline

* Norepinephrine is then methylated by the enzyme N-methyl transferase (NMT) to form epinephrine or adrenaline. S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) is the methyl donor.

The series of reactions involving the production of catecholamines is shown in the image below.

* Formation of thyroid hormones: Tyrosine residues are iodinated to form 3-mono-iodo-tyrosine (MIT) and 3,5-di-iodo-tyrosine (DIT). These are coupled to give rise to triiodothyronine (T3) and tetraiodothyronine (thyroxine or T4)

The derivatives of other amino acids are given in the image below.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 56-year-old male, chronic heavy smoker, presented with breathlessness. On examination, pulse 96/min, BP 112/70 mm Hg and a pansystolic murmur showing Carvallo’s sign with murmur getting louder on deep inspiration. Which one of the following statements is true regarding examination of JVP in him?
options: C wave is attenuated and V wave is accentuated
V wave and C wave merge
V wave and C wave merge and Y descent is blunted
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. V wave and C wave merge

The patient has tricuspid regurgitation (TR), suggested by a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign). In TR, regurgitation of blood into the right atrium during systole produces giant C-V (CV) waves due to fusion of the C and V waves in the JVP.

Why not the other options?

• A. V wave is attenuated: Incorrect. V wave is markedly prominent in TR.
• B. C wave is attenuated and V wave is accentuated: Incorrect. The C and V waves fuse, forming a giant CV wave.
• D. V wave and C wave merge and Y descent is blunted: Incorrect. Y descent is brisk (prominent) in TR due to rapid right atrial emptying; a blunted Y descent is seen in cardiac tamponade.
questions.learning: V wave and C wave merge — The patient has tricuspid regurgitation (TR), suggested by a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not characteristic of the clinical condition given below?
options: Abnormal activity of p53 is seen in the pterygium tissue.
Decreased activity of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases is seen.
Destruction of Bowman's layer occurs when the pterygium invades the cornea.
Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the connective tissue of the conjunctiva occur.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the connective tissue of the conjunctiva occur.

Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the conjunctival connective tissue occurs in pinguecula (and not pterygium).

In pterygium, there is elastotic degeneration of collagen with fibrovascular proliferation.

It is important to distinguish a pterygium from a pinguecula. A pterygium, while histologically similar to a pinguecula, is distinguished by fibrovascular tissue that grows onto the cornea. Pingueculae do not have vascularized tissue and do not cross the limbus.

Pterygium is a subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a degenerative condition of the sub-conjunctival tissue and is never inflammatory. It occurs due to exposure to UV-B radiation and the most common site is the nasal.

It is made up of three parts-a "cap" (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge), a head, and a body.

Clinical features:

* Astigmatism with the rule - most common finding

* Stocker's line - deposition of iron on the advancing edge

* Fuchs islets - small, discrete, whitish flecks consisting of clusters of pterygial epithelial cells, often present at the advancing edge.

The differential diagnosis is pseudo pterygium.

Pterygium
Pseudo-pterygium

Degenerative process
Inflammatory process

Occurs in elderly
Can occur at any age

Situated at the palpebral aperture
Can occur at any site

Either progressive, regressive, or stationary
Always stationary

A probe cannot be passed underneath
A probe can be passed under the neck

The treatment for pterygium is usually excision. To prevent a recurrence, mitomycin C or 5 fluorouracil is used. Other methods:

* Auto-grafting- Conjunctival limbal autograft (CLAG) from the superior limbal conjunctiva is the best method.

* Bare sclera technique- high recurrence rate of 30 to 80%.

* PERFECT surgery- zero rates of recurrence. (PERFECT stands for Pterygium Extended Removal Followed by Extended Conjunctival Transplant)
questions.learning: Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the connective tissue of the conjunctiva occur. Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the conjunctival connective tissue occurs in pinguecula (and not pterygium).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A deceased male was brought to the morgue for a post-mortem examination. His relatives reported that he had a tattoo over his skin, which was not found on examination. Which of the following structures would you examine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymph nodes

The lymph nodes should be examined in this case.

Some amount of material or dye used for creating tattoo marks is transported through lymph to the regional lymph nodes. Hence, in cases where a tattoo mark has disappeared naturally or has been removed, the lymph nodes must be examined.
questions.learning: Lymph nodes — The lymph nodes should be examined in this case. Some amount of material or dye used for creating tattoo marks is transported through lymph to the regional lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man came with complaints of recurrent discharge and pain due to lesions around the anus for 3 years. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fistula in ano

The given clinical scenario of recurrent pain and discharge due to lesions around the anus, shown in the image is likely to be a fistula-in-ano.

A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal connection between the anal canal and the perianal skin, lined with granulation tissue. It may follow the drainage of a perianal abscess or may be seen in association with diseases like tuberculosis or Crohn's disease.

Clinical features are perianal pain, swelling, and intermittent purulent discharge, which might be blood-stained. On examination, one or more external openings may be visible.

Goodsall’s rule can be used as a guide in determining the location of the internal opening of the fistula. Fistulas with an external opening anteriorly connect to the internal opening by a short, radial tract. Fistulas with an external opening posteriorly track in a curvilinear fashion to the posterior midline.

However, exceptions to this rule often occur. Fistulas with an anterior external opening greater than 3 cm from the anal margin usually track to the posterior midline.

The investigations done for fistula-in-ano can include a fistulogram, endoanal ultrasound with hydrogen peroxide, MRI, and computed tomography (CT) scan. An MRI is the gold standard investigation for fistula imaging. It helps us to identify the secondary extensions of the track, which when missed may cause persistence of the fistula.

Surgical management includes fistulotomy, fistulectomy, ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract (LIFT), setons, or advancement flaps.
questions.learning: Fistula in ano — The given clinical scenario of recurrent pain and discharge due to lesions around the anus, shown in the image is likely to be a fistula-in-ano.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient from Uttar Pradesh presented with fever, pallor, and hepatosplenomegaly. Peripheral smear examination showed pancytopenia. Buffy coat examination showed macrophages laden with organisms with a kinetoplast. What is the vector for the likely disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sandfly

From the given clinical features, the most likely disease is visceral leishmaniasis or Kala azar caused by Leishmania donovani, and the vector is sandfly. A patient from Uttar Pradesh presenting with fever, pallor, and hepatosplenomegaly with a smear examination showing pancytopenia and macrophages containing organisms with kinetoplasts point towards the diagnosis.

Leishmaniasis is transmitted by the bite of an infected female Phlebotomus sandfly. In India, it is endemic to Bihar, West Bengal, Jharkhand, and Uttar Pradesh. Patients present with high fever, hepatosplenomegaly, weight loss, and emaciation. The skin becomes dry, rough, and darkly pigmented. There is anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia.

The parasite exists in 2 forms:

• Amstigote form (also called LD bodies)- It is seen within macrophages and contains a kinetoplast.
• Promastigote form- It is the infective form in the sandfly. The kinetoplast is seen at the anterior end.

Kinetoplast are non-nuclear DNA present in addition to nucleus. They consist of blepharoplast and parabasal body. Flagellum originates near the kinetoplast.

Diagnosis of kala-azar is mainly by demonstration of amastigotes within macrophages in tissue aspirates such as blood smears, bone marrow, splenic, or lymph node aspirate. It is the gold standard for diagnosis.

The image below shows amastigotes located intracellularly within macrophages.

Treatment is with a pentavalent antimonial compound. In Bihar, there is resistance to antimony so amphotericin-B-deoxycholate or miltefosine is preferred.

In human beings, different species of Leishmania can cause the following diseases:

• Visceral leishmaniasis, or kala-azar,
• Cutaneous leishmaniasis,
• Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, and
• Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis.

The life cycle of Lesihmania is shown below.

Other options:

Option B: Tse-Tse fly (Glossina species) is involved in the transmission of sleeping sickness or African trypanosomiasis. It is caused by Trypanosoma brucei. The patient can have hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy in the early stages and later on CNS involvement is seen. Blood routine examination would reveal anemia, leucocytosis, and thrombocytopenia.

Option C: Triatomine bug (Reduviid bug/ kissing bug) transmits Trypanosoma cruzi infection leading to Chaga's disease or American trypansomiasis. The acute phase of the disease is characterized by a typical subcutaneous lesion at the site of inoculation called chagoma. In the chronic phase, multiorgan involvement occurs leading to cardiac myopathy, megaesophagus, and megacolon.

Option-D: Female anopheles mosquito leads to the transmission of malaria caused by Plasmodium species. Malaria can present with fever and hepatosplenomegaly but the morphological forms commonly include the ring forms or the gametocytes.
questions.learning: Sandfly From the given clinical features, the most likely disease is visceral leishmaniasis or Kala azar caused by Leishmania donovani, and the vector is sandfly.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a patient with Wilson's disease which of the following is decreased in urine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3-methylhistidine

Urinary levels of 3-methylhistidine are decreased in patients with Wilson disease.

Amino acids in urine exist either in conjugated form (most) or in free form. In Wilson's disease the amount of conjugated amino acids far exceeds the amount of free amino acids. Methyl Histidine largely exists in free form and does not increase in amount on hydrolysis of acids in urine. Hence low amounts is seen in Wilson's disease.

Wilson disease is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by mutation of the ATP7B gene located on chromosome 13. The ATP7B gene, encodes a transmembrane copper-transporting ATPase, expressed on the hepatocyte canalicular membrane.

Deficiency in the ATP7B protein causes a decrease in copper excretion into the bile, impairs its incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and inhibits ceruloplasmin secretion into the blood, leading to the accumulation of toxic levels of copper in the liver, brain, and eye.
questions.learning: 3-methylhistidine Urinary levels of 3-methylhistidine are decreased in patients with Wilson disease. Amino acids in urine exist either in conjugated form (most) or in free form.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient develops numbness after taking a medication for migraine, and his hand appears as shown in the image. Which drug is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The image shows signs of Raynaud's phenomenon (numbness and digital discoloration), which is a classic side effect of ergot alkaloids like dihydroergotamine. These drugs act as partial agonists at 5-HT1B/1D receptors to cause vasoconstriction for treating acute migraine. However, their potent vasoconstrictive properties can extend to the peripheral arteries, leading to digital ischemia and, in severe cases, gangrene. Sumatriptan (Option B) is a more selective triptan that also causes vasoconstriction but is not typically associated with the peripheral vascular compromise and digital discoloration seen here. Butorphanol (Option C) is an opioid that does not cause vasoconstriction. Aspirin (Option D) is an NSAID that lacks significant vasoactive properties. Therefore, the specific development of hand ischemia following migraine therapy points to ergotamine-induced vasoconstriction
questions.learning: The image shows signs of Raynaud's phenomenon (numbness and digital discoloration), which is a classic side effect of ergot alkaloids like dihydroergotamine.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A group of students ate fried rice at a restaurant and began vomiting six hours later. What is the most likely etiological agent?
questions.explanation: The rapid onset of vomiting (within 1–6 hours) following the consumption of fried rice is the classic presentation of the emetic form of Bacillus cereus food poisoning. This form is caused by a heat-stable toxin produced by the bacteria when cooked rice is left at room temperature, allowing spores to germinate. Clostridium botulinum (Option B) causes botulism, which presents with descending paralysis and lacks significant vomiting; symptoms usually appear much later (12–36 hours). Escherichia coli (Option C), specifically ETEC, causes watery diarrhea after a longer incubation period (12–72 hours) and is not primarily associated with rapid-onset vomiting. Shigella dysenteriae (Option D) causes bacillary dysentery, characterized by bloody diarrhea, fever, and abdominal cramps, typically appearing 1–3 days after ingestion. Therefore, the specific combination of a rice-based vehicle and early-onset emesis identifies Bacillus cereus as the most likely causative agent in this scenario
questions.learning: The rapid onset of vomiting (within 1–6 hours) following the consumption of fried rice is the classic presentation of the emetic form of Bacillus cereus food poisoning.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Cyanosis is most likely to be seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Eisenmenger syndrome

Eisenmenger syndrome is the most common cause of cyanosis in patients with congenital heart disease due to reversal of a long-standing left-to-right shunt into a right-to-left shunt following the development of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension. Cyanosis appears because deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs and enters the systemic circulation.

Why is D correct?

• Eisenmenger syndrome results from irreversible pulmonary vascular disease causing right-to-left shunting, leading to:

• Central cyanosis
• Digital clubbing
• Secondary polycythemia
• Exertional dyspnea

Why not the other options?

• A. Atrial septal defect (ASD): Typically produces a left-to-right shunt and is acyanotic unless Eisenmenger physiology develops.
• B. Partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection (PAPVC): Usually causes a left-to-right shunt and is an acyanotic congenital heart disease.
• C. Advanced aortic stenosis: Causes obstruction to left ventricular outflow with syncope, angina, and heart failure but does not cause cyanosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient who suffers from prinzmetal angina requires a formulation of nitroglycerine which has the most rapid onset of action. Which of the following formulations of nitroglycerin can be administered to the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sublingual spray

The sublingual route of administration has a very rapid onset of action (1-3 mins). The onset of action is more rapid when administered as a spray when compared to a tablet.

The sublingual route is used for the termination of attacks. Oral extended-release capsule and transdermal patch are used for prophylaxis. The onset of action is approximately ≥60 min.

Topical nitroglycerine ointment can be used to provide symptomatic relief in patients with anal fissures.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about the management of HIV patient with multiple dog bites?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rabies vaccine + immunoglobuin+ wound management

In the given scenario, an HIV patient with multiple dog bites falls under Category 3 for rabies vaccination and should receive rabies vaccine, immunoglobulin, and proper wound care.

Rabies is a fatal viral disease transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal, primarily dogs. Rabies vaccination is the most effective way to prevent the disease after exposure.

The post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimen includes thorough wound cleaning, administration of the rabies vaccine, and in severe cases (Category 3 exposure), rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) for immediate virus neutralization. The rabies vaccine is administered in a series of intramuscular or intradermal doses, following schedules like the Essen regimen (0, 3, 7, 14, and 28 days) or the Zagreb regimen (0, 7, and 21 days). Immediate treatment is crucial, as rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms appear.

In addition to post-exposure vaccination, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is recommended for individuals at high risk, such as veterinarians, animal handlers, and travellers to rabies-endemic regions. The PrEP schedule consists of two doses on days 0 and 7, with an optional booster if needed. Mass vaccination of dogs and public awareness programs are essential for rabies prevention and control. Since human rabies cases are still reported in many countries, widespread vaccination efforts play a critical role in achieving the WHO goal of eliminating human rabies deaths by 2030.

Pearl PF1934: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules

According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India:

WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately.

One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size.

Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted).

Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG):

* Passive immunization

* Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine

* Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight

* Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG.

* Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus.

Administration of RIG:

* RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites.

* The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration.

* RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated.

Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order):

* Multiple bites

* Deep wounds

* Bites to head, neck, and hands

* Patients with severe immunodeficiency

* Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal

* Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)

PrEP is considered in the following conditions:

* High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions.

* Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult

* Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year

* Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present.

Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of two intramuscular (IM) or two intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0 and 3.

* Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm

* Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended.

* Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers.

For exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP the following guidelines would be applicable:

* Proper wound management should be done.

* There is no need for the administration of RIG.

* One site ID or IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3.

Only adequate wound washing would be required in case of re-exposure where the animal bite victim has documented proof of complete PEP within the last three months.

The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP:

* Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency

* Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment
questions.learning: Rabies vaccine + immunoglobuin+ wound management — In the given scenario, an HIV patient with multiple dog bites falls under Category 3 for rabies vaccination and should receive rabies vaccine, immunoglobulin, and proper wound care.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Posterior interosseous nerve injury causes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of extension at finger

The correct answer is loss of extension at fingers.

The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) supplies the finger and thumb extensors.

Wrist extension is largely preserved due to extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, so wrist drop does not occur.

Supination is mainly by biceps brachii and supinator, which are not significantly affected.
questions.learning: Loss of extension at finger — The correct answer is loss of extension at fingers. The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) supplies the finger and thumb extensors.

questions.text: Testosterone is converted to which of the following hormone by aromatase enzyme?
questions.explanation:

Aromatase (CYP19) converts testosterone to estradiol.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient presented to the emergency room with seizures. He has a history of fever, headache, and confusion. An MRI brain was done, and it showed inflammation involving the bitemporal lobe. What is the most likely etiology for this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Herpes simplex virus

The given clinical vignette suggests the diagnosis of encephalitis caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV).

HSV encephalitis is defined as inflammation of brain parenchyma caused by the Herpes virus and it typically presents as an acute febrile illness.

Patients typically present with acute onset of fever, altered levels of consciousness, personality changes, and evidence of either focal or diffuse neurologic signs and symptoms, especially in the temporal lobe. Focal or generalized seizures occur in many patients with HSV encephalitis. Other most commonly encountered focal findings include aphasia, ataxia, upper motor neuron or lower motor neuron type lesions, and cranial nerve deficits.

HSV-DNA demonstration in CSF by PCR is the investigation of choice for HSV encephalitis. Other investigations that can help include CSF examination, CSF culture, serological studies, MRI, CT, EEG, and brain biopsy.

The T2-weighted MRI of the brain will show hyperintensity in the temporal lobe in most of the patients. Bilateral involvement of the temporal lobe is more common in HSV encephalitis.

The image below is a coronal T2-weighted MR image showing a high signal intensity in the temporal lobes in a patient with HSV encephalitis.

Management includes supportive therapy(monitoring of intracranial pressure, fluid restriction, avoidance of hypotonic IV fluids), anticonvulsants for seizures, and intravenous acyclovir is beneficial in the treatment of HSV encephalitis.

Other options:

Option A: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) encephalitis in adult immunocompromised adult patients often have enlarged ventricles with areas of increased T2 signal on MRI outlining the ventricles (periventricular calcifications).

Option B: In immunocompetent patients, acute toxoplasmosis is usually asymptomatic and self-limited. Immunocompromised patients with Toxoplasma encephalopathy usually have multiple lesions located in both hemispheres, with the basal ganglia and corticomedullary junction most commonly involved in the MRI.

Option D: Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes tuberculous (TB) encephalopathy and it is exclusively seen in children and infants with pulmonary TB. It is characterized by cerebral edema sometimes with features similar to acute disseminated encephalopathy and may manifest with a variety of symptoms ranging from focal neurological deficits to convulsions and decreased conscious state.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby assessed 5 minutes after birth is found to be pink, with blue extremities, and irregular respiration. Heart rate is 80 beats per minute. There is grimace and some flexion. What is the Apgar score for this baby?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 5

The Apgar score for this baby will be 5.

• Color; body pink, extremities blue: score-1
• Heart rate; 80 beats per minute: score 1
• Grimace: Score-1
• Some flexion: Score-1
• Irregular respiration: Score-1

The Apgar score is a systematic way of assessing the infant after birth at 1 and 5 minutes of life. It gives a maximum score of 10 which indicates the newborn is in the best possible condition. Scores between 0-3 require immediate resuscitation.

Changes in the Apgar scores denote the response of the infant to resuscitation. If the score at 5 minutes remains less than 7, the infant should be assessed again every 5 minutes for the next 20 minutes.

Causes for false positive Apgar score are:

• Prematurity
• Drugs like analgesics, narcotics, sedatives, magnesium sulfate
• Acute cerebral trauma
• Precipitous delivery
• Airway obstruction (choanal atresia)
• Congenital pneumonia or sepsis
• Hemorrhage- hypovolemia

False-negative Apgar score is seen in maternal acidosis and high fetal catecholamine levels.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is called as Australia antigen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HBsAg

HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) is also known as the Australia antigen. It is called so because it was first isolated from the serum of an Australian person.

Sera from hepatitis B patients when observed under an electron microscope show three types of particles:

• A spherical particle: 22nm, most abundant, contains only HBsAg.
• Filamentous or tubular particle: 22nm, contains only HBsAg.
• A double-walled spherical structure: 42nm diameter, is the complete Hepatitis B virus. It was described by Dane and is called Dane particle.
questions.learning: HBsAg HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) is also known as the Australia antigen. It is called so because it was first isolated from the serum of an Australian person.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under which category of bioterrorism is Anthrax classified?
questions.explanation: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) classifies biological agents into three categories based on their potential to pose a threat to public health. Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) is classified as a Category A (CAT A) agent. This highest-priority category includes organisms that are easily disseminated or transmitted from person to person, cause high mortality rates, and have the potential for major public health impact. Other CAT A agents include Plague, Botulism, and Smallpox. Category B (Option B) agents are moderately easy to disseminate and cause moderate morbidity (e.g., Vibrio cholerae). Category C (Option C) includes emerging pathogens that could be engineered for mass dissemination in the future (e.g., Hantavirus). Category D is not a standard CDC classification for bioterrorism. Anthrax is particularly dangerous because its spores are highly resilient and can be aerosolized. Recognizing these classifications is essential for national security, emergency preparedness, and the rapid deployment of medical countermeasures
questions.learning: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) classifies biological agents into three categories based on their potential to pose a threat to public health.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A soldier presents to a referral hospital one day after sustaining a high-velocity shrapnel injury to his right thigh. He complains of severe pain at the wound site. On examination, crepitus is present. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Clostridium perfringens

The most likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario is gas gangrene/ clostridial myonecrosis, which is caused by clostridium perfringens.

Military wounds provide an ideal environment for gas gangrene as the kinetic energy of high-velocity missiles or shrapnel causes extensive tissue damage. Patients who are immunocompromised, diabetic, or have malignant disease are also at greater risk. The usual incubation period is <24 hours of injury.

Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus (gas in the tissues). The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate, in which Gram staining will reveal bacteria. Edema and spreading gangrene occur due to the release of collagenase, hyaluronidase, other proteases, and alpha-toxin. Early systemic complications like circulatory collapse and organ failure can occur without adequate treatment.

Management includes high doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues. Amputations should be performed under antibiotic prophylaxis.

Other options:

C. difficile, a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus, causes Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium) difficile infection (CDI) after ingestion of spores of the organism. The more severe form of the condition is known as pseudomembranous colitis (PMC). It is most commonly associated with prolonged antimicrobial use which interferes with the commensal colonic microflora. The most commonly implicated antibiotics are cephalosporins, ampicillin, and clindamycin.
questions.learning: Clostridium perfringens — The most likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario is gas gangrene/ clostridial myonecrosis, which is caused by clostridium perfringens.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The most sensitive indicator of environmental iodine deficiency is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urinary iodine excretion

Urinary iodine excretion (UIE) is the most sensitive indicator of current environmental iodine deficiency because more than 90% of ingested iodine is excreted in urine. It reflects recent iodine intake and is the preferred method for assessing the iodine status of a population.

• A. Prevalence of goitre ✗

• Goitre reflects long-term iodine deficiency and changes slowly after iodine supplementation.
• It is not a sensitive indicator of current iodine status.

• B. Prevalence of neonatal hypothyroidism ✗

• Used as an indicator of severe iodine deficiency, but is less sensitive than UIE for population surveillance.

• C. Prevalence of cretinism ✗

• Indicates very severe, longstanding iodine deficiency.
• It is a late manifestation and unsuitable for monitoring current iodine status.

• D. Urinary iodine excretion ✓

• Most sensitive and preferred indicator of environmental iodine deficiency in a community.
questions.learning: Urinary iodine excretion Urinary iodine excretion (UIE) is the most sensitive indicator of current environmental iodine deficiency because more than 90% of ingested iodine is excreted in urine.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid cancer. Following, surgery the patient develops perioral numbness and spasm of the muscles of her hand. The latter change is due to a change in the resting membrane potential of cells. Which of the below mentioned conditions will have a similar effect on the RMP of a cell?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conn’s syndrome

Tetany after thyroidectomy occurs due to hypocalcemia.

Low extracellular Ca²⁺ decreases the threshold potential of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, making nerves and muscles hyperexcitable, leading to carpopedal spasm and tetany.

Additionally, associated alkalosis can worsen tetany because alkalosis increases binding of Ca²⁺ to albumin, thereby decreasing free ionized calcium, which is the physiologically active form. Thus neuromuscular excitability further increases.

So the sequence is:

• Thyroidectomy → parathyroid damage/removal
• ↓ PTH → hypocalcemia
• Alkalosis may further ↓ ionized Ca²⁺
• ↓ extracellular free Ca²⁺ lowers Na⁺ channel threshold
• Increased neuromuscular excitability → tetany/carpopedal spasm.
questions.learning: Conn’s syndrome Tetany after thyroidectomy occurs due to hypocalcemia. Low extracellular Ca²⁺ decreases the threshold potential of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, making nerves and muscles hyperexcitable, leading to carpopedal spasm and tetany.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults?
questions.explanation: In adults, Malignant Choroidal Melanoma (often part of uveal melanoma) is definitively the most common primary intraocular malignancy. It typically arises from melanocytes within the choroid and occurs most frequently in middle-aged and elderly individuals. Clinically, it may be asymptomatic or present with blurred vision, floaters, or visual field defects depending on its location. Retinoblastoma (Option A) is the most common intraocular cancer in children, not adults, and is rare after age five. Reticulum cell sarcoma (Option C, now classified as primary intraocular lymphoma) is much rarer and often mimics chronic uveitis. Neurofibroma (Option D) is a benign nerve sheath tumor, not a primary intraocular malignancy. Diagnosis of choroidal melanoma involves dilated fundus examination, ultrasound (showing a characteristic "collar-stud" or "mushroom" shape and low internal reflectivity), and sometimes MRI. Management options include plaque brachytherapy, proton beam radiation, or enucleation in advanced cases. Early detection is critical, as these tumors carry a significant risk of hematogenous metastasis, primarily to the liver

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young male who is a professional trumpet blower presented with a swelling on the left side of the neck. On examination, there is a gurgling sound while compressing the swelling. X-ray of the neck is seen below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Laryngocele

The given image along with the examination finding of Bryce's sign is suggestive of laryngocoele.

Laryngocele is an air-filled cystic swelling in the neck due to dilatation of the saccule. It is more commonly seen in trumpet players, glass-blowers, or weight lifters due to a raised transglottic air pressure in these people. It can be classified into internal, external, or combined types of laryngocele.

* Internal laryngocele is limited within the larynx and appears as a distension of the false cord and aryepiglottic fold.

* External laryngocele has a distended saccule that herniates through the thyrohyoid membrane and appears as a swelling in the neck.

* Combined or mixed laryngocele has both internal and external laryngoceles as its components where the air-filled sac extends both within the larynx and externally through the thyrohyoid membrane into the neck, and potentially into the mediastinum.

It presents with hoarseness of voice, cough, and airway obstruction (if large). External laryngocele presents as a reducible swelling in the neck that increases in size on coughing or performing the Valsalva maneuver. On pressing the neck swelling, a gurgling sound is heard, indicating a positive Bryce's sign. Adult laryngoceles can be associated with carcinoma.

Diagnosis is based on an indirect laryngoscopy and CT scan. Internal laryngocele is managed by marsupialization and external laryngocele is managed by a surgical excision through an external neck incision.

Other options:

Option A: The pharyngeal pouch(Zenker diverticulum) is a pulsion-pseudodiverticulum and results from herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the Killian triangle (or dehiscence of Killian). Killian's triangle is an area of muscular weakness between the transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus and the oblique fibres of the thyropharyngeus.

Option C: A tracheoesophageal fistula is an abnormal fistula communication between the oesophagus and the trachea. Type C lesion is associated with proximal oesophagal atresia and distal TEF, the proximal blind pouch ends approximately at the distance of one or two vertebral bodies from the distal TEF.

Option D: The tonsillar cyst is due to blockage of a tonsillar crypt and appears as a yellowish swelling over the tonsil. Very often it is symptomless. It can be easily drained.
questions.learning: Laryngocele — The given image along with the examination finding of Bryce's sign is suggestive of laryngocoele. Laryngocele is an air-filled cystic swelling in the neck due to dilatation of the saccule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the most probable nerve to be injured based on the clinical image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Long thoracic nerve

The above image shows winging of the scapula, which is caused by injury to the long thoracic nerve.

When the patient is asked to push against a wall with both hands, medial border of the scapula on the affected side becomes prominent and this is known as ‘winging of scapula.’

Scapular winging is almost always caused by damage to one of three nerves that control muscles in your arms, back, and neck:

* The long thoracic nerve, which controls the serratus anterior muscle

* The dorsal scapular nerve, which controls the rhomboid muscles

* The spinal accessory nerve, which controls the trapezius muscle

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Re-infection with which of the following will lead to catastrophic symptoms even in the presence of antibodies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dengue

Re-infection with Dengue virus will lead to catastrophic symptoms even in the presence of antibodies.

The DENV-1/DENV-2 sequence of infection has a 500-fold risk of DHF than primary infection.

DENV-3/DENV-2 sequence has a 150-fold risk and DENV-4/DENV-2 has a 50-fold risk of DHF.

This shows that multiple infection with different serotypes of the dengue virus leads to severe forms of dengue such as DHF/DSS.

Recent update: Dengvaxia is the WHO endorsed first ever vaccine for dengue fever, which is currently licensed in twenty countries.

Other options: Re-infection with Yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis and Zika will not cause catastrophic symptoms in the presence of antibodies.
questions.learning: Dengue Re-infection with Dengue virus will lead to catastrophic symptoms even in the presence of antibodies. The DENV-1/DENV-2 sequence of infection has a 500-fold risk of DHF than primary infection.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A cohort study was carried out involving individuals who consumed green tea and those who did not, aiming to examine its impact on diabetes mellitus. The calculated risk ratio stood at 0.84. Which of the subsequent statements is accurate?
options: Green tea increases the risk of diabetes
Green tea decreases the risk of diabetes
Data insufficient to establish causal association
The value (0.84) tends to be close to 1, hence there is no effect
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Green tea decreases the risk of diabetes

A risk ratio (relative risk) of 0.84 indicates that the exposed group (green tea consumers) has 16% lower risk of developing diabetes compared to the unexposed group.

A value less than 1 signifies a protective effect, while a value greater than 1 indicates increased risk.

Although causality requires further evaluation, the correct interpretation of the given RR is that green tea consumption is associated with a reduced risk of diabetes.
questions.learning: Green tea decreases the risk of diabetes — A risk ratio (relative risk) of 0.84 indicates that the exposed group (green tea consumers) has 16% lower risk of developing diabetes compared to the unexposed group.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A new drug is introduced into the market after which phase of the clinical trials?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phase III

A new drug is introduced into the market after phase III of the clinical trial.

Phase III of the clinical trial checks the efficacy and monitors the adverse reactions of a new drug and thus a new drug is introduced after this phase.

Phase II takes place over a short duration. During this period, the most prominent side effects are assessed. However, less common side effects might have gone undetected due to the shorter duration and smaller study group.

Phase III takes place over a longer duration and includes more population as compared to Phase II. Because these studies are larger and longer in duration, the results are more likely to show long-term or rare adverse effects. Hence, this phase is used to monitor adverse effects.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 32-year-old farmer was brought to the emergency after he suddenly became unconscious while working in the field. On examination, his temperature was 105 degrees Fahrenheit and his skin turgor was decreased. Which of the following would not be seen in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sweating

| Finding | Interpretation

| ------- | --------------

| Temp = 105°F | Severe hyperthermia

| Unconscious | CNS dysfunction

| Decreased skin turgor | Dehydration

This presentation is heat stroke, characterized by hyperthermia (>40°C), dehydration, and altered sensorium. Types of Heat Stroke

| Type | Example

| ---- | -------

| Exertional | Athletes, farmers

| Non-exertional | Elderly

Heat stroke shows hot, dry skin due to failure of thermoregulatory sweating.

Patients develop tachypnea, hypotension, and red hot skin from peripheral vasodilation.

| Feature | Heat Stroke | Heat Exhaustion

| ------- | ----------- | ---------------

| Temperature | >40°C | <40°C

| CNS symptoms | ✅ Severe | Mild

| Sweating | ❌ Absent | ✅ Present

| Skin | Hot, dry | Sweaty

| Severity | Emergency | Less severe

Sweat glands fail due to:

• Hypothalamic dysfunction
• Severe dehydration

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with lower back pain and a 1–1.5 mm osteolytic lesion at the T10 vertebra. Histopathological findings are provided. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture of a 50-year-old with back pain and a "punched-out" osteolytic lesion is highly suggestive of Multiple Myeloma. The histopathology confirms this, showing a dense infiltrate of malignant plasma cells (large cells with eccentric nuclei and clock-face chromatin). A hallmark of multiple myeloma is the overproduction of monoclonal light chains. When these small proteins are excreted in the urine, they are known as Bence-Jones proteins. Rouleaux formation (Option B) is actually present in multiple myeloma due to high protein levels causing RBCs to stack like coins. Multiple myeloma is the primary cause of systemic AL (Amyloid Light-chain) amyloidosis, so saying it's absent (Option C) is incorrect. Multiple myeloma causes increased calcium levels (hypercalcemia) due to the osteolytic destruction of bone, not decreased levels (Option D). The "CRAB" mnemonic is essential for this diagnosis: Calcium elevation, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, and Bone lesions

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which amongst the following is true about Turner's syndrome?
options: Webbing of hands and toes are associated with risk of visceral anomalies
Noonan syndrome is more associated with cardiac defects
Absence of neck webbing is associated with higher risk of co-arctation of aorta
Webbing of neck is associated with higher risk of cardiac anomalies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Webbing of neck is associated with higher risk of cardiac anomalies

In Turner's syndrome, webbing of the neck is associated with a higher risk of cardiac anomalies.

The image below summarises the clinical features of Turner's syndrome.

The image given below shows the webbing of neck.

Noonan syndrome is characterised by mutations in the RAS-MAPK pathway. The most common of these is the PTPN11 which encodes a protein tyrosine phosphatase on chromosome 12.

Clinical features include:

• Short stature
• Short webbed neck
• Cystic hygroma
• Tall forehead
• Low posterior hairline
• Dental malocclusion

Although it shares many clinical features with Turner’s syndrome, Noonan syndrome affects both sexes. It follows an autosomal dominant pattern and it also has a different pattern of congenital heart disease, typically involving right-sided lesions.
questions.learning: Webbing of neck is associated with higher risk of cardiac anomalies In Turner's syndrome, webbing of the neck is associated with a higher risk of cardiac anomalies.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Apocrine glands are present in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Axilla

Apocrine glands are present in the axilla.

Exocrine glands can be classified into three subtypes, based on the manner in which their secretions are poured out of the cells:

1. Apocrine
2. Merocrine
3. Holocrine

In apocrine glands, the apical parts of the cells are shed off to discharge the secretion. Examples of apocrine glands are :

• Secretion of milk fat by mammary glands
• Atypical sweat glands in the axilla, perianal region, periumbilical skin, mons pubis.
• Ceruminous glands of the external auditory meatus are modified apocrine glands

Apocrine glands are large glands found in the dermis or subcutaneous fat. They are a type of sweat gland. It consists of a basal secretory coil followed by a straight duct that opens into the pilary canal above the duct of the sebaceous gland. In hairless skin, it directly opens onto the skin surface.

Apocrine activity is minimal before puberty, after which it is androgen-dependent and responsive to emotional stimuli. It is controlled by adrenergic nerves and is sensitive to adrenaline and noradrenaline. The secretion is initially sterile and odorless, but it undergoes bacterial decomposition to generate odorous and musky compounds. Obstruction of apocrine sweat ducts and associated upper hair follicles in the axillae, breast areolae, and pubic region, mainly in women, is thought to cause Fox–Fordyce disease. It is also implicated in the causation of a painful, occasionally debilitating condition called hidradenitis suppurativa.

The given image shows an illustration of apocrine secretion.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the most common form of arthritis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis.

Osteoarthritis is strongly associated with age and is highly prevalent among older individuals. Studies suggest that over 80% of people aged 55 and above have osteoarthritis in at least one joint.
questions.learning: Osteoarthritis Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis. Osteoarthritis is strongly associated with age and is highly prevalent among older individuals.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: For standards of ventilation, the widely quoted standard is that of De Chaumont who advocated a fresh air supply of 3000 cubic feet per person per hour. It is calculated based on which parameter?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CO2 content of air

For standards of ventilation, CO2 content of air is the paramater used to calculate fresh air supply of 3000 cubic feet per person per hour which was advocated by De Chaumont.

Ventilation involves the quality control of incoming air but not quality control of outgoing air. It also involves the replacement of vitiated air(air with decreased oxygen content) by a supply of fresh outdoor air. It aims to provide a comfortable thermal environment and reduce the risk of infections.

Fresh air supply of f 3000 cubic feet per person per hour is a good standard for air requirement. It is observed that the amount of CO2 due to respiration is not more than 2 parts in 1000 parts of air, then the air in the room is considered fresh.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Lady with 28 weeks of gestation presents with fever, acute pain abdomen, and mild leucocytosis. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Red degeneration of fibroid

In the given scenario history of acute pain abdomen with fever and mild leukocytosis in a 28-week pregnant woman is suggestive of red degeneration of fibroid.

Red degeneration is the most common complication of fibroids in pregnancy. It is due to the breakdown of the fibroid resulting in ischemia and pain. Key clinical features in this condition are:

• Low-grade fever
• Tender uterus on palpation
• Elevated leukocytes
• Elevated ESR

The diagnosis is confirmed with an ultrasound. It is usually self-limiting and can be managed with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Other options

Option A - Uterine torsion is defined as rotation of more than 45 degrees around the long axis of the uterus. The most usual symptoms of uterine torsion are birth obstruction, abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, shock, and urinary and intestinal symptoms. The treatment in the earlier months of pregnancy is immediate laparotomy and detorsion of the uterus. Near-term or during labor cesarean section is carried out, and elimination of the possible etiologic factors.

Option B - Infection is common in submucous and myomatous polyps if they project into the cervical canal or the vagina. An infected polyp can cause blood-stained purulent discharge. Infection is more likely in the postpartum and postabortal state.

Option D -Preterm labor is diagnosed with the help of the following criteria

• Regular uterine contractions with or without pain (at least one in every 10 minutes)
• Dilatation (> 2 cm) and effacement (80%) of the cervix
• Length of the cervix (measured by TVS) < 2.5 cm and funneling of the internal os
• Pelvic pressure, backache and/or vaginal discharge or bleeding.
questions.learning: Red degeneration of fibroid — In the given scenario history of acute pain abdomen with fever and mild leukocytosis in a 28-week pregnant woman is suggestive of red degeneration of fibroid.
